description: Evaluation question set for the Seerah RAG system. Tiered by how many passages an answer requires: T1 one chunk, T2 several chunks in one lecture, T3 several lectures (cross_episode marks lectures far apart in the series rather than consecutive parts of one arc). supporting_quotes are CANDIDATE evidence proposed at authoring time - verified verbatim against the transcripts, but the claim that a quote actually supports its question has not been independently checked. The set of lectures a question draws on is the set of lecture_number values across its supporting_quotes.

A1.scope: Lectures 1-12: the Prophet's specialities, sources of the seerah, pre-Islamic Arabia and the origins of idolatry, his lineage and the Year of the Elephant, his birth, childhood and youth, marriage to Khadija, the rebuilding of the Ka'bah, Zayd ibn Haritha, the first and second revelations, and the start of public preaching.

A2.scope: Lectures 13-24 (late Meccan period: Quraysh opposition, persecution, the two Abyssinian migrations, the satanic-verses controversy, conversions of Hamza and Umar, the boycott, the Year of Sorrow, Ta'if, the Night Journey and Ascension, and the first contacts with Yathrib)

A3.scope: Lectures 25-35: the two pledges at Aqaba, the early emigrations, the Hijrah itself, why Madinah was chosen, the demographics of Madinah, the first mosques, the brotherhood pairing, the Constitution of Madinah, the change of Qiblah, and the expeditions leading up to Badr.

A4.scope: Lectures 36-47 (Badr 1-7, the period between Badr and Uhud, the Meccan-period summary, and the opening of Uhud). Every question is answerable from a single lecture.

A5.scope: Lectures 48-58: close of the Uhud arc (48-50), the massacres of al-Raji and Bir Ma'una (51), the Prophet's wives and Dhat al-Riqa (52), the expulsion of Banu Nadir (53), the al-Muraysi/Banu al-Mustaliq campaign (54), the slander of Aisha (55-56), and the opening of the Battle of the Trench (57-58). Every question is answerable from a single lecture.

A6.scope: Lectures 59-70: close of Khandaq (59-60), Banu Qurayza (61), minor expeditions before Hudaybiyya (62), the Hudaybiyya arc (63-67), Khaybar (68, 70), and the marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh (69). Every question is answerable from a single lecture.

A7.scope: Lectures 71-81 (letters to rulers, Umrah al-Qada, Mu'tah, Dhat al-Salasil, Conquest of Makkah). Every question is answerable from a single lecture.

A8.scope: Lectures 82-93: Hunayn and the siege of Ta'if (82-83, 86), Ka'b ibn Zuhayr / Adi ibn Hatim (84), miracles (85), the Tabuk campaign (87-88, 90-92), Ka'b ibn Malik (88-89), and Surat At-Tawbah after Tabuk (93). Every question is answerable from a single lecture.

A9.scope: Lectures 94-104 (delegations of the ninth year, Maria and Ibrahim, the marital dispute, Abu Bakr's Hajj, the Farewell Hajj, the Prophet's final illness and death, his grave, and the succession). Every question is answerable from a single lecture.

B1.scope: Battle of Badr arc (lectures 36-42) and Battle of Uhud arc (lectures 46-50)

B2.scope: Khandaq/Ahzab (58-60), Treaty of Hudaybiyya (64-67), Khaybar (68, 70), Mu'tah (73-74)

B3.scope: Conquest of Makkah (76-81), Hunayn and Ta'if (82-83), Tabuk (87, 88, 90, 91, 92), Year of Delegations (94-96), Night Journey and Ascension (21-23)

C1.scope: Whole 104-lecture series, theme: PEOPLE. Cross-episode T3 questions tracking individuals across widely separated lectures (Makkan period through Madinah, the conquest, and beyond the Prophet's death).

C2.scope: Whole 104-lecture series. Recurring threads spanning distant lectures: tribes (Banu Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Qurayza, Thaqif, Aws/Khazraj), treaties (Aqaba pledges, Hudaybiyya clauses), places (Abyssinia, Ta'if, Khaybar, Makkah), and individuals whose story restarts many lectures later (Ja'far, Amr ibn al-As, the Negus, Bilal/Umayya, Mut'im, Salman, Urwa ibn Mas'ud, Wahshi, Mus'ab, Khalid, Abbas, Suhayl, Zayd, Umm Salama, Huyayy).

questions.question: The Roman emperor of the time apparently worked out for himself that a prophet had appeared in Arabia. So why did he never become Muslim?
questions.reference_answer: Heraclius questioned Abu Sufyan, who happened to be in Jerusalem with a Meccan caravan, and concluded from the answers that this was the prophet his scriptures had predicted; a bishop he trusted confirmed it. He still refused to accept Islam, because doing so would have cost him the throne, and the temptation of being the most powerful man on earth was too much for him. He therefore died on his old faith.

supporting_quotes.quote: yet Heraclius did not accept Islam because he realized if he accepted Islam then he'd have to give up being the emperor and when you're the most powerful man on earth, then it's too tempting

questions.question: The Prophet's grandfather wasn't actually born with the name everyone knows him by. How did he end up with it?
questions.reference_answer: His real name was Shaybat al-Hamd, given because he was born with a streak of white hair. He was raised in Yathrib after his father Hashim died on a trading trip. His uncle Muttalib eventually came, recognised him, and carried him off to Mecca on his camel. When the Meccans saw Muttalib arriving with an unknown boy they assumed he had bought a new slave, so they called the child Abd al-Muttalib, meaning Muttalib's slave, and the name stuck.

supporting_quotes.quote: And when the people saw him with a young lad, they assumed the young lad was a new slave he had purchased. So that is why they called him, Oh this is, Muttalib has an Abd, Abdu'l-Muttalib.

questions.question: Nobody in Mecca was called Muhammad at the time. What did his grandfather say when people asked him about the choice?
questions.reference_answer: Abd al-Muttalib named the child on the seventh day, when he circumcised him and held a feast. The name was known but very uncommon, and there was nobody in Mecca who bore it, so people asked why he had not used one of the family's usual names. He answered that he wanted the boy to be praised by the people of the earth just as he wanted him praised by the people of the heavens, the name itself meaning the one who is praised.

supporting_quotes.quote: He said, I want him to be praised by the people of the earth as I want him to be praised by the people of the heavens.

questions.question: A woman taken prisoner after one of the later battles insisted she was the Prophet's sister. How did she prove it?
questions.reference_answer: She was Shayma, the daughter of his foster mother Halima, captured when the Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr were defeated at Hunayn. When she was brought to him he asked for a sign, and she reminded him of the marks still on her from a bite he had given her as a baby while she carried him on her back. He recognised the story as something only she could know, freed her, and gave her many gifts.

supporting_quotes.quote: So she said, I still have the marks of the bite that you bit me when I was carrying you as a baby on my back. I still have that. So the Prophet ﷺ realized that this is Shayma.

questions.question: What did the Prophet do for a living as a young man, and what was he paid for it?
questions.reference_answer: He worked as a shepherd. In a hadith in Bukhari he said that every prophet Allah sent had been a shepherd, and when the companions asked whether that included him he confirmed that he had tended the flocks of the people of Mecca in return for qararit, a handful of the smallest coins. He named the valley of Ajyad, near the Haram, as where he grazed them.

supporting_quotes.quote: So he said, yes, I was. I was a shepherd. And I used to tend to the flock of the people of Mecca in return for some qararit, some pennies. The smallest denomination.

questions.question: A man travelled up from Yemen wanting to follow the new preacher, and was told to go home instead. Why the refusal?
questions.reference_answer: The man was Amr ibn Abasa, who had heard rumours in Yemen and came to Mecca, where he found the Prophet still keeping a low profile. The preaching was at that point still confined to trusted people in Mecca, and Amr, as a non-Qurayshi with no clan to protect him, would simply have been killed. So the Prophet told him to go back to his own people and to come to him when he heard that he had prevailed. Amr waited years and finally joined him in Medina, where the Prophet still recognised him.

supporting_quotes.quote: don't you see my situation I have to hide from my own people. You're not able. You're not a Qurashi. You're gonna be killed. You can't do this now.
Go back to your people. And when you hear that I have been victorious over my people, then come back to me.

questions.question: When his uncle finally begged him to drop the whole thing, what did the Prophet say back?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Talib, under enormous pressure from the Quraysh, pleaded with him to have mercy on an old man and stop. Overwhelmed with emotion, the Prophet answered that even if they placed the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left he would not abandon the message until Allah made it prevail or he died in the attempt. In another version he pointed to the sun and told his uncle he was no more able to stop preaching than Abu Talib was to light his stick from it.

supporting_quotes.quote: if they were to give me the sun in my right hand, and the moon in my left hand, Wallahi, I could not give up this message until I succeed in what I'm doing, or I die a death in this path

questions.question: The Prophet is known by two names that sound almost the same, Muhammad and Ahmad. Is there any real difference between them?
questions.reference_answer: Both come from the root hamd, praise, and both are among the names he listed for himself, and they are the only two proper names for him in the Quran. Muhammad is the form that means being praised again and again, so it refers to the quantity of praise; Ahmad means being given the very highest praise, so it refers to its quality. Ibn al-Qayyim explained the split in the earlier scriptures this way: Musa foretold him as Muhammad because the Israelites were the largest genuine community after this one, while Isa foretold him as Ahmad because his true followers were few but outstanding in quality. Both meanings meet in the praiseworthy station, al-Maqam al-Mahmud, that he will be given.

supporting_quotes.quote: Muhammad means that he is being given continuous praise, continuously, time after time, praise after praise. So Muhammad is for the quantity of praise.
So, the Prophet Musa alayhi salam, his people were the largest ummah of true Muslims. after our ummah. And therefore they were given quantity because they have quantity.
And so for them, they were given the name Ahmad, because they were people of quality.

questions.question: Once wealth started flowing to the Muslims and he was effectively ruling Arabia, did the Prophet's own way of living get any easier?
questions.reference_answer: No. Umar once walked in on him in his small compartment, which held nothing but a jug of water and a bed of bare palm branches that had left red marks in his side, and wept; the Prophet rebuked him and asked whether he was not content that the disbelievers had this world while the Muslims had the next. Aisha described his bed as a leather skin sometimes stuffed with palm leaves, and when a wife folded it over to make it softer he made her undo it so it would not keep him from tahajjud. Weeks would pass without meat, and Aisha said they lived on the two dark things, dates and water. Years later Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf wept over a dish of meat and bread, saying the Prophet died without ever eating even plain wheat bread to his fill, and Aisha would cry the same way over good food.

supporting_quotes.quote: Umar, aren't you happy that they have the dunya and we have the akhira?
So she said, by eating al-aswadan, the two dark things, dates and dirty water.
He said, the Prophet ﷺ, till the day that he died, he never ate wheat bread. Forget this fine refined bread. He never ate wheat bread to his fill.

questions.question: Who first wrote down the life of the Prophet, and do any of those earliest books still exist?
questions.reference_answer: The first to write were children of the companions. The greatest of them was Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, who had direct access to his aunt Aisha and produced a small pamphlet; Aban ibn Uthman wrote a booklet too, and then Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri wrote an early treatise. None of these survive, because later and larger compilations absorbed them and, in an age of hand-copying, people copied the bigger book. The great work is that of Ibn Ishaq, born about 85 AH in Medina, who arranged everything chronologically and with chains of narration, filling ten to fifteen volumes. It was too long to copy, so Ibn Hisham abridged it by cutting poetry and long genealogies, and it is his version that survives. Ibn Ishaq's own text was thought lost until Dr Hamidullah found and published roughly a quarter of it from manuscripts in Europe, which confirmed that Ibn Hisham had only cut, not altered.

supporting_quotes.quote: And of the greatest of those who wrote was Urwa, the son of Az-Zubayr.
Ibn Hisham realized that Ibn Ishaq is too big. 10-12 volumes. So, he decided to summarize it.
he discovered around one fourth of Ibn Ishaq and so he edited it and published it

questions.question: If the Arabs traced their religion back to Abraham, how did they end up worshipping idols at all?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet named the man responsible: Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i, whom he said he saw punished in the fire as the first to change the religion of Ismail. Amr travelled to Syria, was impressed by the Amalekites who attributed their power to their idols, was gifted one called Hubal, and set it before the Ka'bah; Hubal became the chief idol of the Quraysh. Three things let one man pull this off: an inferiority complex toward a civilisation that looked stronger and therefore seemed right about everything, his own standing as the respected chieftain of Khuza'a, who then controlled Mecca, and the ignorance of a people who had gone perhaps two thousand years without a prophet. From there it spread, with caravans chipping stones off the Ka'bah to worship on their travels and the five idols of Nuh's people reappearing among the tribes.

supporting_quotes.quote: So they gave him an idol by the name of Hubal. and so Hubal became the first idol of the Arabian Peninsula and it also became the main idol of the Quraysh

And these are the three factors then. Number one, inferiority complex. You think that a civilization is better, everything must be right about them. Number two, the person who says it has credentials.
We learn from the traditions that whenever a caravan left Mecca, they would chip away and take a rock from the Ka'bah.

questions.question: The well of Zamzam had been lost for generations. How was it found again, and what trouble did that stir up?
questions.reference_answer: When Khuza'a drove the tribe of Jurhum out of Mecca, Jurhum buried and destroyed the well on their way out, and nobody could relocate it, so for three hundred years or more the Meccans had to bring water in from wells further away. Abd al-Muttalib was shown the spot in a dream, ignored it at first, and finally dug there with his only son at the time, Harith, while the Quraysh mocked him. When water came up his relatives immediately claimed a share and it nearly came to bloodshed; it was then that he vowed to sacrifice one of his sons if Allah gave him ten. They agreed instead to travel to a priestess to arbitrate, got lost on the way and nearly died of thirst, and when Abd al-Muttalib struck water again while digging his own grave, the others took it as a sign and handed him the rights to Zamzam without ever reaching her.

supporting_quotes.quote: they did a very dastardly deed they buried the well of Zamzam they destroyed it and they buried it and no matter how much Khuza'a tried and they tried and tried and tried they could not find the well
That he saw it in a dream. Allah showed him in a dream. That if you go to such and such a place next to this idol between that stone and marker.
And as Abdul Muttalib is digging his own grave, he strikes water again.

questions.question: How certain are we really about the exact day the Prophet was born?
questions.reference_answer: Two things are firm. He told us himself, when asked why he fasted Mondays, that Monday was the day he was born and the day revelation began; and companions such as Qubath ibn Ashyam and Suwayd ibn Ghafla place it in the Year of the Elephant, generally reckoned as around 570 CE. The day of the month is not settled at all: the earliest books give more than ten opinions. The familiar 12th of Rabi al-Awwal comes from Ibn Ishaq, writing some two centuries later with no chain of narration, while the 2nd, 8th and 10th are backed by earlier and weightier authorities such as al-Waqidi, Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn Hazm, Imam Malik, al-Zuhri and Ja'far al-Sadiq. The 12th became dominant partly because everyone leans on Ibn Ishaq and partly because the first public birthday celebrations, begun by the Fatimids of Egypt around 517 AH, fixed on that date. The only timing detail with any narration behind it is that he was born at high noon.

supporting_quotes.quote: He said, this was the day I was born on. And this was the day that revelation began to me.
Ibn Kathir says the fourth opinion is that he was born on the 12th of Rabi'ul-Awwal and this is the opinion of Ibn Ishaq But there is no isnad on this matter.
But he said that it has been narrated to me that the Prophet ﷺ was born at high noon.

questions.question: Something happened while the Prophet was being raised out in the desert that frightened his foster mother into sending him back. What was it?
questions.reference_answer: At about four years old, while he was playing with the other children, Jibreel came to him. The other children fled but he stood his ground; the angel wrestled him to the ground, opened his chest, took out his heart, removed from it a black portion that he called Shaytan's share, washed the heart in zamzam in a golden vessel and put it back. The children ran home screaming that a man had killed him, and Halima found him sitting there pale but not crying. Anas ibn Malik said he could still see the line on his chest as an old man. Halima, unnerved by what was happening around this child, quietly returned him to Aminah. The same washing happened again decades later before the Night Journey, but with no black portion to remove the second time.

supporting_quotes.quote: And he took out a black slither, a black portion from the heart. And he threw it away.
So they come screaming and running that our brother has died, our brother has been killed, a man has abducted him, a man has killed him.
And she decided before anything else happens, let me quietly return the Prophet ﷺ to Amina.

questions.question: A trader from Yemen was cheated out of his money in Mecca and had no clan there to back him. What did he do about it?
questions.reference_answer: The man, from the tribe of Zubayd, had sold goods to al-As ibn Wa'il, who kept putting off payment. None of the Qurayshi sub-tribes would take on a rich and powerful chieftain on his behalf, so he composed a poem and proclaimed it aloud in front of the Ka'bah at the hour when everyone gathered, shaming the Meccans for abusing a stranger in ihram in their own sanctuary. Al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib took it up and convened the senior men of Quraysh at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an, where they swore to stand with the oppressed against the oppressor whatever tribe he came from, sealing it by dipping their hands in perfume and marking the Ka'bah. Al-As dismissed it as none of their business, which is one explanation of the name it carried. The Prophet, about twenty and the youngest present, later said he would answer such a call even as a Muslim and would not trade his place in it for a herd of red camels.

supporting_quotes.quote: So they convened in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an, And here is where they agreed to a pact, a treaty.
They would side with the oppressed against the oppressor, regardless of which tribe the oppressor belonged to.
I witnessed in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an a treaty that were I asked to uphold it even in Islam, I would do so.

questions.question: Khadija was wealthy and had turned down plenty of suitors. How did she end up marrying the Prophet?
questions.reference_answer: She first heard of him through her sister, who had hired him to graze her flock; when the wages were due he was too shy to ask a woman for them himself and sent his companion, and the sister praised his modesty and honour so warmly that Khadija took notice. She then hired him to take her caravan to Busra on half the profits, and her servant Maysara came back reporting both his conduct and a return far larger than she had ever had. She sent an older woman, Nafisa, to sound him out; when Nafisa asked what he would say if Khadija wanted him, he did not refuse but wondered why she would want someone like him. Her uncle Amr ibn Asad acted as her guardian, Abu Talib delivered the marriage sermon, and the dower was twelve uqiyah of silver. He was about twenty five; the lecture argues she was most likely twenty eight rather than the commonly quoted forty, given the earlier authorities and the six children they had.

supporting_quotes.quote: So the Prophet ﷺ said, why don't you go on my behalf because I am too shy to go because she's a woman.
And so Nafisa said, what if Khadija wanted to marry you?
the more authentic version mentions that her uncle Amr ibn Asad was the one who performed the nikah

questions.question: Why is a strip of ground fenced off just outside the Kaaba rather than being inside the building?
questions.reference_answer: After a fire and then a flood wrecked the structure, the Quraysh rebuilt it using timber and marble bought from a Byzantine ship wrecked at Jeddah. There was not enough of it to lay the foundation of the original building, which was a rectangle rather than a square, so they built a square and marked off the leftover stretch with two posts and a low barrier, expecting a later generation to restore it. In the same rebuild they doubled its height, raised the door above ground level so they could control who entered, and added a water spout. The Prophet later told Aisha that only the newness of the Quraysh in Islam stopped him from pulling it down and rebuilding it on Ibrahim's foundations with a door at ground level. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr did rebuild it that way, but Hajjaj ibn Yusuf destroyed it and restored the pre-Islamic square, and Imam Malik later refused to change it back, saying the Ka'bah should not become a plaything for rulers.

supporting_quotes.quote: The original Ka'bah was not a square, it was a rectangle.
So they decided to build a square instead. And to mark the other two angles, if you like, or the other two corners with two posts.
Imam Malik said no I don't want the Ka'bah to become a toy that kings come along and they put their whims and desires on it

questions.question: Zayd ibn Haritha's father tracked him down in Mecca and offered to pay whatever it took to bring him home. Why did Zayd stay?
questions.reference_answer: Zayd had been snatched as a boy of seven or eight by his mother's own relatives during a feud and sold at the fair of Ukaz for four hundred dirhams to Hakim ibn Hizam, who bought him for his aunt Khadija; she gave him to the Prophet when they married. Years later his father and uncle found him and came with ransom money. The Prophet said the choice was Zayd's, and that if he chose them he could leave for nothing, but that he could not turn away someone who had turned to him. Zayd, by then a grown man, said he could never choose anyone over him, that this man was more to him than a father and an uncle together, and refused even when his father called him mad for preferring slavery to his own tribe. The Prophet then took him to the Hijr by the Ka'bah and publicly declared him free and his adopted son, and he was known as Zayd ibn Muhammad until the verse in Surah al-Ahzab restored his father's name.

supporting_quotes.quote: So the Prophet ﷺ said, it is up to him. I will leave the matter to him. And if he chooses you, then I will send him back without any ransom.
I can never choose anyone over you, for you are to me more than a father and an uncle combined.
O people of Mecca I want you all to testify that from now on Zayd is a free man and I have adopted him as my son

questions.question: After that first encounter in the cave, nothing more came for a while. What happened during that gap and how did it end?
questions.reference_answer: Revelation stopped after Iqra. Ibn Abbas describes the Prophet wandering the valleys and mountains around Mecca hoping to see Jibreel again and seeing nothing; Ibn Abbas and al-Zuhri put the break at around forty days, and the lecture rejects the claims of two or three years. This is the period in which he feared for himself, worrying that he might be losing his mind. It ended when he was coming down from the mountain and heard his name called, looked around and finally upward, and saw the same angel seated on a throne between heaven and earth. He trembled, in one report fell to his knees, and rushed home to Khadija asking to be covered. It was there, wrapped in his cloak, that Jibreel gave him the opening verses of Surah al-Muddaththir, telling him to rise and warn. The gap is explained as a preparation, letting him recover and long for the next meeting.

supporting_quotes.quote: Ibn Abbas says that for many days, the Prophet ﷺ would wander around Mecca and the valleys of Mecca and the mountains of Mecca wanting to see Jibreel again. But Jibreel would not appear.
he heard his name being called so he says I looked in front and I couldn't see anybody. He heard the name again, he looked behind him, there was nobody.
Scholars say that this was to prepare him for the second meeting. To make him recover, to recollect his energies, to make him feel enthused.

questions.question: Once the preaching became public, the Quraysh went to Abu Talib rather than confronting his nephew directly. How did that play out?
questions.reference_answer: They came first with soft words, and he put them off without taking a side. When that failed they returned with an ultimatum: either he silence his nephew himself or hand him over to them, since by Arab custom they could not touch a man of the Banu Hashim without their chief's consent. Abu Talib passed the pressure on, begging his nephew to have mercy on an old man, and got the answer about the sun and the moon; seeing that resolve he told him to do as he wished and promised never to raise it again, a promise he kept even through the boycott. The Quraysh then came back as a full delegation offering a swap, their finest young man Umara ibn al-Walid in exchange for the Prophet, which Abu Talib rejected as an absurd bargain, asking whether he was to feed their son while they killed his. Mut'im ibn Adi, the most senior man in Mecca, took their side and told him he had to accept one of the offers, but Abu Talib accused him of a staged plot, refused to budge, and composed poetry shaming his relatives, and the Quraysh backed down.

supporting_quotes.quote: we cannot bear this anymore you either stop him from preaching yourself or you hand him over to us and we do as we please
Here is the son of Al-Walid, Al-Umara Ibn Walid. And one son for one son will hand over Al-Umara to you.
he said to him do what you will my nephew, fa wallahi I will never come to you again to stop what you are doing

questions.question: Did Abu Jahl ever admit why he personally refused to follow the Prophet?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. Asked point blank for his honest verdict on what he had heard, Abu Jahl explained that his clan, the Banu Makhzum, had spent generations locked in a status race with the Banu Abd Manaf / Banu Hashim, matching them in feeding and watering the pilgrims, in bravery and in carrying the war banner, until the two were neck and neck. Now that his rivals claimed a prophet who received revelation from heaven, he said there was no way to compete with that, and so he swore he would never accept him as long as he lived. The lecture notes that this was an honest answer: his objection was tribal rivalry and pride, not any belief that the message was false.

supporting_quotes.quote: the Banu Manaf and us, we have always been in competition with one another. And when they began to give food to the pilgrims, we also began to give food.
and now they come and they tell us they have a prophet whom Allah inspires from the heavens. How can we compete with that? How can we win the race?

questions.question: What price did Suhayb the Roman have to pay before the Quraysh would let him leave Mecca?
questions.reference_answer: They stopped him on the outskirts as he set out and told him he had arrived among them with nothing and was now leaving as a wealthy man with what they considered their money, so he had to hand it all over. Suhayb gave up everything, including the mount he was riding, and told them where the rest of his buried wealth was. He is described as the only Companion known to have made the emigration on foot, arriving at Quba destitute, and the Prophet told him his transaction had been the most profitable one.

supporting_quotes.quote: you came to us penniless. You came to us without any money, without anything. And now you're leaving us as a rich man, taking our wealth? Give us back all of this money, and then we'll let you go.
the only Sahabi that we know of who performed the Hijrah on foot. Walking in the desert without any, not just the clothes on his back, that's all he owned.

questions.question: How many Muslims left for Abyssinia the first time, and who was the first to go?
questions.reference_answer: Fifteen people made the first crossing: eleven men and four women. The first to leave was Uthman ibn Affan, together with his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's daughter, so the first couple to emigrate were the Prophet's own son-in-law and daughter. The permission was given in Rajab of the fifth year of the public call, and others in the group included Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Mus'ab ibn Umayr, Uthman ibn Maz'un, and Abu Salama with Umm Salama.

supporting_quotes.quote: And therefore, when the Prophet ﷺ gave this command, 15 people immigrated. 11 men and 4 women. 11 men and 4 women. Amongst them, the first to migrate was Uthman ibn Affan.

questions.notes: The lecture also reports a competing count of 12 men and 5 women (17 total) mentioned in lecture 17.

questions.question: When the Negus demanded to know what the Muslim refugees believed about Jesus, what answer did Ja'far give, and how did the king react?
questions.reference_answer: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib said they held Jesus to be the servant of God, His messenger, His word cast to Mary the chaste virgin, and a righteous prophet. He deliberately stopped there and did not go on to attack the Trinity. The Negus picked up a small twig lying in front of him and swore that what Ja'far had said did not exceed what Jesus himself had said by so much as the width of that twig, and he then dismissed the Quraysh envoys for good and returned their gifts.

supporting_quotes.quote: our Prophet told us that Jesus Christ is the Abdullah and Rasulullah and Kalimatullah that he gave to Maryam. Al-Batul Al-Adhra, the virgin, the innocent, the chaste Maryam. And that he was a righteous Prophet.
he picks up a little branch that was in front of him a twig and he says Wallahi what you have just said does not exceed what Jesus Christ said by this much of a branch

questions.question: Aisha once said something about Khadija that upset the Prophet. What was it, and what did he say back?
questions.reference_answer: After Khadija's sister Hala came to visit and the Prophet became visibly flustered at hearing a voice like hers, Aisha's jealousy got the better of her and she asked how long he would keep remembering an old woman of the Quraysh, adding that Allah had given him someone better than her. That last phrase is what angered him. He answered that Allah had not given him anyone better than her: she believed in him and supported him when no one else did, she spent her wealth on him when everyone else boycotted him, she comforted him when the world gave him grief, and Allah gave him children through her when He gave him none through his other wives. Aisha said she never spoke about Khadija again after that.

supporting_quotes.quote: Allah has not given me someone better than her. Don't say this, O Aisha. Allah has not given you someone better than her. She supported me when no one else supported me.

questions.question: On the night journey the Prophet was offered a choice between two drinks. Which did he take, and what was he told about his choice?
questions.reference_answer: Jibreel presented him with two vessels, one of wine and one of milk, and told him to choose for himself and for his community. He took the milk, and Jibreel told him he had chosen correctly and had chosen the natural, uncorrupted state. Wine was still lawful at the time, so this was a genuine choice; the lecture reads the milk as a symbol of purity and the wine as a symbol of what has been corrupted. Reports differ on whether this happened in Jerusalem or during the ascent.

supporting_quotes.quote: So the Prophet ﷺ chose the milk, and Jibreel says, you have chosen the fitrah. Asabtal, you have chosen the right one, and that is the fitrah.

questions.question: Why was the civil war between the Aws and the Khazraj later seen as a blessing in disguise?
questions.reference_answer: Aisha described the day of Bu'ath as a gift Allah gave to the Prophet. The battle, the climax of more than a decade of fighting between the two Yathrib tribes, shattered their unity and killed off the bulk of their senior leadership, leaving mostly a younger generation that was sick of a decade of bloodshed and open to something new. Only one senior figure survived, Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, who later became the head of the hypocrites. Without that decimation of the old leadership, the message would have had a much harder time taking root in the city.

supporting_quotes.quote: the day of Bu'ath, i.e. the civil war, was a gift that Allah gave to the Prophet ﷺ.

it was because of Bu'ath that their unity had been completely fragmented and their leaders had been completely decimated the battle of Bu'ath killed the bulk of the senior members of the Aus and the Khazraj

questions.question: Utbah ibn Rabi'ah once went to the Prophet as a negotiator on behalf of the Quraysh. What was he authorised to offer, and how did the meeting end?
questions.reference_answer: Utbah volunteered at a gathering of the Quraysh, pointing out that nobody had actually tried to negotiate, and went to the Prophet as their representative. He opened with loaded questions about whether the Prophet considered himself better than his father and grandfather, warned that the city was on the brink of civil war, and then laid out his offers: if it was money he wanted they would collectively make him the richest of the Arabs, if it was power they would make him their king, if it was women he could choose any woman and they would arrange the marriage, and if he was ill they would pay for the best doctors. The Prophet let him finish without interrupting, asked whether he was done, and then recited Surah Fussilat to him; when he reached the verse warning of a destruction like that of Ad and Thamud, Utbah put his hand over the Prophet's mouth and begged him by their kinship to stop. He went back to the Quraysh and told them to leave the man alone, saying he had heard speech unlike anything he had heard before, that this man would amount to something, and that if he prevailed over the Arabs his victory would be their victory. They accused him of having been bewitched.

supporting_quotes.quote: If you wish for money, if that's why you're doing this, then I have the power of the Quraysh invested in me, we will give you more money than anybody of us have.
If you want power, we will make you our king. The Arabs did not have a king. The Quraysh did not have a king.
Leave this man alone. Because I have heard a speech from him that I have never heard before.

questions.question: How was Khabbab ibn al-Aratt treated by his owner, and what eventually happened to her?
questions.reference_answer: Khabbab was an Arab slave and a swordsmith owned by a woman, Umm Anmar. When she learned he had become Muslim she gathered a group to beat him at his workplace, and afterwards she would repeatedly take iron he had just drawn out of the furnace and press it onto his back. The Prophet passed by while this was happening and prayed for Allah to help him against his enemy. Shortly afterwards she was struck with an illness that left her behaving like a rabid dog, crawling and panting around the house; the doctors of Mecca said the only remedy was cauterisation, so she was burned on the back and head and died from it. Years later Khabbab showed his scarred back to Umar during his caliphate, and Umar said he had never seen anything like it and seated him with honour.

supporting_quotes.quote: she would take some of that iron that he had just taken out, and she would use it to burn the back of Khabbab ibn al-Arat.
she had a type of sickness and disease that she was acting like a rabid dog. Panting around and crawling around the house, she became like, completely she lost senses.

questions.question: Why did the Prophet pick Arqam's house as the secret gathering place for the Muslims in Mecca?
questions.reference_answer: The lecture notes that the sources do not state the reasons, so they are inferred from who Arqam was and where he lived. He was a nobleman of the Quraysh but from Banu Makhzum, Abu Jahl's clan, so nobody would suspect a Makhzumi of sheltering a Hashimi; he was among the first ten to accept Islam and so completely trustworthy; he was a young man of about eighteen or nineteen who had inherited the property, which nobody would expect; and by one report he had never announced his Islam, adding another layer of cover. Crucially the house sat just behind Mount Safa in the middle of downtown Mecca, a stone's throw from the Ka'bah, so people walking to and from it looked like ordinary traffic to the sanctuary, whereas forty people converging on an isolated house outside the city would have been obvious. It also had to have been a fairly large house, since at least forty people gathered there.

supporting_quotes.quote: he was from the nobleman of the Quraysh, but he was not from the tribe of Banu Hashim. He was from the tribe of Banu Makhzum.
According to another report, Al-Arqam had not announced his Islam. He had kept it secret. And so yet another added, if you like, cover of secrecy.
Imagine if 40 people are walking towards a small house outside of Mecca. Traffic. Traffic. Everybody has to go to downtown.

questions.question: The Muslims who fled to Abyssinia came back to Mecca after only about three months. What made them return, and what did they find?
questions.reference_answer: They came back on the strength of a rumour that the Quraysh had accepted Islam. The rumour grew out of a real event: the Prophet recited Surah An-Najm in front of the Ka'bah, and when he reached the closing command to prostrate, the sheer power of the surah swept up the whole gathering so that the pagans prostrated alongside the Muslims. By the time the story travelled to Abyssinia it had become the claim that the Quraysh had all embraced Islam and united behind him. Homesick and unsettled in a foreign land, the emigrants packed up without any way to verify it, and on the road home they met a caravan that told them nothing had changed and the persecution was continuing. Some argued for turning back immediately, but being so close they went on into Mecca, each having to find a new protector to re-enter.

supporting_quotes.quote: They returned back because of one rumor. And that rumor was, the Quraysh have accepted Islam.
the Quraysh were so overwhelmed with emotion, they too fell into sajda. And Muslim and non-Muslim for the first time united together in worshipping Allah.
By the time it reached Abyssinia, the rumor had become what? They've all accepted Islam, they've united behind.

questions.notes: Lecture 17 also recaps the return and the caravan that told them the rumour was false; lecture 16 covers it in full.

questions.question: Abu Bakr set out for Abyssinia with the others but never got there. What stopped him, and how did that arrangement fall apart?
questions.reference_answer: On the road towards the port he was met by Ibn al-Dughunnah, the chief of a neighbouring tribe and a former trading partner, who told him a man like him should not have to leave Mecca and offered to extend his own tribe's protection. He went back with him and publicly asked the Quraysh to accept it. They agreed, but on one condition: Abu Bakr must not pray in public. Abu Bakr worked around this by building an extension onto his house as a place of worship and praying aloud there, and because he wept easily and recited beautifully, women and children began gathering outside to listen. The Quraysh then sent word that he could not even pray in his own house, and Ibn al-Dughunnah told him he must either stop or release him from the protection. Abu Bakr handed the protection back and said he accepted the protection of Allah, after which he lived in Mecca unprotected until the emigration, which is why he could be beaten almost senseless when he intervened to save the Prophet from being strangled.

supporting_quotes.quote: someone like you does not deserve to leave the land of Mecca. And if your people have persecuted you, then let me intercede on your behalf.
we're only going to allow this with one condition and that is Abu Bakr cannot pray publicly because Abu Bakr was of the elite of the Quraysh before this, he would pray in front of the Kaaba.
So Abu Bakr said, okay, you know, thanks but no thanks, take your protection back, and I trust in the protection of Allah.

questions.question: How did Hamza come to accept Islam?
questions.reference_answer: He accepted it almost by accident, out of tribal anger rather than conviction. While he was away hunting, Abu Jahl met the Prophet near Mount Safa and abused him publicly at length, cursing his ancestors, and the Prophet said nothing back. The women of Banu Hashim, insulted on the clan's behalf, taunted Hamza when he returned about the family's honour. He marched to the Ka'bah with his bow still on him, struck Abu Jahl across the face with it hard enough to draw blood, and blurted out that he too followed his nephew's religion, a claim he had not planned to make. Abu Jahl told his clansmen to leave him alone, admitting he had provoked him. Hamza went home in confusion and prayed that if the matter were true Allah would open his heart to it and if not that He take his life; the next morning he went to the Prophet, who talked with him and convinced him, and he then affirmed the truth of the message and never went back to the religion of his forefathers.

supporting_quotes.quote: he marched straight to Abu Jahl and took his bow and smacked him across the face with his bow caused a huge gush of blood to come out and he said how dare you curse my own nephew
Oh Allah, you know that I am one of the leaders of the Quraysh and I have now said something that I don't know, I cannot take it back.

questions.question: What finally brought the boycott of the Banu Hashim to an end?
questions.reference_answer: Several things converged. The Prophet had prayed against the Quraysh for a famine like the famine of Yusuf, and conditions in Mecca became so bad that people were reduced to eating carcasses and chewing hides, which they connected to that prayer. At the same time a group of sympathetic Qurashis, organised by Hisham ibn Amr and Zuhayr and including Mut'im ibn Adi and Abu al-Bukhtari, planted themselves around the assembly and stood up one after another to denounce the boycott, leaving Abu Jahl without support and realising he had been outmanoeuvred. The decisive moment came when the Prophet told Abu Talib that Allah had informed him the treaty hanging inside the locked Ka'bah had been eaten away by termites except for the words in the name of Allah. Abu Talib staked everything on it, offering to hand his nephew over if it proved false; the document was produced and found exactly as described, and although the Quraysh called it sorcery they had given their word, so the Banu Hashim returned to Mecca in the tenth year of the call.

supporting_quotes.quote: the Prophet ﷺ made a dua against them and said, Oh Allah, send upon them a famine like the famine of Yusuf.
for how long are we going to starve our own kith and kin to death?
Allah has informed me, that the treaty that they wrote, has been eaten up by termites or ants.

questions.question: After Abu Talib died, Abu Lahab briefly took over protecting the Prophet. Why did he do it, and what made him drop it?
questions.reference_answer: With Abu Talib dead, Abu Lahab was the eldest surviving pagan son of Abd al-Muttalib and so became chief of the Banu Hashim. When an outsider abused the Prophet particularly harshly, Abu Lahab told him to carry on exactly as he had in Abu Talib's day and that he would have the same privileges for as long as he lived. He was acting out of a chieftain's duty to his own clan, not any sympathy for the message, and when people asked whether he had become Muslim he said no, he was simply protecting his flock. Abu Jahl and Utbah then set a trap: they told him to ask his nephew where his father Abd al-Muttalib had ended up. The Prophet answered non-committally that he was with his people; Abu Lahab took this as good news until Abu Jahl pointed out that according to the Prophet his people were in the Fire. Enraged that the man he was protecting in his father's name consigned that father to hell, he withdrew his protection within about a week, leaving the Prophet unprotected in Mecca and prompting the journey to Ta'if.

supporting_quotes.quote: go and do as you used to do in the time of Abu Talib. I.e. be as you were. Be as you were.
So Abu Jahl and Utbah came together and they devised a plot. And they said to Abu Lahab, why don't you ask your nephew about the fate of your father Abdul Muttalib?
you fool. Where are his people according to the Prophet ﷺ except in the fire of hell?

questions.question: After the people of Ta'if drove the Prophet out, he was offered the chance to have them destroyed. Who made the offer and what did he say?
questions.reference_answer: Once he reached Qarn al-Manazil outside Ta'if, a cloud shaded him and Jibreel called out that Allah had heard what his people had said to him and had sent with him the angel of the mountains, placed at his disposal. The angel greeted him and said he was at his command, offering to crush the city between the two mountains it lies between. The Prophet declined and said instead that he hoped Allah would bring forth from their descendants people who would worship Him alone. The lecture stresses that this came only days after the three chiefs had mocked him and while his sandals were still soaked with his own blood, and that the real miracle of the episode was that mercy rather than the angel's offer.

supporting_quotes.quote: he has sent me with the Malakul Jibal. This hadith is in Bukhari. He has sent me with the Malak, or the angel of the mountains, to put at your disposal, and to do with as you please.
Rather, I hope that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala will extract from their progeny, from their children, those who will eventually worship Him without associating partners with Him.

questions.question: Who was the Christian servant who accepted the Prophet's message on the way back from Ta'if, and what convinced him?
questions.reference_answer: He was Addas, a Christian slave from Nineveh in Iraq, owned by Utbah and Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah. Bloodied and exhausted, the Prophet had sat down beside a wall belonging to their orchard, and the two men, feeling a tribal sympathy for a fellow Qurashi treated that way by Thaqif, sent Addas over with a bowl of grapes. When the Prophet said the name of Allah before eating, Addas was startled because it was not a local expression; asked where he was from, he said Nineveh, and the Prophet identified it as the city of Jonah son of Matta and called Jonah his brother, since both were prophets. Addas, the only practising Christian for hundreds of miles, was astonished that anyone in Arabia knew of Jonah, began kissing his hands and feet and believed in him on the spot. When his masters accused him of being bewitched he told them there was no one on earth better, and he later refused to march with them to Badr, where both of them were killed.

supporting_quotes.quote: Adas was shocked and he goes, what is this phrase, Bismillah? This is not the phrase of the local Arabs, Bismillah.
I am from Nineveh. I am from Nineveh. So the Prophet ﷺ smiled and he said, from the city of Yunus ibn Matta.
Adas instantaneously began kissing the feet of the Prophet ﷺ, as the Christians did to respect their elders and their rabbis and their priests.

questions.question: How did the number of daily prayers end up at five?
questions.reference_answer: At the divine audience the Prophet was told his community should pray fifty times a day. On the way back down he passed Musa, who asked what his Lord had commanded for his community; hearing fifty, Musa told him to go back and ask for a reduction, saying that from his own experience with the Children of Israel his community would not manage it. The Prophet glanced at Jibreel as if seeking a second opinion and Jibreel nodded, so he went back, and this repeated several times, Musa sending him back again and again as the number came down. When it reached five Musa still urged him to return, but the Prophet said he was now content and would not ask again. A voice then announced that the obligation was settled and had been made light for His servants: it is five, but it will be rewarded as fifty. The lecture adds that the Prophet's own daily routine nevertheless added up to about fifty units of prayer.

supporting_quotes.quote: 50 salawat every single day now you know the story from here and he goes back down and he meets Musa
And tell him to lower this because I have more experience than you with the Bani Israel and your ummah will not be able to do 50 times a day.
My faridah has been established, and I have made things easier for my servants. It is five, but it shall be rewarded with fifty.

questions.question: When the Prophet told the Meccans he had gone to Jerusalem and back in one night, how did they try to catch him out?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Jahl found him sitting anxious by the Ka'bah, got him to repeat the claim, then gathered the Quraysh to hear it. Their reactions ranged from clapping in disbelief to snickering, until one of them who had actually been to Jerusalem challenged him to describe the city, since everyone knew he had never been there. He began describing it but they pressed him on details he could not recall, and he says he was more terrified at that moment than he had ever been. Then Jerusalem itself was raised up before his eyes, appearing beyond the house of Aqeel ibn Abi Talib, and he answered every question they put to him while looking at it, until the man conceded that his description was accurate. He also gave them a further proof, describing three caravans he had passed on the way back, including one that had lost a camel and one whose water vessel he had drunk from, and told them when the nearest would arrive; it came in exactly as described, and Abu Jahl could only call it sorcery. When the news reached Abu Bakr he said that if the Prophet had said it then it was true, and that he believed him in things more astonishing than that, which is how he earned the title as-Siddiq.

supporting_quotes.quote: and he had been there to Baytul Maqdis can you describe it for us because everybody knew that the Prophet ﷺ had never been to Baytul Maqdis
I began describing the Baitul Maqdis until they began to ask me about specifics that I wasn't able to recall.
I saw in the distance, Baytul Maqdis rising up in front of me. Baytul Maqdis rising up in front of me. Until I saw it descending beyond the house of Aqeel ibn Abi Talib
if he said that then it must be true because I don't know what you're saying

questions.question: The Banu Shayban were interested in the Prophet's message but did not accept it. What held them back?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Bakr, who knew Arab genealogy better than anyone, introduced the Prophet to them and told him beforehand that they were among the noblest and most intelligent of the Arabs. Their elder Hani ibn Qays said the message was good and that the Quraysh had lied about him, but that changing religion after a single meeting would be hasty and they had people at home whose counsel they had not sought, so both sides should wait a year. Their military leader, al-Muthanna ibn Haritha, raised the real obstacle: they lived on the Persian frontier and had treaties both with neighbouring Arab tribes and with the Persian emperor, under which they were bound to stay neutral in Arabian affairs. He offered to accept the message only in their dealings with the Arabs and not with the Persians. The Prophet refused a half-commitment, saying Allah's religion is only helped by those who embrace it fully, and as he was leaving he asked whether they would accept if he promised them victory over the empire of Kisra and its lands and wealth. They did not believe it possible and so did not embrace Islam then, though the lecture notes that the same generation went on to bring down the Sasanian empire.

supporting_quotes.quote: we will not take any hasty decision in this matter. And there is another matter as well.
we have a deal with him to be neutral in all affairs in the Arabian Peninsula. We have a deal with him to be neutral.

your response has been good, and has been sincere. You're being fair. And you're being fair about your concerns, but, listen to this Allah's religion will only be helped by those who have embraced it fully
Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala will grant you victory over the kingdom of Kisra and you will enjoy their land and their money

questions.question: The men from Yathrib who pledged to shelter the Prophet knew they were taking on a war. Did he offer them anything for it?
questions.reference_answer: When the terms of the second pledge had been laid out, someone in the group called out asking what they would receive for it. The Prophet's answer was a single word: Paradise. He told them plainly that he could not give them money, fame or fortune; all he could promise was Allah's pleasure and Jannah. That was exactly what they wanted to hear, and they came forward one by one to give the oath.

supporting_quotes.quote: a voice cried out from amongst them and what shall we get in return? what is in it for us and the Prophet s.a.w. said the one word that they wanted to hear Al-Jannah I can't give you any money I can't promise you fame and fortune

questions.question: How did Suhayb al-Rumi get past the Quraysh when they came out to stop him leaving Makkah?
questions.reference_answer: A militia of Quraysh surrounded Suhayb outside the city. He drew his bow and told them he had forty arrows and that none of them would reach him before he had used all of them, and that his sword would be waiting afterwards. Rather than risk it, they accepted his offer: he told them where he had buried all his wealth in exchange for being let go. He reached Madinah with nothing but the clothes on his back, and the Prophet greeted him by telling him his transaction had been a profitable one.

supporting_quotes.quote: O people of Quraysh, I have 40 bows in my quiver. And I swear by Allah that none of you will get to me until I've used all 40. And then when you get to me, here is my sword.
So Suhaib said, what if I were to tell you where I hid all of my wealth?

questions.notes: The transcript says 40 bows in the quiver, which is presumably a slip for 40 arrows.

questions.question: Once the Quraysh realised the Prophet had slipped out of Makkah, what price did they put on him?
questions.reference_answer: The Quraysh announced a bounty of one hundred camels for the Prophet and the same for Abu Bakr, dead or alive, with no questions asked. The lecture stresses how enormous a sum that was: a camel was the equivalent of a car, and the Prophet did not own even one until the Hijrah itself.

supporting_quotes.quote: the booty, the bounty the war money of a hundred camels had been placed on Abu Bakr and the Prophet ﷺ dead or alive, anybody who finds them gets a hundred camels That's a lot of money.

questions.notes: Quote contains the transcript's Arabic honorific glyph after 'the Prophet'.

questions.question: On the road north a passing caravan recognised Abu Bakr and asked who the other traveller was. What did he tell them?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Bakr answered that this was his guide, guiding him along the path. The caravan understood him to mean a hired road guide, whereas Abu Bakr meant that the Prophet was guiding him to the straight path. This is described as tawriya, a deliberate double meaning rather than a lie, which is why it was permissible.

supporting_quotes.quote: And so Abu Bakr said, he is my guide guiding me to the path. He is my guide guiding me to the path. And of course, what Abu Bakr meant was, he is my guide to Siratul Mustaqim.

questions.question: The Prophet used to stand on an old palm trunk when he addressed people. What happened to it after a proper pulpit was made for him?
questions.reference_answer: An Ansari woman's carpenter built him a three-step pulpit, and during the first sermon he gave from it the companions heard a wailing like the crying of a baby camel coming from the abandoned stump. The Prophet interrupted the sermon, came down and embraced it until it quietened, and said that had he not done so it would have kept crying until the Day of Judgement. He then ordered it to be uprooted and buried underneath the new pulpit.

supporting_quotes.quote: the sahaba said, we began to hear a wailing, a crying, like that of a baby camel. And we found that the source of this noise was the tree. This stump. And the Prophet ﷺ interrupted his khutbah and came down and hugged the tree.
if I didn't hug it if I hadn't hugged it it would have cried until the day of judgment and he ordered that the tree then be uplifted and uprooted and then dug underneath his actual mimbar

questions.question: How did the Muslims settle on a way of announcing that it was time to pray?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet consulted the companions, and suggestions such as a bell like the Christians used or a horn like the Jews used were all rejected, so the meeting broke up with nothing decided. That night two men, Abdullah ibn Zayd and Umar ibn al-Khattab, independently saw the same dream in which they were taught the wording of the call. Abdullah ibn Zayd reached the Prophet first, who declared it a true dream and told Bilal to go up and call it out because he had the loudest voice, with Abdullah prompting him phrase by phrase.

supporting_quotes.quote: One of them said, let us use a bell like the Christians. But this was discarded.
that night two people saw a dream one of them was Umar ibn al-Khattab the other was Abdullah ibn Zayd and their dreams were the same

questions.question: Is the story true that everyone spun around mid-prayer on the day the direction of prayer changed?
questions.reference_answer: Not in the Prophet's own mosque. That version is described as a myth: the command came in the early morning, so he prayed Fajr facing Jerusalem and then Dhuhr facing Makkah, and the front of his mosque simply became the back. The turning around during a prayer happened at the mosque of the Banu Salama, later known as Masjid al-Qiblatayn, when a man who had prayed Dhuhr with the Prophet arrived while they were praying Asr and called out the news from the back of the mosque.

supporting_quotes.quote: there's a common myth that he was praying one day and Jibreel came down and told him to pray the other way so he turned around and the whole masjid turned around. This is a myth. This is not true.
So he cried out from the back of the Masjid. that, O people of the masjid, I have just come from the Prophet ﷺ's masjid, and I prayed with him dhuhr, and he was praying facing Mecca.

questions.question: How did Sa'd ibn Mu'adh end up becoming Muslim?
questions.reference_answer: After twelve men from Yathrib pledged allegiance at Aqaba, the Prophet sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr back with them to teach the Qur'an and lead the prayer, and he stayed in the house of As'ad ibn Zurara. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, a leader of the Khazraj, sent his friend Usayd ibn Hudayr with a spear to drive Mus'ab out, but Usayd agreed to listen first and converted on the spot. Sa'd then came himself, armed and angry, and Mus'ab made the same offer: hear me out and if you disagree I will stop. He recited Surah al-Zukhruf, and Sa'd immediately asked how to convert. With the two of them Muslim, their whole sub-tribe, Banu Abd al-Ashhal, converted within weeks, the largest mass conversion up to that point.

supporting_quotes.quote: The Prophet ﷺ chose Mus'ab ibn Umayr to send back with them to go to Yathrib. He chose Mus'ab ibn Umayr to teach them the Qur'an and to lead them in salah.
And once again he sat him down, and this time he recited Surah Zuhruf.

And with the conversion of Sa'd and Usaid, the entire tribe of the Banu Al-Ashhal it is called, which is one of the sub-tribes of the Khazraj, the entire tribe converted along with them, because these two were their leaders.

questions.notes: The lecture places Banu Abd al-Ashhal under the Khazraj; other sources make them a sub-tribe of the Aws.

questions.question: What happened to Umm Salama when her husband tried to take the family out of Makkah?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Salama packed openly and set out with his wife and small son, but the Quraysh confronted him: he was not a Qurayshi so they had no claim on him, yet they refused to let him take Umm Salama, who was one of theirs. His own tribe then came to seize the boy, and in the tug of war between the two sides the child's arm was dislocated. Umm Salama was left alone in Makkah for more than sixteen months, going out every day to al-Batha to weep, until her relatives persuaded the elders to release her. She set out alone with her son and was met at Tan'im by Uthman ibn Talha, still a pagan, who led her camel on foot the whole way to Madinah, turning his back whenever she dismounted, until her husband's home was in sight.

supporting_quotes.quote: As for your wife, she is ours. She's a Quraishi. And we will not let you take her or her son because he is our son now. This is pure dhulm.
she said for more than 16 months, every day, year and a half. I would go to Al-Bathha, which is the farthest place outside of Mecca that is still within view of the city.

He walked the entire way and he led the camel with his hand. He's walking from Mecca to Medina and he didn't say a word to me but when it was time to stop, he would tell the camel to come down and he would go forward and turn his back on me.

questions.question: What did the Quraysh decide to do about the Prophet at their late-night meeting, and who was kept out of it?
questions.reference_answer: The chiefs gathered secretly at Dar al-Nadwa, their assembly house, and deliberately left out Banu Hashim, including Abu Lahab, and also Mut'im ibn Adi, since Mut'im had given the Prophet his protection and could not be asked to break his word in private. Three options were floated: imprison him, exile him, or kill him. An unrecognised old man claiming to be a chief from Najd, identified in the reports as Iblis, shot down the first two. Abu Jahl then proposed that every tribe supply one young man so that they would strike as one and his blood would be on all their swords, leaving Banu Hashim unable to make war on everyone and forced to accept blood money. That was the plan they adopted, and Jibril came that same night telling the Prophet to leave.

questions.question: A man caught up with the Prophet and Abu Bakr in the desert hoping to collect the reward. What became of him?
questions.reference_answer: Suraqah ibn Malik, a tribal chief, heard where the three riders had been sighted, misled his own tribesmen so he would not have to share the hundred camels, and rode after them. Three times his horse sank into the ground and threw him, and his divining arrows told him not to proceed; on the third throw he realised this was beyond him and called out asking for safe conduct instead. He asked for a written guarantee of security, which the guide Abdullah ibn Arqat wrote out for him, and Abu Bakr's only request was that he tell nobody. As he left, the Prophet asked him how he would be on the day he wore the bracelets of Kisra. Years later, when the treasures of the Persian capital reached Madinah, Umar called Suraqah forward and placed those bracelets on his hands.

questions.question: Out of all the places the Muslims could have gone, why Madinah?
questions.reference_answer: Several reasons are given. Its location was strategic: close enough to Makkah to matter but far enough that no army could arrive by surprise, and central to the Hijaz. It was naturally defensible on three sides, walled in east and west by lava fields that no army could cross and to the south by dense date plantations, leaving only one open stretch, which is precisely where the trench was later dug. Its people had never been conquered by anyone, so they still had their independence and fighting spirit. The wars of Bu'ath had wiped out the older leadership and left a younger generation tired of bloodshed and open to change. And the Prophet had a blood tie there, since his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib's mother Salma was from the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj, making him a distant cousin of the people who took him in.

questions.question: How did Jewish tribes come to be settled in an oasis in the middle of Arabia?
questions.reference_answer: Nobody knows for certain, and several theories are laid out. One early Muslim view is that Musa himself sent a group to the Hijaz to await the coming prophet, which is treated as unlikely. The more reasonable theory ties them to the expulsions from Jerusalem: the first when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Solomon's temple in 587 BCE, then the destruction under Titus in 70 CE, and the massacre under Hadrian around 132-135 CE, after which refugees wandered south and settled in the date-growing land of Yathrib and Khaybar, with the largest group continuing to Yemen. An alternative reverses the direction, bringing them up from Yemen. Evidence that they were Karaites rather than Rabbinic Jews would date their arrival before about 400 CE, supporting the expulsion theory. The lecturer's own suggestion is that the three tribes represent three separate waves of migration, which would explain why they behaved as distinct tribes and even fought on opposite sides.

questions.question: How was the Prophet's mosque in Madinah actually put up, and who owned the ground it stood on?
questions.reference_answer: As the Ansar competed to host him, the Prophet let his camel go, saying Allah had charge of it, and it knelt on an open patch that the locals used for drying dates. The land belonged to two orphan boys who offered it as a gift, but he refused and insisted on paying its price. The few date palms on the plot were cut down, and some old pagan graves there had the remains moved elsewhere. The felled trunks formed two of the walls and mud bricks the other two, with the Prophet joining the work line himself while they chanted verses asking Allah's mercy on the Ansar and the Muhajirun. It took around two weeks. There was no roof at first, only later a covering of palm thatch over one section, which still leaked.

questions.question: What did the Prophet actually talk about in the first Friday sermon he gave after reaching Madinah?
questions.reference_answer: He gave it on the Friday he left Quba for the city, stopping among the Banu Salama on the way. The first part was about generosity: he reminded them of the certainty of death and of standing before Allah, who would ask each of them what they had been given and what they had done with it, and said that whoever can shield himself from the fire even with a scrap of a date should do so, and if he has not even that, then with a good word. The second part opened with the khutbat al-haja and was purely spiritual: love Allah with your whole heart, never tire of His speech and His remembrance, do not let your hearts harden, worship Him alone, be truthful, love one another, and remember that Allah hates a broken promise. The whole thing takes only two or three minutes to deliver.

questions.question: The emigrants arrived in Madinah with nothing. What did the Prophet do to get them settled?
questions.reference_answer: He paired each emigrant with an individual from the Ansar, a bond so strong that at that early stage the two even inherited from each other, until Surah al-Anfal after Badr restored inheritance to blood relatives. Over a hundred such pairings are recorded, and they were made deliberately, matching people with something in common. He also refused the Ansar's offer to hand over half their land outright, insisting instead that the emigrants work it and share the produce so that nobody was living on handouts. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf is the classic case: his partner Sa'd ibn al-Rabi offered him half of everything he owned and Abd al-Rahman asked only to be shown the way to the marketplace. The pairing was not a one-off; it continued for years, right through to companions who accepted Islam after the conquest of Makkah.

questions.question: Why does the Muslim year begin with Muharram when the emigration didn't take place in that month?
questions.reference_answer: The calendar was fixed under Umar around seventeen years after the Hijrah, prompted by practical confusion: a court case where two men disputed whether a debt due in Sha'ban meant this year or next, and a similar complaint from one of his governors. The companions debated which year to start from, and Ali's suggestion of the year of the Hijrah was accepted because that was the turning point from humiliation to honour. The Prophet actually emigrated in Safar, so the choice of Muharram as the first month needed its own reason. Uthman proposed Muharram, and two explanations are offered: the announcement to emigrate came after the Hajj, so the bulk of the companions began leaving in Muharram; and returning from Hajj at the end of Dhul Hijjah felt like a fresh start, so the new life begins in Muharram. Later scholars tried to read a Qur'anic support for it into Surah al-Tawbah 108, which is treated as a stretch.

questions.question: What did the agreement the Prophet drew up in Madinah require of the Jewish tribes living there?
questions.reference_answer: Each Jewish group is named individually and declared an ummah alongside the believers. Domestically they were left to themselves: their own internal disputes, their own poor, their own blood money, their own crimes were their business, and only matters involving both communities went to the Prophet for judgement. Militarily and financially they were bound to the Muslims: if Madinah was attacked both sides would spend and defend together. No Jew could leave Madinah without the Prophet's permission, which in that context meant renouncing membership of the community rather than simply travelling. And any Jew who wished to accept Islam was to be helped and protected, with no one permitted to harm him for it.

questions.question: Why was the direction of prayer switched from Jerusalem to Makkah, and how did people take it?
questions.reference_answer: For about sixteen months after the Hijrah the Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem, which in Madinah meant turning their backs on the Ka'bah. As relations with the Jewish tribes soured, the Prophet was told to differ from them in various matters, and he privately longed to pray towards Makkah. He asked Jibril, who replied that he was only a servant like him and could only bring Allah's command, so the Prophet took to gazing up at the sky in supplication at night, and the Qur'an says Allah had seen his face turning towards the heavens and would give him a direction that pleased him. The change caused real confusion: the Qur'an quotes the foolish asking why they had turned from their former direction, and the objections included mocking a prophet who kept changing which way he faced and asking whether their qiblah was not good enough. The companions themselves asked what would become of those who had died praying towards Jerusalem, and the answer came that Allah would not let their faith go to waste.

questions.question: There was a small scouting party sent out shortly before Badr that caused a scandal. What went wrong?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet handpicked eight Muhajirun under his cousin Abdullah ibn Jahsh, sent them off north-east with a sealed letter and told him not to open it for two days. The letter told them to double back to Nakhla, near Makkah, and report on Quraysh movements, and gave anyone who wished the freedom to turn back. Two men lost their camel on the way and were left behind, so six arrived, and before they could even pitch camp a lightly guarded Quraysh caravan appeared. It was the thirtieth of Rajab, a sacred month, with only an hour or two of daylight left; they attacked anyway, killed one of the drivers, took two prisoners and brought the goods back. The Prophet was angry, said he had not ordered them to fight, and refused the booty, while the Quraysh broadcast the scandal across Arabia. Then Surah al-Baqarah 217 came down: fighting in the sacred month is grave, but barring people from Allah's path, disbelieving in Him, and expelling the people of the sacred mosque is graver still. Only then did he accept the goods, and he held the prisoners until his own two missing men returned safely before allowing them to be ransomed.

questions.question: Who was left running Medina while the Prophet was away at Badr?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet left Medina on the 12th of Ramadan in the second year of the Hijrah and put Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind companion, in charge of the city. This was not a one-off arrangement: he was given charge of Medina at least a dozen times because he was regarded as a sensible, wise man. The lecture treats the appointment as evidence that a physical disability was no bar to responsibility in Islam, at a time when the blind were usually treated as outcasts.

questions.question: How did Abu Lahab get out of marching with the Quraysh army to Badr?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Lahab did not go himself. He sent a substitute, al-As ibn Wa'il, who owed him an outstanding loan of 4,000 dirhams, and Abu Lahab cancelled that large debt in exchange for the man going in his place. The classical sources do not say why he stayed behind; the lecture suggests that besides fear, he may have felt a tribal conflict about fighting his own Banu Hashim.

questions.question: Whose idea was it for the Muslims to take up position by the water at Badr?
questions.reference_answer: It was the suggestion of al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir, a companion known as a desert scout. He first asked the Prophet whether the chosen campsite was something Allah had instructed or simply his own military judgement; told it was his own opinion, he proposed moving past the midpoint of the plain so that the wells of Badr lay behind the Muslims and the Quraysh would be left dependent on the water they had carried from Mecca. The Prophet accepted the advice, moved camp, and had the smaller wells emptied and blocked so the main well sat inside the Muslim camp; in one version Jibril told him to follow Hubab's advice.

questions.question: Did anything significant happen elsewhere in the world on the same day as the battle at Badr?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. A report in Sunan al-Tirmidhi says that on the very day of Badr, hundreds of miles away, the Byzantine Romans and the Sassanid Persians were at war, and in an unexpected reversal the Persians were badly defeated. This matched the prediction at the opening of Surah al-Rum that the Romans, who had been losing, would prevail, so the believers were given two victories on the same day.

questions.question: When Abu Sufyan asked Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf which faith was better, the Meccans' or the Muslims', what did Ka'b tell him?
questions.reference_answer: Ka'b, a monotheist from the Banu Nadir, told the pagan Abu Sufyan that the Meccans were the better guided of the two: 'you are more rightly guided than them.' The lecture notes that the pagans felt an inferiority complex towards the Jews as a people of scripture, which is why Abu Sufyan asked him at all, and that the Qur'an quotes this private exchange in Surah an-Nisa verse 50.

questions.question: Was Abu Bakr older or younger than the Prophet, and by how much?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Bakr was two years younger than the Prophet. The figure was cloaked, so from behind he assumed it was a man; when he raised the sword the person turned round and let out the women's wail, and it was Hind bint Utbah. questions.question: How did Abu Sufyan work out that his caravan was being watched, and what did he do once he knew?
questions.reference_answer: Already on alert after the earlier near-miss at al-Ushayra, Abu Sufyan inspected a spot where riders had camped and broke open camel dung, finding date stones he recognised as coming from Yathrib. Realising the Muslims were monitoring him, he did two things: he swung the caravan off its usual route and bypassed the danger area altogether, and he sent his fastest rider, Damdam ibn Amr al-Ghifari, racing to Mecca to warn the Quraysh that the caravan would be seized unless they sent reinforcements. Damdam staged his arrival dramatically, mutilating his camel, smearing blood, tearing his clothes and riding in backwards while crying out that the caravan was under attack.

questions.question: Before the fighting began, how did the Muslims find out how many men the Quraysh had brought with them?
questions.reference_answer: The Muslims captured two Quraysh slaves who were water carriers for the army. The companions beat them each time they said they belonged to the army, because the Muslims wanted to hear that they were with the caravan; the Prophet rebuked this, pointing out that they were beating them for telling the truth and letting them go when they lied. He then asked the captives a question they could answer from their own work: how many camels the Quraysh slaughtered each day. They said nine or ten, and he concluded the army was between nine hundred and a thousand men, since one camel feeds about a hundred. He then asked which of the Quraysh nobles were present, and the roll-call of leading Meccans that followed alarmed the Muslims.
