questions.question: How did the single combats at the start of Badr play out?
questions.reference_answer: Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, his brother Shaybah and his son al-Walid stepped forward and challenged the Muslims. Three young Ansar answered first, but the Quraysh refused them, saying they had no quarrel with them and wanted opponents of their own blood. The Prophet then sent out three of Quraysh stock: Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, Hamza and Ali, paired with their opposite numbers by age. Hamza and Ali killed their opponents without taking a wound, while Utbah sliced Ubaydah's leg; the other two then came to his rescue and killed Utbah. Ubaydah was carried off on the shoulders of Hamza and Ali and died of the wound a few days later, so all three Quraysh champions were killed and the Muslims took the encounter as a first, morale-lifting victory.

questions.question: Who actually killed Abu Jahl, and how did he die?
questions.reference_answer: He was brought down by two Ansari teenagers, roughly sixteen and seventeen years old: Mu'adh, who struck the blow that took off Abu Jahl's leg, and Mu'awwidh ibn al-Afra. Ikrimah, Abu Jahl's son, cut Mu'adh's arm in the exchange, and Mu'adh pinned it down with his foot and tore it off so it would not get in his way, then fought on with his left hand. After the battle the Prophet had the body searched for, and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud found Abu Jahl at his last breath, put his foot on his chest and asked whether he now admitted Allah had disgraced him; Abu Jahl was defiant to the end, complaining only that he had been killed by his own people. questions.question: What did the Muslims disagree about once the fighting at Badr was over, and how was it settled?
questions.reference_answer: This was the first time they had captured spoils, and three groups each claimed a prior right to them: those who had gathered the goods from the field, those who had chased the fleeing Quraysh to make sure they did not return, and those who had stayed around the Prophet to guard him. Individual claims were made too, such as Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asking to keep a fine sword he had taken from a man he killed. The opening verse of Surah al-Anfal was then revealed on the battlefield itself, declaring that the spoils belong to Allah and His Messenger rather than to the fighters personally, followed by the rule of the khums, one fifth set aside and itself divided into five shares. At Badr the remainder was divided in equal shares, and Uthman was given a share even though he had stayed behind with the dying Ruqayyah.

questions.question: Did the Prophet's uncle Abbas have to pay a ransom like the other captives taken at Badr?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, and the Prophet insisted on the full amount. Abbas was assessed at 4,000 dirhams for himself and also had to cover the ransoms of his nephews Aqil and Nawfal. When he protested that he had no money, the Prophet asked him about the wealth he had secretly buried with his wife Umm al-Fadl, telling him he had instructed her that if he died it should be divided among his sons al-Fadl, Abdullah and Qutham. Abbas swore that no one but the two of them had known of it and took this as proof of prophethood. The lecture links Qur'an 8:70, revealed about Abbas, promising that if Allah knows good in the captives' hearts He will give them better than what was taken from them.

questions.question: What happened to the Prophet's daughter Zaynab when she left Mecca for Medina after Badr?
questions.reference_answer: Her husband Abu al-As had been captured at Badr, and about a month later he was released on the condition that he send Zaynab to her father; the Prophet sent two companions to wait for her outside Mecca. When she set out, a crowd of Quraysh gathered to stop her while her brother-in-law Kinana tried to protect her camel. Zaynab was pregnant, and Habbar ibn al-Aswad thrust a spear at the camel; it reared, she fell about fifteen feet, began to bleed and miscarried. The injuries were said to have stayed with her and to have contributed to her death a few years later. Abu Sufyan intervened, telling Kinana not to make a public spectacle of it and to bring her out quietly a few nights later.

questions.question: How did Abu Lahab die?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Lahab had not gone to Badr and refused to believe the first deserters' reports, so he waited to hear it from Abu Sufyan, questioning him at Abbas's house; Abu Sufyan described being overwhelmed by riders between heaven and earth whom no one could resist. Abbas's slave, who was already Muslim, showed his delight at the news, and Abu Lahab set on him and beat him. When Umm al-Fadl, Abbas's wife, tried to stop him he turned on her too, and she shamed him publicly for attacking the household of a man who was absent. He left the house humiliated, was struck by a disease, and died of it within a few days.

supporting_quotes.quote: she comes out and she physically tries to stop Abu Lahab from killing the slave. And he turns on her and he begins beating her up.
He fled from the house in a state of humiliation and guilt. And he was afflicted with a type of disease.
But within a few days after this incident, he passed away, he died.

questions.question: Someone travelled to Medina after Badr intending to kill the Prophet. Who was he and what became of him?
questions.reference_answer: Umayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi, sitting with his cousin Safwan ibn Umayyah and grieving the losses at Badr, said he would go and kill the Prophet himself if not for his debts and his dependants. Safwan offered to clear his debts and provide for his family exactly as he provided for his own, and Umayr swore them both to secrecy, poisoned his sword and travelled to Medina alone. Umar recognised him at the mosque and warned the Prophet, who had him brought in. Umayr claimed he had come to negotiate his captive son's ransom, but the Prophet recounted the secret conversation he had held with Safwan in the Hijr. Convinced no one but Allah could have told him, Umayr accepted Islam on the spot; the Prophet ordered that he be taught the religion and the Qur'an and that his son be released free of charge. He returned to Mecca to preach, and years later, at the conquest, he obtained the Prophet's protection for Safwan, who also became Muslim.

supporting_quotes.quote: He sharpened his sword and he poisoned it such that if the tip had just entered into anybody's body it would have been enough poison to die.

questions.question: What led to the Banu Qaynuqa being expelled from Medina?
questions.reference_answer: After Badr the Banu Qaynuqa were openly resentful, and when the Prophet gathered them in their market and reminded them of the treaty, one of their leaders told him not to be deceived by his victory, since he had fought people with no experience of war and would find it different against real men. The final trigger came in the same market: a goldsmith flirting with an Ansari woman had her garment pinned so that it fell away when she stood, and when she screamed a Muslim killed the man who had done it, whereupon the Banu Qaynuqa killed the Muslim. The Prophet sent word that the treaty was annulled, as the Qur'an requires rather than a surprise attack, and besieged their fortresses for half a month until they surrendered. Abdullah ibn Ubayy, their old ally, physically seized the Prophet's armour and would not let go until he was promised their lives; Ubadah ibn as-Samit, their other ally, publicly disowned them. They were given three days to leave and had to abandon most of their property, and Surah al-Ma'idah 51-56 was revealed about the episode.

supporting_quotes.quote: one of their leaders stood up and said, O Muhammad ﷺ, don't be fooled or deceived by your recent victory.
And so for half a month, the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims surrounded them. For half a month, they laid siege to the tribes of the Banu Qaynuqa until finally they decided there is no alternative.
And then the verdict came, you have three days, to pack your stuff and leave. Get out of here. And whatever remains will be ours.

questions.question: How did Muhammad ibn Maslama manage to get Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf out of his fortress alone at night?
questions.reference_answer: When the Prophet asked who would deal with Ka'b, Muhammad ibn Maslama volunteered, then stopped eating and drinking for three days out of anxiety that he might fail; the Prophet told him he only had to try, and gave him permission to say whatever the plan required. He was chosen partly because he was from the Aws, who had old ties with the Banu Nadir, so the killing would not reopen the Aws-Khazraj feud. He visited Ka'b and complained bitterly about the Prophet, which delighted Ka'b, then asked for a loan. Ka'b demanded a pledge; Muhammad ibn Maslama refused to pledge their women or their sons and offered their weapons instead, which gave the party a reason to arrive armed without arousing suspicion. They came on a moonlit night, the 14th of Rabi al-Awwal; Ka'b's new wife warned him that he was a man at war and should not go out, but he went down, and after Abu Nailah, his foster brother, asked to smell his perfume and took hold of his hair, they killed him. Al-Harith ibn Aws was badly wounded in the struggle and the Prophet healed him with his saliva.

supporting_quotes.quote: so he said, what if I bring you weapons my weapons you see where he's heading with this what if I bring you my weapons swords and spears

And that is that he will through some ruse or tactic hold on to his head and have him in an arm grip and then the others will do the deed.

questions.question: How many uncles did the Prophet have, and how many of them were still alive to see him preach?
questions.reference_answer: He had at least twelve uncles, probably more than ten in any case; the common idea that there were only ten comes from Abdullah being the tenth son of Abd al-Muttalib, but more sons were born after him, including Abbas, who was about the Prophet's own age. By the time he turned forty and began preaching, all of them had died except four: Abu Talib, Abu Lahab, Hamza and Abbas. Hamza and Abbas accepted Islam while Abu Talib and Abu Lahab did not, and the shaykh notes as a curiosity that the two who refused were the two whose given names, Abd al-Uzza and Abd Manaf, were names of idols.

supporting_quotes.quote: by the time the process is 40 years old all of his uncles have died except for four
these four are of course who are they Abu Lahab and Abu Talib and Hamza and Abbas
by the way Abu Lahab, his name was Abdul Uzza and Abu Talib, his name was Abdi Manaf. And it is perhaps just a coincidence but both of those were named after idols and they did not accept Islam.

questions.notes: Lecture 45 is a recap of the Meccan period, so much of its material duplicates lectures 3-28; this particular tally of the uncles appears to be specific to it.

questions.question: The Prophet's own preference was not to meet the Meccan army in open ground at Uhud. Why did the Muslims end up marching out anyway?
questions.reference_answer: In the consultation the Prophet proposed staying inside Medina and using the city's natural defences, which would have forced the attackers into street fighting the defenders knew and even allowed women and children to fight from the rooftops. Abdullah ibn Ubayy, a seasoned warrior, agreed, arguing from precedent that Medina had never been beaten when its people stayed inside it. But a group of younger companions who had missed Badr kept pressing to go out and fight like brave men rather than sit at home like cowards, while the senior companions stayed silent, and when it seemed to the Prophet that the majority wanted this he agreed and went in to put on his armour. The older companions then rebuked the young men, who sent Hamza in to say they had changed their minds; but the Prophet had already fastened his armour and replied that it is not fitting for a prophet who has put on his armour to take it off before fighting.

supporting_quotes.quote: So, the Prophet ﷺ suggested to remain in Medina. And amazingly, Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul agreed. Not because he was somebody who appreciated the Prophet ﷺ, but because it was the correct opinion.
they said why should we remain in our houses like cowards rather we should go out like brave men and fight them on the battlefield
it is not possible once a Prophet has worn his armor that he takes it off until he fights the enemy

questions.question: Who was the man who became Muslim on the very morning of Uhud and was killed in the battle without ever having prayed a single prayer?
questions.reference_answer: He was al-Usayrim, Amr ibn Thabit, one of the last few pagans left in Medina. On the morning of the battle he went around asking where the leaders he looked up to were, found that all of them had gone to Uhud, and accepted Islam on the spot. The Muslims initially told him to keep away because they knew him as a pagan, but he told them he had accepted Islam and was allowed to fight, and he was killed as a martyr. Because the battle began early and Dhuhr had not yet come in, he died without performing a single prayer, and Abu Hurayrah used to test his students by asking who entered Paradise without ever making one prostration.

supporting_quotes.quote: and so Usayrim accepted Islam on Saturday morning the 15th of Shawwal the morning of Uhud he accepts Islam right then and there and he takes his armor and sword

questions.question: What became of the man who killed Hamza? Did he ever accept Islam, and how did the Prophet deal with him afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: Hamza was killed by Wahshi, an Abyssinian slave of Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who had been promised his freedom if he did it; Jubayr also wanted revenge because Hamza had killed his uncle Tu'ayma at Badr. Wahshi later fled to Ta'if when Mecca was conquered, and only accepted Islam after someone told him that the Prophet never kills anyone who enters his religion. He came veiled to Medina and gave the shahada, and the Prophet asked him to describe how he killed Hamza, wept until his beard was wet, and then told him to keep himself hidden from his sight. The corpus adds that Wahshi struggled with drinking and was punished for it under Umar, but that he sought to expiate his deed by killing Musaylimah in the Ridda wars with the very same spear.

questions.question: How did Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah end up losing some of his teeth?
questions.reference_answer: At Uhud two objects were embedded in the Prophet's cheeks, and Abu Bakr wanted to pull them out but Abu Ubaydah begged to be allowed to do it instead. Rather than yanking them with his hand, he gripped the arrow with his teeth and eased it out, biting so hard that he broke his own teeth in the process, and then insisted on doing the same for the second wound. He was left missing at least three, possibly four, of his teeth for the rest of his life.

supporting_quotes.quote: so what does Abu Ubaidah do he decides to bite onto the arrow with his teeth and gently nudge it out to pull it out and he bites so hard that he loses his own two teeth in the process
And Abu Ubaidah therefore remained without at least three, maybe four of his teeth for the rest of his life.

questions.question: When the Prophet got separated from the bulk of his army at Uhud, who was still with him, and how did that small group keep him alive?
questions.reference_answer: When Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry swung back, only nine men were around the Prophet: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Talha ibn Ubaydullah, and seven Ansar whose names are not preserved. They retreated up the mountain toward a narrow crevice, and the Prophet sent the Ansar out one at a time to fight and draw the enemy away, so that all seven were killed one after another while Talha kept asking to go and was told to stay. In the end only Talha and Sa'd were left; Sa'd shot arrows that the Prophet himself handed him, and the Prophet said to him the phrase he never used for anyone else, that his mother and father be sacrificed for him. Talha shielded the opening with his own body and lost some fingers fighting off the last attacker.

supporting_quotes.quote: And this continued to happen until finally all seven of the Ansar, and that's why we don't know their names, All seven of the Ansar, one by one, died a shaheed.

May my mother and father be given in ransom for you. Shoot, O Sa'ad, shoot.

questions.question: Did the Muslims take any captives at Uhud, and what happened to him?
questions.reference_answer: Only a single prisoner was taken out of the three thousand who came, a man named Abu Uzza, found cowering on the battlefield, and he was executed there. He had been captured at Badr and released without ransom after pleading that he had only daughters to support, on the sole condition that he never fight the Muslims again, but Abu Sufyan tempted him back with a promise of a share of the spoils and of looking after his daughters if he died. Breaking that promise is presented as the reason Allah singled him out for humiliation.

supporting_quotes.quote: Now very interesting, very interesting that no prisoners of war were taken except for one. They found him on the battlefield, cowering on the battlefield. One person.
he was the one person that was captured and then executed on the battlefield

questions.question: The Quraysh very nearly turned around and came back to finish off Medina after Uhud. What stopped them?
questions.reference_answer: The day after the battle the Prophet called for volunteers from those who had actually fought, and seventy men went out under Ali to camp at Hamra al-Asad as a forward guard, with instructions to watch whether the enemy rode horses (meaning they were coming back) or camels (meaning they were going home). Meanwhile the Quraysh had regrouped and were arguing, with Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl pushing hard to return while Safwan ibn Umayyah warned that the Muslims would be enraged. The deciding factor was Ma'bad al-Khuza'i, a sympathetic non-Muslim tribal elder who had just visited the Prophet, met Abu Sufyan on the road and painted a terrifying picture of Medina's fury, telling him to flee as fast as his horses would carry him. The Quraysh withdrew, and the Qur'an praises those who answered the call after their wounds.

supporting_quotes.quote: therefore 70 of them volunteered 70 of them volunteered at the head of them was Ali ibn Abi Talib
And the most adamant amongst them was Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, the son of Abu Jahl.
So Abu Sufyan said, what do you advise we do? So he said, I advise you flee as fast as your horses will take you.

questions.question: How did Amir ibn Tufayl, the Najdi chieftain who had the Prophet's messenger and his companions killed, eventually die?
questions.reference_answer: He met a miserable end. He was struck with a kind of leprosy that began under his arm and spread over his whole body, driving him to delusion and making him an outcast whose own family and people abandoned him. He died alone in the desert in great pain, which the corpus presents as Allah punishing him in this world before the next, especially since the Prophet had supplicated against him.

supporting_quotes.quote: he was inflicted with a type of leprosy that spread over his whole skin. It started from under the arm and then it spread and it caused him to become delusional and it caused him to become a pariah.

questions.question: Two of the ambushed companions were taken alive and sold to families in Mecca to be put to death. What happened to each of them?
questions.reference_answer: They were Khubayb and Zayd, taken after the rest of their group was killed; a third, Abdullah ibn Tariq, refused to cooperate and was killed on the roadside. Khubayb was bought by the Banu Harith because he had killed one of them at Badr, and while a prisoner he asked for a bath and a razor to meet Allah clean, refused even to touch a child who crawled to him with the razor in his hand, and was seen eating grapes when there were no grapes in Mecca. Before his execution he asked to pray two units and then cut them short so no one would think him afraid, and this became the practice for anyone facing execution. Zayd was bought by Safwan ibn Umayyah in revenge for his father Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and the Meccans made a public spectacle of his killing; when Abu Sufyan asked whether he would rather be home with the Prophet in his place, he answered that he would not accept even a thorn pricking the Prophet in exchange for his own life.

questions.notes: The lecture uses the names Bir Ma'una and al-Raji somewhat interchangeably when narrating this ambush; the question deliberately avoids naming the site.

questions.question: Did any of the Prophet's wives pass away during his own lifetime?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, two: Khadijah in Mecca, and Zaynab bint Khuzaymah of the Banu Hilal, who died in Medina. Zaynab was married to the Prophet only a few months and died in Rabi al-Awwal of the fourth year of the Hijrah, which is why almost nothing is known about her. She was already known in the days of ignorance as Umm al-Masakin, the mother of the poor, because she cared for orphans and the needy, and she was the first of the wives to be buried in al-Baqi.

She was known as Ummul Masakin, because she used to take care of the orphans and the poor.

questions.question: Why did Uthman and then Abu Bakr both turn Umar down when he offered them his widowed daughter in marriage?
questions.reference_answer: Hafsa was widowed young when her husband Khunays died of wounds after Uhud, and once her waiting period ended Umar offered her to Uthman, who was himself widowed. Uthman asked for time and came back saying he did not wish to marry at that point, which wounded Umar deeply. He then went to Abu Bakr, who said nothing at all and never came back with an answer, which hurt Umar even more. The reason was that the Prophet had already mentioned Hafsa to both of them and they could not disclose his intention; he then proposed to her himself. Abu Bakr later apologised to Umar and explained that he had been keeping the Prophet's confidence, and that had the Prophet not proposed he would have taken her himself.

Hafsa will marry someone better than Uthman. And Uthman will marry someone better than Hafsa.
and I could not inform you of his secret

questions.question: What made the Prophet decide to drive the Banu Nadir out of Medina, and how were they finally forced to go?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet went to them with Abu Bakr, Umar and others to ask for help paying blood money owed for two men killed by mistake. They welcomed him and sat him beneath their fortress wall while they went inside, where they agreed to drop a rock on him from the roof; he suddenly stood up and left without a word, having been warned. He then sent Muhammad ibn Maslamah to confront them with the plot and give them ten days to leave. They first agreed, but Abdullah ibn Ubayy sent word promising to fight alongside them and even go into exile with them, so they sent back a defiant message telling the Prophet to do as he pleased. The Muslims mobilised the same day and besieged their fortresses for roughly a week to ten days, no help came from Ibn Ubayy, and the burning of their prized date palms broke their morale. They surrendered and were allowed to leave with their lives, their families and whatever their camels could carry, on the single condition that they take no weapons; out of spite they demolished their own houses before departing.

questions.question: Did the Prophet ever tell one of his companions to learn a foreign language, and why?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. He instructed Zayd ibn Thabit to learn Hebrew because he wanted a trustworthy person of his own who could read and verify incoming correspondence rather than relying on others. Zayd said he mastered it in fifteen days. He was well chosen: he was very young, had already memorised much of the Qur'an as a boy, and had grown up among Jewish neighbours, even attending their school as a child.

supporting_quotes.quote: he wanted someone trustworthy. He did not trust the correspondence. He wanted somebody to know the Hebrew language in order to communicate if they write anything or if anything goes on.
And so Zayd said, I learned it in 15 days. Two weeks. Took him two weeks to learn.

questions.question: How did Juwayriyah come to be married to the Prophet, and what did that marriage mean for her people?
questions.reference_answer: She was captured with her tribe after the raid on the Banu al-Mustaliq and allotted to Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, with whom she negotiated a price to buy her own freedom. As the daughter of the tribal chief she then came to the Prophet asking for help raising the money, and he offered her something better: he would free her himself and marry her, making her freedom her dowry. When the Ansar heard that the Prophet had married into the tribe, they refused to keep his in-laws as captives and freed every single prisoner. Her father al-Harith came to ransom her, the Prophet left the choice to her and she chose to stay, which so moved him that he accepted Islam, and with him the whole tribe. Aisha said she knew of no woman who brought greater blessing to her people.

supporting_quotes.quote: and she agreed with Thabit to purchase her own freedom
He said, I will free you myself. Not a loan, forget that. I will free you myself and marry you.
So one by one they began freeing every single captive until all of them were freed down to the last person.
And Aisha comments, that I don't know of any lady who brought more blessings to her tribe than Juwadia.

questions.question: What did Abdullah ibn Ubayy say on the way back from the Banu al-Mustaliq campaign, and what happened to him because of it?
questions.reference_answer: A scuffle between an Ansari and a Muhajir youth over water blew up into a standoff between the two groups, which the Prophet shut down as a call of ignorance. Ibn Ubayy, angry that the division had been quelled, said in his tent that the Muhajirun were like a dog you fatten only for it to bite you, and that when they returned to Medina the honourable would expel the lowly. A young man present, Zayd ibn Arqam, reported this; Ibn Ubayy swore the strongest oaths that he had never said it and the Prophet accepted his denial, leaving Zayd devastated. Umar asked permission to kill him and the Prophet refused, saying he did not want people saying that Muhammad kills his own companions. The Prophet then marched the army non-stop for about twenty hours so exhaustion would kill the gossip, and that morning outside Medina the whole of Surah al-Munafiqun was revealed, quoting Ibn Ubayy's words and vindicating Zayd. Ibn Ubayy's own believing son offered to execute his father himself and then blocked him at the gate of Medina until the Prophet gave him permission to enter.

but there was a young lad amongst them whose heart was full of iman and his name was Zayd ibn Arqam

And right that morning, outside of Medina, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala revealed all of the entirety of Surah Al-Munafiqun.
he stood at the gate of Medina waiting for Abdullah ibn Ubayy his own father to come

questions.question: How did the Prophet try to establish the truth of the accusations made against Aisha?
questions.reference_answer: He first sought testimony privately from the two people closest to his household, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Usama ibn Zayd. Usama said flatly that he knew the family and none of them had such a character; Ali said Allah had not restricted him and there were other women, but advised calling her maidservant Barira, who would know best. Barira, terrified, could only report that Aisha sometimes fell asleep while kneading dough and a goat would eat it. Once Aisha had moved to her parents' house the Prophet took the matter public in the mosque, asking who would excuse him regarding a man who had harmed him through his own family, and declaring that he knew nothing but good of his wives and of Safwan. That gathering then collapsed into a tribal argument between Sa'd ibn Mu'adh of the Aws and Sa'd ibn Ubadah of the Khazraj, which the Prophet had to calm down.

supporting_quotes.quote: So Usama testified, it's not possible that I know all of them, and none of them have such a character.
if you want to know her character why don't you call her maid servant Barira, Barira will know more than us
Except that sometimes, Ya Rasulullah, she is supposed to knead the dough, and she falls asleep. And the goat comes and eats the dough when she is supposed to be kneading it.
And wallahi, I know nothing but good from my wives.

questions.question: Was anyone actually punished for spreading the rumour about Aisha?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. Once the verses of Surah al-Nur came down, three Muslims who had repeated the rumour without inventing it were given the prescribed punishment of eighty lashes for slander: Hassan ibn Thabit, Hamnah bint Jahsh, and Mistah. The hypocrites who started it, chiefly Abdullah ibn Ubayy, were not punished at all in this world; scholars explain that Allah left their full punishment for the hereafter.

supporting_quotes.quote: And Allah revealed in the Quran that those who spread it, they should be lashed 80 times.
as for the munafiqun and the one who instigated it they were let off

questions.question: Whose idea was the defence the Muslims used when the allied armies marched on Medina, and how did that man come to be free to take part?
questions.reference_answer: The idea came from Salman al-Farisi, who told the Prophet that back home in Persia they would dig a trench as a barrier between themselves and an enemy, a tactic never used in Arabia before. Salman had spent a long life moving from Zoroastrianism through a succession of Christian monks before being brought to Medina as a slave, and he had agreed with his master to buy his freedom for an enormous number of date palms that would take many years to mature; the Prophet planted every seedling himself and Salman was freed within a few years. He had therefore missed Badr and Uhud as a slave, and the Battle of the Trench was the first battle he could take part in. The corpus draws from this that Islam freely adopts useful worldly innovations from other cultures even though it rejects innovation in ritual.

supporting_quotes.quote: He said, back in our hometown in Iran, in Persia, back in our home, we have a tactic we used to do, and that is to dig a trench and basically use this as a means of protection against us and our enemy.
And for the first time in Arabia, this idea was imported.
And Salman agreed with his master to be freed for a preposterous sum.
So he was not able to participate in Badr and Uhud because he's a slave. Now in Khandaq he becomes free. And Khandaq was his first battle.

questions.question: Where were the women and children of Medina kept while the city was under siege, and what happened when the enemy came to scout the place?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet had them sent to al-Fari, the fortress of the Banu Harithah, the strongest stronghold the Ansar owned, because he feared the Banu Qurayza inside the city might turn. Only some elderly or infirm men went with them, plus the poet Hassan ibn Thabit, who by his own community's account was not a fighter. When the Banu Qurayza did switch sides they first sent two scouts at night to see whether the fortress was guarded. Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's aunt, heard someone climbing, and when Hassan declined to go out she wrapped herself in a man's shawl, took a dagger in her mouth, climbed down, surprised the intruder and cut his throat, then threw the head down to his companion, who fled believing the place was defended.

questions.question: What happened when Jabir ibn Abdullah invited the Prophet home for a meal while the Muslims were digging Medina's defences?
questions.reference_answer: There was a severe food shortage from the first days of the digging; the companions were eating dried barley with foul-smelling oil and even date pits, and Jabir saw that the Prophet had tied a stone against his stomach from hunger. Distressed by this, Jabir went home, slaughtered the small goat he and his wife owned and had her prepare some bread, then quietly invited the Prophet and one or two others. Instead the Prophet stood up and announced the meal to everyone at the trench. Jabir panicked, but his wife pointed out that the Prophet had made the announcement, not him. The Prophet came first, told them not to lift the pot until he arrived, made supplication over the food, and then let people in ten at a time until everyone had eaten their fill. Jabir later estimated they numbered about a thousand, and the lecture uses this as the clearest illustration of what barakah means.

questions.question: How did the Muslims find out that the Banu Qurayza had gone over to the enemy while Medina was surrounded?
questions.reference_answer: Huyayy ibn Akhtab, the exiled chief of the Banu Nadir, slipped back into the city he had grown up in and worked on Ka'b ibn Asad of the Banu Qurayza, who at first refused because he had given his word three times, until repeated promises of protection and reward wore him down. Zubayr ibn al-Awwam volunteered to go and see what was happening and came back reporting that they had broken the covenant, which is when the Prophet called him the disciple of every prophet being his own. Because he would not act on one man's observation, the Prophet sent four Ansari leaders who had old ties with the tribe to confront them directly; they got only evasive answers and confirmed the betrayal. questions.question: How did Sa'd ibn Mu'adh get the injury that eventually killed him, and who was responsible?

The wound would not close and kept bleeding for weeks until he died. The man who shot him from across the trench was Hibab ibn al-Ariqah, who called out mockingly as he did it, 'take this from me and I am Ibn al-Ariqah.' questions.question: Which of the Prophet's marriages had the most generous wedding feast, and what was actually served?
questions.reference_answer: The feast for Zaynab bint Jahsh was the most lavish of any of his marriages, and this is reported in all the books of hadith. When Anas was asked what was served he said meat and bread until everyone had eaten their fill. questions.question: Abu Hurayrah is the most prolific narrator of hadith, but when exactly did he join the Prophet?
questions.reference_answer: He arrived at Khaybar after the fighting was already over, having travelled up from Yemen as a man of the tribe of Daws on his way to Medina. Because the campaign was finished he had no claim to the spoils, so the Prophet asked the companions whether they minded the Dawsis being given a share, and they agreed. So Abu Hurayrah received a fortune from Khaybar without having fought at all. He only accompanied the Prophet for about three years, yet narrated more hadith than any other companion.

questions.question: How did the Muslims find out that Banu Qurayza had gone over to the enemy, and how did the Prophet react when it was confirmed?
questions.reference_answer: Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, sent out as a scout, brought back the first report that something was wrong, but he had only seen things from a distance and was not an eyewitness, so the news was not certain. The Prophet then sent a delegation of senior Ansar with the closest ties to the tribe, the two Sa'ds, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh of the Aws and Sa'd ibn Ubada of the Khazraj, along with Abdullah ibn Rawaha and Khawwat ibn Jubayr, telling them to signal the answer indirectly if it was bad so as not to frighten the army, but to announce it out loud if the treaty still held. The delegation was met with mockery and outright denial that any treaty existed. They returned and simply named two tribes notorious for earlier treachery as their coded signal. On hearing it the Prophet said Allahu Akbar and called it good news, because he was certain their turning would end in the Muslims' favour.

questions.question: How did one man manage to break the trust between the tribes besieging Medina?
questions.reference_answer: Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud of Ghatafan, who had only just accepted Islam and was still trusted by both sides, was given permission to use wartime deception. He went first to Banu Qurayza and advised them that the Quraysh might abandon them, so they should demand seventy of their nobles as a guarantee. He then went to Abu Sufyan and warned him confidentially that Banu Qurayza were having second thoughts and had offered the Prophet seventy Qurayshi heads as expiation, so he should be especially wary if they asked for noblemen. He told his own tribe the same thing. When Banu Qurayza's envoy duly demanded the seventy nobles, Abu Sufyan stalled and then told the Quraysh to hand over nobody. Nu'aym went back and reported to Banu Qurayza that Abu Sufyan had said he would not hand over even a baby camel, which left both sides convinced the other was about to betray them.

questions.question: Who went out on the freezing, windy night at the end of the siege of Medina to see what the enemy was doing, and what did he find?
questions.reference_answer: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. He later described how bitterly cold, dark and windy that night was, and how the Prophet asked three times for a volunteer, offering to be that man's companion on the Day of Judgement, and nobody stood up out of sheer exhaustion and fear. The Prophet then called Hudhayfah by name, so he had no choice, and was told to bring back news without giving himself away. He was chosen partly because the Quraysh would not recognise him. He made a prayer for his protection, and Hudhayfah said all his fear left him. He slipped into the enemy camp, worked out which man was Abu Sufyan, and twice had a clear shot at him but held back because of the instruction not to expose himself. He heard Abu Sufyan announce that their animals were dying, their pots and fires were being wrecked by the wind, and that Banu Qurayza had betrayed them, and that he was leaving whatever anyone else did. questions.question: Why did Abu Lubaba tie himself to a pillar in the mosque, and how did that end?
questions.reference_answer: Banu Qurayza, under siege, asked for him specifically because he was an old friend and ally of theirs. When he went in, the women and children were weeping and begging, his heart softened, and when they asked whether they should surrender he said yes but also drew his hand across his throat to indicate what awaited them. He said that before his feet had even moved he realised he had betrayed Allah and His Messenger. He walked straight past the army and the Prophet to the mosque and tied himself to a pillar, vowing not to be released until Allah accepted his repentance and never to return to that place. When the Prophet heard, he said that had Abu Lubaba come to him he would have asked forgiveness for him, but since he had bound himself by a vow nothing could be done. He stayed tied there, probably over a week. One morning before Fajr the Prophet was laughing, and told Umm Salama that Abu Lubaba's repentance had been accepted. She ran to tell him, but he refused to be freed by anyone except the Prophet, who untied him with his own hands and then led the prayer.

questions.question: Why was Sa'd ibn Mu'adh the one who decided the fate of Banu Qurayza, and what did he rule?
questions.reference_answer: When the tribe finally agreed to surrender, the Aws, who had been their allies since before Islam, pressed the Prophet for the same leniency shown to earlier Jewish tribes. Rather than impose his own decision he asked whether they would be satisfied if one of their own men judged, and when they agreed he named their leader Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. Sa'd was carried over on a mule from the hospital tent of Rufayda, still bandaged and bleeding from his wound. On the way his own people kept urging him to be merciful, and one said he had only been chosen because he would be lenient; he answered that this was the moment for Sa'd not to care about the criticism of any critic where Allah and His Messenger were concerned. He first made both the Aws and the Prophet commit to accepting the verdict without argument, then gave it instantly: the men to be executed, the property distributed, the women and children taken captive. The Prophet told him he had judged with the decree of Allah from above the seven heavens.

questions.question: Zaynab bint Muhammad's husband stayed a pagan for years after she became Muslim. What finally brought him to Islam?
questions.reference_answer: Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi was captured a second time when Zayd ibn Haritha intercepted a Quraysh caravan he was travelling with. At Fajr the next morning Zaynab called out from the women's side of the mosque that she had granted him her protection, which took even the Prophet by surprise; he confirmed afterwards that the least of the Muslims can grant protection and that all Muslims are bound by it. The Prophet then asked the Ansar who held the captured goods to return his share if they were willing. They agreed but suggested he accept Islam first, and he refused, saying it would be an evil thing to change his faith and betray a trust for the sake of money. He carried the wealth back to Mecca, returned every single deposit to its owner, publicly asked whether anyone was still owed anything, and only then declared the shahada in front of the Quraysh, so that nobody could say he had converted for money or safety. He then returned to Medina and was reunited with Zaynab.

questions.question: What did the Prophet do on the journey towards Mecca in the sixth year to convince the Quraysh he was not coming to fight?
questions.reference_answer: He deliberately timed his departure for the first of Dhul Qa'dah, the day the sacred months begin, when fighting is forbidden and the Quraysh had never in their history barred anyone from the Kaaba. He entered ihram at Dhul Hulayfa and consecrated a large number of sacrificial animals, seventy camels in one report, marked and garlanded so that everyone could see they were dedicated to Allah and the poor of Mecca. Unlike his other expeditions, where he would leave in the opposite direction to disguise his target, he travelled straight down the road to Mecca to show he had nothing hidden. The companions carried weapons on the baggage animals but did not wear them, since they were in ihram. He also sent Busr ibn Safwan al-Khuzai, an unknown Muslim from a neutral tribe, ahead to Mecca to find out how the Quraysh were reacting.

questions.question: The chief of Thaqif came to negotiate on behalf of the Quraysh and went home saying something completely different from what he arrived believing. What changed his mind?
questions.reference_answer: Urwa ibn Mas'ud arrived contemptuous, telling the Prophet that the mixed rabble around him would scatter at the first sign of battle. What he then saw over the next hour overturned that. Abu Bakr, of all people, snapped and hurled an extraordinarily vulgar curse at the idol Allat, whose guardian Urwa was. His own nephew Mughira, standing armed by the Prophet, beat his hand away from the Prophet's beard and threatened to cut it off. And he watched the companions compete for the Prophet's spittle and wudu water and refuse even to look him in the face. He went back and told the Quraysh that although he had entered the courts of Caesar, Khosrow and the Negus, he had never seen any king revered the way Muhammad was revered by his companions, that he had taken their measure and if the Quraysh wanted the sword they would get it, and that this was a man who had come honouring the sanctuary with sacrificial animals and was being turned away. The Quraysh were furious, said they wished anyone but him had said it, and insisted he would not enter Mecca that year.

questions.question: Why was Uthman the one sent into Mecca to negotiate, and what happened to him there?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet first chose Umar, because of his strength and nerve. Umar did not refuse but pointed out that his enmity with the Quraysh was notorious and that his clan, Banu Adi, had nobody left who could protect him, so the mission would fail; he suggested Uthman instead, who was of Banu Umayya, closely related to the Quraysh leadership and to Abu Sufyan personally. When Uthman reached the Baldah road the men blocking it mocked him and turned him back, but his older cousin Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-As put him on his own horse and personally sponsored his safe entry. Uthman met Abu Sufyan and the other leaders, all of whom refused to let the Muslims in that year, and he also sought out the persecuted converts still trapped in Mecca to tell them relief was coming. The talks dragged on far longer than anyone expected, and with no news for most of a day the camp convinced itself he had been killed, which is what led to the pledge under the tree.

questions.question: What became of the Muslims who escaped Mecca after the truce but were refused shelter in Medina?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Basir was the first to arrive and, when two men came to collect him under the terms of the agreement, the Prophet handed him back, telling him he would not be treacherous and that Allah would make a way out for him. On the road Abu Basir flattered one of his escorts into handing over his sword, killed him on the spot, and the other fled back to Medina. Abu Basir returned too, but the Prophet would not address him directly, remarking only that he was a kindler of war who would set off a conflict if he had anyone to help him, which Abu Basir understood as a signal to leave. He set up a camp on the coast near Mecca, Abu Jandal joined him, word spread, and around eighty men gathered there and began raiding Quraysh caravans. Within about a year and a half the Quraysh were desperate enough to send a delegation begging the Prophet to take these men into Medina after all. He sent for them; Abu Basir himself died of illness before he could make the journey, but the rest came.

questions.question: The agreement struck outside Mecca felt like a humiliation to the companions at the time. Why is it counted as such a great success in hindsight?
questions.reference_answer: Because the peace it created did what fighting could not. For the first time Muslims and pagans across Arabia could travel, trade and talk without fear of bloodshed, so the message spread by persuasion and conversions surged. Al-Zuhri said there had been no victory in Islam greater than it, since once people mixed and heard about Islam every intelligent person who heard it entered it. Ibn Hisham backed that up with numbers: 1,400 men gave the pledge under the tree, and two years later 10,000 marched on Mecca, so the difference must have converted in between. With the Quraysh neutralised the Prophet could also turn to the remaining threat at Khaybar and, for the first time, begin writing to foreign rulers as the head of an independent political entity. And without the treaty there would have been no legal basis for the later conquest of Mecca.

questions.question: Khaybar was a cluster of heavily built fortresses. How did the Muslims manage to take it?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet marched with around 1,600 to 1,700 men, camped away from Khaybar overnight and moved before dawn so as to arrive unannounced; the farmers coming out with their tools ran back shouting that Muhammad and his army had come. The defenders sealed themselves into their separate fortresses, and that turned out to be their undoing, because the strongholds were scattered and could not support one another, so each faced the whole army alone. The Muslims took them one at a time. Na'im held out about ten days, and Mahmud ibn Maslama was killed there by a log dropped from the wall. The Prophet then announced he would give the banner to a man loved by Allah and His Messenger, cured Ali's eyes and sent him forward; Ali killed the champion Mirhab and the fortress fell, followed by al-Sa'b, whose stores of grain fed the starving army. When only the last great fortress remained, its people negotiated rather than be taken, agreeing to hand over half their produce, bear all the costs themselves, and accept that the Muslims could cancel the arrangement whenever they wished.

questions.question: Safiyya lost her father, her brother and her husband to the Muslims. How did she end up married to the Prophet?
questions.reference_answer: As one of the Banu Nadir at Khaybar she was taken as part of the spoils and allotted to Dihya al-Kalbi, but companions objected that the daughter of Huyayy was too high in status for that, so the Prophet paid Dihya her price and took her himself. Nobody knew at first whether she was a concubine or a wife, until he knelt so she could mount his camel and then covered her with his cloak, which was the covering reserved for his wives. He tested her by telling her plainly that her father had been the most openly hostile of all his enemies until Allah caused his death; she answered from the Quran that no soul carries another's burden. He then gave her the choice of accepting Islam and staying with him or keeping her faith and being freed to return to her people, and she said she had already inclined to Islam before he asked, and that Allah and His Messenger were dearer to her than freedom and her own people. He freed her and married her, making her freedom her dowry.

questions.question: What did the Persian emperor do when Muhammad's letter was delivered to him?
questions.reference_answer: Khosrow Aparviz, the Sassanid emperor, was an arrogant man; he scoffed at the letter, mocked the messenger who brought it, and tore the letter up in front of him. When word of this got back to the Prophet, he said that just as Khosrow had torn up his letter, Allah would tear apart his kingdom. The letter itself had been sent via the ruler of Bahrain and carried the same phrase used to other rulers: accept Islam and you will be safe, otherwise the sin of the Magians would be on him.

questions.question: When Amr ibn al-As came to accept Islam he hesitated at the last moment. What was worrying him, and how was he reassured?
questions.reference_answer: As the Prophet stretched out his hand, Amr held back and said he had a condition first: that everything he had done in the past be wiped clean and never brought up again. The Prophet told him that Islam erases whatever came before it, and so does migration, and so does Hajj. Amr had just migrated, so his slate was already clear.

questions.question: Who was the Muslim messenger whose killing prompted the campaign to Mu'tah, and who was responsible?
questions.reference_answer: The envoy was al-Harith ibn Umair al-Azdi, sent north with a letter for the Romans. He was seized by the Ghassanids, the Christian Arab vassals of Rome, and brought before their chieftain Sharhabil ibn Amr. Although al-Harith identified himself as an ambassador, Sharhabil mocked him, tied him up, tortured him and killed him with his own hands. Killing a diplomat this way was an unmistakable declaration of war, and al-Waqidi gives this as the main reason for the expedition.

supporting_quotes.quote: revenge for the killing of Al-Harith ibn Umair Al-Azdi, who is the messenger of the messenger of the Prophet ﷺ
and Sharahbil mocked him tied him up tortured him brutally and with his own hands killed him

questions.question: Amr ibn al-As once led the morning prayer on a bitterly cold expedition without performing the full washing that was required of him. How did the Prophet react when his men complained about it?
questions.reference_answer: Amr woke up needing a ritual bath during the winter campaign against Quda'ah, but feared that stripping and bathing in the desert cold would kill him, so he did dry ablution instead and led Fajr. His men complained to the Prophet that their commander had led them while in that state. When the Prophet asked him about it, Amr explained that he had recalled the verse forbidding killing oneself. The Prophet simply laughed at the explanation and did not rebuke him at all.

supporting_quotes.quote: And I was worried that if I took a bath, I would end up killing myself. So therefore I did tayammum, and I didn't take a bath.
He laughed at my explanation, and didn't say anything to rebuke me.

questions.question: How did Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah try to get his warning to Mecca without it being discovered?
questions.reference_answer: Hatib picked an obscure, non-Muslim woman who was travelling back to Mecca, paid her money to carry a sealed letter, and deliberately did not tell her what was in it. She untied her hair and hid the folded letter inside her braids, where nobody would think to look. It would never have been found had Jibril not told the Prophet, who sent Ali and Zubayr to intercept her caravan outside Medina.

supporting_quotes.quote: And so she took this letter and folded it up and took, untied her hair and put it in the middle of her hair. And then through the braids, she tied the letter inside the braids of her hair.

questions.question: Who ended up holding the keys to the Kaaba after Mecca was taken?
questions.reference_answer: Ali asked the Prophet to give the custodianship of the Kaaba to Banu Hashim so that it would sit alongside the job of watering the pilgrims. The Prophet did not answer him; instead he called for Uthman ibn Talha of Banu Abd al-Dar, the traditional key-holder, and handed the keys back to him, saying this was a day of keeping trusts and giving people their due. Since then the key has stayed with Uthman ibn Talha's descendants.

supporting_quotes.quote: Go ahead and take your keys, Ya Uthman. Today is the day of Al-Wafa' wa Al-Birr, fulfilling the promises and giving back what is due.

questions.question: Where did the Prophet actually live during the time he spent in Mecca after the conquest?
questions.reference_answer: He had no house left in Mecca. Ali suggested he return to Abu Talib's old house, but the Prophet pointed out that Aqeel had sold off the property; Abu Talib had died a pagan, so his non-Muslim sons Talib and Aqeel inherited it and Ali and Ja'far got nothing. So the Prophet pitched a tent instead, in the small valley of al-Hujun a few minutes' walk from the Kaaba, and stayed there for the nineteen days he remained in the city. Al-Hujun was where the Quraysh had once gathered to sign the boycott document against him.

supporting_quotes.quote: And did Aqeel leave any property for us to live in?
He sets up a tent to live in for the next 19 days. And the place that he chooses is the famous mini valley close to the Kaaba

questions.question: Before the Byzantine emperor would have Muhammad's letter read out, he first interrogated a Meccan trader about him. How did he make sure he was getting honest answers, and what did he conclude?
questions.reference_answer: Heraclius was in Jerusalem when the letter arrived via Basra, and he summoned a group of Arab traders, asking which of them was closest in kinship to the man claiming prophethood. Abu Sufyan was the only Qurayshi, so he was seated in front while the others were placed behind him and told to signal if he lied. Knowing he would be exposed, Abu Sufyan answered truthfully about the Prophet's noble lineage, his honesty, that the poor were the ones following him, that his followers kept increasing and never left the faith. Heraclius then explained why each answer pointed to genuine prophethood and said that if it were all true, the man would one day rule the very ground beneath his feet.

questions.question: Hamza's orphaned daughter ran after the Muslims as they were leaving Mecca. Three men each argued that she was theirs to raise. Who were they, and how was it settled?
questions.reference_answer: The girl was Umara bint Hamza, whose mother Salma bint Umays had stayed behind in Mecca. Ali took her by the hand and gave her to Fatima, saying she was their orphan to care for. Zayd ibn Haritha then claimed her because the Prophet had made him and Hamza brothers, making her his niece. Ja'far claimed her both as a cousin and because his wife Asma bint Umays was the girl's maternal aunt. The argument got heated, so the Prophet praised each of the three in turn to soften the blow, then awarded custody to Ja'far on the principle that a maternal aunt takes the place of the mother.

questions.question: What finally convinced Khalid ibn al-Walid to become Muslim, and what happened when he told people in Mecca?
questions.reference_answer: Khalid said that in every battle he fought against Muhammad he felt something supernatural turning him away, and that after being outmanoeuvred at Hudaybiyyah he realised the man was protected and would win. He considered fleeing to Abyssinia or to Rome but rejected both. The decisive push came when the Prophet asked after him during the make-up Umrah and his brother al-Walid, who had accepted Islam as a prisoner at Badr, wrote urging him not to waste any more time. When Khalid sounded out Safwan ibn Umayyah, Safwan refused outright; when he told Ikrimah, Ikrimah panicked and called in the Quraysh leaders, and by one account swords were drawn on him. He slipped out of Mecca that night with Uthman ibn Talha and met Amr ibn al-As on the road, all three heading to the Prophet.

questions.question: Before the army set out for Mu'tah the Prophet named a whole succession of leaders. Who were they, and what became of each one?
questions.reference_answer: This was the only expedition where the Prophet named three commanders in advance: Zayd ibn Haritha, then Ja'far if Zayd was killed, then Abdullah ibn Rawaha if Ja'far was killed, with one narration adding that the Muslims should then choose someone themselves. All three died. Zayd charged in holding the banner and was surrounded and killed. Ja'far fought until his horse was hamstrung, then held the flag with one hand until his right hand was cut off, caught it with his left, and when that too was severed clutched it between his stumps before a Roman soldier cut him down; Ibn Umar later counted over ninety wounds on his body. Ibn Rawaha hesitated, recited poetry urging his own soul forward, then charged in and was killed. In Medina the Prophet announced all three deaths, weeping, before any messenger arrived.

questions.question: With all its commanders dead, how did the Muslim army at Mu'tah avoid being wiped out?
questions.reference_answer: Khalid ibn al-Walid, chosen on the spot, judged that no real victory was possible and that saving the army was the only win available. He launched a short sharp attack to halt the Roman advance, using archers positioned to check them, and fought so hard in the melee that nine swords broke in his hand. By nightfall the two armies had separated beyond bow range and the martyrs could be buried. The next day, by one later account, he created the impression that reinforcements were arriving from Medina, which made the Romans pause long enough for the Muslims to withdraw safely. Out of roughly three thousand men only around fifteen to twenty were lost.

questions.question: How were the men who came back from Mu'tah received in Medina?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet welcomed them, but within days a smear campaign started against those who had returned: they were taunted as men who had fled the path of Allah. When the Prophet noticed Salama was missing from the mosque, his wife explained that he would not leave the house because people mocked him every time he stepped out. The Prophet addressed the whole mosque and said they were not runaways but qurrar, meaning those who would come back and fight again, changing a single letter to turn the insult into praise. The lecture draws the lesson that martyrdom is a genuine aim but reckless, pointless death is not part of the religion.

supporting_quotes.quote: Ya Rasulullah, he has not come out of his house. Because every time he exits, people make fun of him.

questions.question: On the raid against Quda'ah, reinforcements turned up under a far more senior companion. Who ended up commanding the combined force, and how was the disagreement resolved?
questions.reference_answer: Amr ibn al-As had been sent with 300 men, travelled only by night and banned campfires so the enemy would not see how few they were. Realising 300 was not enough, he asked for reinforcements, and the Prophet sent 200 more, including Abu Bakr and Umar, under Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, telling Abu Ubaydah to make sure the two of them agreed. When Abu Ubaydah stepped forward to lead the prayer, Amr objected that Abu Ubaydah commanded only the reinforcements while he commanded the army, and tension flared. Abu Ubaydah, far senior in Islam, gave way rather than disobey the Prophet's instruction to stay united, so Amr led both the prayer and the army. The subsequent surprise attack scattered Quda'ah and brought considerable spoils with almost no casualties.

questions.question: Abu Sufyan travelled to Medina to try to patch things up after his allies broke the truce. Who did he turn to, and what did he get out of the trip?
questions.reference_answer: The Quraysh had refused the ultimatum after the Khuza'ah massacre, so Abu Sufyan went to Medina himself to reaffirm the Hudaybiyyah treaty. The Prophet gave him no answer at all. Abu Bakr flatly said he could not help; Umar openly mocked the idea of interceding for him; Ali told him nobody would try to change the Prophet's mind once it was made up, and Fatima refused to let her five-year-old son Hasan grant protection on the Quraysh's behalf. On Ali's advice he stood up in the mosque and publicly asked anyone to grant him protection, which nobody did. He even visited his daughter Umm Habiba, who pulled the Prophet's bedding away so he could not sit on it. He went home with nothing, and the Quraysh told him he had been made a fool of.

questions.question: What reason did Hatib give for warning the Quraysh, and why was he not executed for it?
questions.reference_answer: Confronted with the intercepted letter, Hatib admitted writing it but insisted he had not left his faith or preferred disbelief; he said he knew for certain Allah would fulfil his promise and that the letter could not harm the Prophet. His motive was that, unlike the other emigrants, he was an outsider with no clan in Mecca to shield his family and property, so he wanted to earn a favour with the Quraysh that would protect them. Umar twice asked permission to kill him, first as an apostate and then as a spy. The Prophet said Hatib had told the truth and that nobody should speak ill of him, and reminded Umar that he had fought at Badr and that Allah may well have forgiven the people of Badr entirely. Umar wept, and Surah al-Mumtahina was revealed about the incident.

questions.question: How did Abu Sufyan end up inside the Muslim camp on the eve of the conquest, and what finally made him accept Islam?
questions.reference_answer: With the army camped at Marr al-Zahran and ten thousand fires lit on the Prophet's orders, al-Abbas, a very recent convert, rode out on the Prophet's own mule hoping to prevent bloodshed. In the dark he came across Abu Sufyan out scouting with Budayl and Hakim, who could not imagine the fires belonged to the Muslims. Abbas told him whose army it was and warned that he would be executed if Mecca were taken by force, then rode him back through the camp; the Prophet's mule meant nobody challenged them. Umar recognised him and demanded his execution, but Abbas invoked the protection he had granted. The Prophet postponed the meeting to the morning, and Abbas argued with Abu Sufyan all night. In the morning Abu Sufyan praised the Prophet's kindness and conceded that if other gods existed they would have helped him by now, accepting there is no god but Allah; he still hesitated over the messengership until Abbas pressed him hard, and he said the testimony reluctantly.

questions.question: A short list of people in Mecca were excluded from the general pardon. Who was on it, and what actually happened to them?
questions.reference_answer: The sources differ, giving somewhere between six and nine names out of a city of perhaps two thousand. They included Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Abdullah ibn Khatal, Miqyas ibn Subaba, Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh, two singing slave women named Fartana and Sara, and figures such as Habbar ibn al-Aswad and Huwayrith ibn Nuqaydh, plus Wahshi, the killer of Hamza. In the event more than half were spared. Ibn Khatal clung to the covering of the Kaaba and was still executed on the Prophet's order, as was Miqyas. Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh was brought by his foster brother Uthman and pardoned after a long silence, and later became governor of Egypt. Of the two women Fartana was executed and Sara forgiven. Ikrimah fled by sea, was caught in a storm, and came back to accept Islam; Wahshi was forgiven but asked to keep out of the Prophet's sight.

questions.question: Some of the Ansar were afraid the Prophet would settle back in Mecca now that it was his again. How did that come to light, and what did he say to them?
questions.reference_answer: After taking the pledge from the men and women of Quraysh, the Ansar started muttering among themselves that now he was home among his own relatives he had gone soft on them and would forget the people of Medina. Jibril told the Prophet exactly what had been said, but he still went to them and asked them directly whether they had said it, which the lecture presents as a lesson in verifying before judging, and as a way of heading off a bigger rift. They admitted it. He answered that he was the servant and messenger of Allah, that he had emigrated to them, and reminded them of the promise made at Aqaba: my life is your life and my death is your death. The Ansar wept and apologised, and he accepted their excuse.

questions.question: Khalid ibn al-Walid's mission to the Banu Jadhimah ended badly. What went wrong, and what did the Prophet do about it?
questions.reference_answer: Khalid was sent out from Mecca on a series of errands, one of which was to invite the Banu Jadhimah to Islam. He had an old blood feud with that tribe, so when they saw him approaching with an army some of them drew weapons, and Khalid, a brand-new Muslim who did not know the rules, responded in the old pre-Islamic way. To make it worse, when the rest of the tribe tried to submit they used the word for having become Sabians rather than saying they had accepted Islam, which Khalid did not understand. He ended up killing people who should not have been killed. Senior companions including Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Ibn Umar refused his order to attack, and he cursed Ibn Awf for it. When the news reached Medina, the Prophet faced the Kaaba, raised his hands and declared himself free of what Khalid had done, then sent Ali with money to pay blood compensation and apologise to the families. He also told Khalid not to insult his companions.

questions.question: Before marching against Hawazin the Prophet needed more armour than he had. Where did he get it, and on what terms?
questions.reference_answer: He turned to the Meccans who had stayed on after the conquest, including men who were not yet Muslim. He asked Safwan ibn Umayyah, who was still in his trial period as a non-Muslim, for the armour he had stockpiled. Safwan asked whether it was being confiscated or borrowed, and the Prophet answered that it was a loan he guaranteed to repay, meaning that anything damaged would be compensated. He borrowed armour and money from others as well, and everything borrowed was later returned.

questions.question: The tribes that fought the Muslims at Hunayn brought their wives, children and herds with them to the battlefield. Did anyone in their own camp object to that?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. Durayd ibn as-Simma, an elderly blind veteran of Thaqif who had been brought along for his blessing and counsel, heard babies crying and animals in the camp and demanded to know who had ordered it. The young chief Malik ibn Awf said he wanted every man fighting with his family and property behind him so he would fight harder. Durayd told him that women, children and flocks win nothing, only men with swords do, and pointed out that the sub-tribes he trusted most had refused to come at all. He advised sending the families back to the fortress. Malik mocked him as senile and, when the people began to be persuaded, threatened to kill himself with his own sword in front of them if they did not obey, so the families stayed.

questions.question: Why did the siege of Ta'if end without the city ever being taken?
questions.reference_answer: Ta'if was walled, stocked with about a year of supplies, had its own water, and had devices for pouring burning oil from the walls. The Muslims had prepared by sending men to the tribe of Jurash to learn to build catapults, battering rams and a large covering shield, and used a catapult for the first time there, but the covering shield failed when burning oil got through and the defenders killed men with arrows. In desperation some Muslims began burning the crops outside the walls; when the people of Ta'if begged them to stop, the Prophet forbade any more burning and announced protection for anyone who came over and freedom for any slave who defected. After further losses demoralised the army the Prophet proposed leaving a second time and the companions agreed. The siege probably lasted under two weeks, and as he left he prayed for Thaqif's guidance rather than against them.

questions.question: Someone accused the Prophet to his face of being unfair when the spoils from Hunayn were handed out. What became of him?
questions.reference_answer: A man with a scraggly beard and a large forehead addressed the Prophet by his first name and told him to be fair in the distribution. The Prophet answered, who will be just if I am not just, and asked whether the man would refuse to trust him when the One in the heavens trusted him. Umar wanted to execute him, but the Prophet refused, saying people must not be able to say that he kills his own companions. He then warned that from this man's type would come people whose recitation would not pass their throats, whose prayer and worship would look better than everyone else's, yet who would pass out of Islam like an arrow passing through its target. The lecture treats this man as the prototype of the Kharijite mentality.

questions.question: What did the Prophet give Ka'b ibn Zuhayr after hearing him recite his poem, and what did he ask of him afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet was so moved by the poem that he took off his own cloak and gave it to Ka'b. He also told him that since he had harmed the Ansar with his tongue in the past, he should now praise them, and Ka'b duly composed verses in their honour. Ka'b died a Muslim and became a celebrated poet; Umar ibn al-Khattab used to quote him constantly.

questions.question: Adi ibn Hatim was a Christian chieftain who fled north rather than face the Muslims. What eventually brought him round?
questions.reference_answer: His sister was taken prisoner when Ali's expedition subdued Tayy, and the Prophet freed her and gave her money and transport out of respect for her father Hatim al-Ta'i. She went to Adi and urged him to go, arguing that the man was either a prophet, in which case he should believe early, or a king, in which case he should win his favour. When Adi came and refused Islam three times on the grounds that he already had a religion, the Prophet told him he knew Adi's religion better than Adi did, and showed it by pointing out that Adi took a quarter of his people's income although his own faith forbade it. Adi was then struck by his humility, stopping in the road for an old woman with a child and giving Adi the only mat in the house while he sat on the ground. Finally the Prophet answered Adi's real objection, the weakness and poverty of the Muslims, by predicting security so complete that a woman would travel alone to Mecca, the treasures of Kisra distributed among them, and a time when a man would look in vain for anyone to accept his charity. Adi accepted Islam and later said he had personally seen two of the three come true.

questions.question: Qatadah was hit in the eye by an arrow while shielding the Prophet at Uhud. What happened to that eye?
questions.reference_answer: The eye came out of its socket. The Prophet made a special supplication for him, asking Allah to restore the eye better than it had been, since Qatadah had put his own face in front of the Prophet's. The eye healed immediately, and Qatadah said it remained the sharper of his two eyes for the rest of his life.

questions.question: What happened to the young chief who led the attack on the Muslims at Hunayn?
questions.reference_answer: Malik ibn Awf, the man who had insisted on bringing the families to the battlefield and who planned the ambush, escaped into Ta'if. After his tribe surrendered and accepted Islam, the Prophet sent word that if Malik came to him as a Muslim he would get his family and property back and be given a hundred camels on top. Having lost his tribe, family and wealth, Malik came, accepted Islam, and was reinstated as chieftain of his own people. He then composed verses saying that only a true prophet, not a king, would have been so generous.

questions.question: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari came asking for mounts so his people could join the northern campaign, and was turned away with an oath. How did that end?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet was in an angry mood over something unrelated, had nothing to give, and swore he would not give Abu Musa anything to ride on, so Abu Musa went back to his people distressed and assuming he had done something wrong. Shortly afterwards Bilal came to call him back, and the Prophet handed him six camels he had just purchased from Sa'd. Abu Musa felt uneasy about accepting them after the oath and came back to clarify; it was explained that the Prophet had simply had nothing at the time, and that an oath said in that sense is not the kind of binding oath a person is held to.

questions.question: Was there actually a Byzantine army coming for Medina, or was there some other reason for marching all the way north in the worst of the summer?
questions.reference_answer: The lecture works through the reasons the classical sources give and finds none of them convincing. The report that Jews goaded the Prophet into going to Syria is dismissed outright, since no Jews remained in the area, the Prophet would not have been tricked so crudely, and the verse cited for it is Makkan. The report that forty thousand Roman troops were being sent down is not established and makes little sense, since Rome had no interest in the Arabs and could have moved against them at any point in previous centuries. A Ghassanid threat has slightly more basis, since Umar's first fear on hearing alarming news was that the Ghassanid king had attacked, but that does not explain why the march was launched in the fiercest heat and at harvest time rather than in winter. The conclusion drawn is that there was no immediate threat and the expedition was a direct command from Allah to test the believers, with support taken from Surat At-Tawbah 123.

questions.notes: The same conclusion (Tabuk as a divine test) is restated briefly in lectures 92 and 93, but the survey and rejection of the proposed causes is only in 87.

questions.question: Ka'b ibn Malik was a sincere believer with no excuse at all. How did he end up not going to Tabuk?
questions.reference_answer: He simply kept putting it off. He was strong and unusually well off, owning two riding camels, so illness and poverty did not apply to him, but his fruit was ripening and the shade was pleasant and he admits his heart was more inclined to those than to the march. During the roughly ten days of preparation he went out every day meaning to get ready and came back each evening having done nothing. When the army left he told himself he would sort himself out and catch up in a day or two, and two more days passed with nothing done, by which point it was too late to overtake them. Walking around Medina afterwards he was grieved to find that the only men left were the infirm and those known for hypocrisy. questions.question: While Ka'b ibn Malik was being shunned in Medina, a foreign king tried to lure him away. What did Ka'b do about it?
questions.reference_answer: A Nabataean trader selling grain in the market sought Ka'b out and handed him a letter from the king of Ghassan, saying that he had heard Ka'b's companion had treated him coldly, that Allah would not have him live somewhere he was humiliated and his rights lost, and inviting him to come and be consoled. Ka'b recognised at once that this was another part of the test he was undergoing, and took the letter straight to his oven and burned it so that he could not second-guess himself.

questions.question: What happened on the day Ka'b ibn Malik learned that his repentance had been accepted?
questions.reference_answer: By then he was so isolated that he prayed Fajr alone on his own roof. A man climbed the mountain outside the mosque and shouted the good news to him from the top, and Ka'b fell straight into prostration. A horseman also galloped out to tell him in person, and Ka'b, who had given away all his cash during the boycott, gave the man the only garment he was wearing and had to borrow a robe from a neighbour to go out. People received him in batches in the mosque, and Talha ibn Ubaydullah stood up and rushed over to shake his hand, the only one of the Muhajirun to do so, a gesture Ka'b never forgot. The Prophet's face shone like the full moon and he told Ka'b to rejoice at the best day since his mother bore him; Ka'b asked whether the forgiveness was from him or from Allah, and was told it was from Allah. Ka'b then offered to give away all his remaining property and was told to keep some, so he kept his share of Khaybar, and he vowed never to tell a lie again as long as he lived.

questions.question: Why was a newly built mosque near Quba torn down and burned on the Prophet's orders?
questions.reference_answer: The hypocrites built it while the Prophet was raising funds for Tabuk, giving nothing to the campaign but finding money for their own building, and it stood within walking distance of Quba with Abdullah ibn Ubayy as its intended leader. Behind it was Abu Amir al-Rahib, the Medinan turned Christian ascetic who had failed at Uhud, fled to Rome and got access to the Caesar, and who wrote to Ibn Ubayy asking him to establish a base in Medina for an insurrection. They invited the Prophet to pray two units in it to open it, claiming it was for the weak and the elderly and for rainy days; he did not refuse outright but said he was busy preparing to travel and would see when he returned, and he never prayed there. On the way back Jibril brought Surat At-Tawbah 107 to 108, which describes the building as raised for harm, for disbelief, to divide the believers and as an outpost for one already at war with Allah and His Messenger, and forbids the Prophet from ever standing in it. He then sent Ammar ibn Yasir and others to destroy and burn it.
