questions.question: Abu Dharr set out after the army on foot when his camel failed him. What did the Prophet say about him then, and did it come true?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Dharr's camel was either sick or had not been returned to him, so he loaded the camel's baggage onto his own back and walked for days until the army saw a lone figure trudging towards them. The Prophet said, let it be Abu Dharr, and when it was, he said that Allah have mercy on Abu Dharr, he walks alone, he will die alone and he will be resurrected alone. Years later, after his austere views on wealth had caused so many complaints that Uthman asked him to leave Medina, Abu Dharr went to live in the desert with only his wife and an old servant. On his deathbed he consoled his weeping wife with a prophecy that one of that gathering would die in the wilderness and a group of believers would pray over him, and told her to place his body beside the caravan road. A caravan that included Ibn Mas'ud and Ammar ibn Yasir came upon it; Ibn Mas'ud wept, recalling exactly what the Prophet had said, and they shrouded him from their own garments and prayed over him there.

questions.question: Ali was left behind in Medina when the army marched north, and the hypocrites taunted him for it. What did the Prophet say to him?
questions.reference_answer: Ali put on his armour and caught up with the army outside the city, asking whether he was being left with the women and children while the hypocrites mocked him as unfit to fight. The Prophet consoled him by asking whether he was not content that his position with him was like Harun's with Musa, except that there is no prophet after him. He added that the hypocrites were lying, and that he had left Ali specifically to take charge of his household. Command of the city itself had been given to Muhammad ibn Maslama.

questions.question: Heraclius sent a messenger down to the Prophet while the army was camped at Tabuk. What was that messenger told to watch for, and what did he report back?
questions.reference_answer: Heraclius had first gathered his patriarchs and priests behind a locked door and suggested following the Prophet or at least paying rather than fighting; when they rushed the door in outrage he told them it had only been a test of their firmness. He then had an Arabic-speaking man of the tribe of Tanukh brought to him and told him to memorise three things: whether the Prophet mentioned the earlier letters, whether he said anything about night or darkness on reading the new one, and whether there was something startling on his back. All three came about. Before opening the letter the Prophet invited the man to Islam and then said that Kisra and the Najashi's successor had torn up his letters so their kingdoms would be torn up, while Heraclius had kept his so his rule would be preserved. Mu'awiyah read the letter aloud, which asked where Hell could be if Paradise is as wide as the heavens and the earth, and the Prophet answered, where does the night go when the day comes. The Prophet apologised for having no gift while travelling and Uthman gave the man a garment, and as the messenger was leaving the Prophet called him back and drew his garment aside to show him the seal between his shoulder blades.

questions.question: On the way home the army passed the old rock-cut dwellings of Thamud. What instructions did the Prophet give there?
questions.reference_answer: Some of the men went in to look around, and he had them called back with the announcement that prayer was gathering. He asked why they would want to enter upon a people on whom Allah's anger had descended, and when they said they found the place amazing he told them that something far more amazing was among them, a man informing them of what has happened and what will happen. He said not to enter the dwellings of people who wronged themselves and were punished unless one enters weeping, and he covered his face with his turban and hurried his mount through the valley without stopping. He forbade them from drinking the water they had drawn from the wells there, telling them to give it and the dough kneaded with it to the animals. He also warned them not to demand miracles, recalling how the people of Salih were given the she-camel and hamstrung it anyway, and ordered that nobody leave the tents at night alone; two who disobeyed came to harm.

questions.question: A companion died during the stay at Tabuk and the Prophet climbed into the grave to bury him himself. Who was he?
questions.reference_answer: Abdullah Dhul Bijadain, whose nickname means the man of the two coarse cloths, because when he became Muslim his tribe stripped him of everything and he left with a single cheap garment which he tore in two out of embarrassment so it would look like two. questions.question: When the leader of the hypocrites of Medina died, did the Prophet pray over him?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. Abdullah ibn Ubayy asked for the Prophet to visit him on his deathbed and to seek forgiveness for him. Umar objected that he was an enemy of Allah, and the Prophet answered that he hoped a thousand of the man's people would embrace Islam through the gesture. He gave his own shirt to be used as a shroud, and when the body was brought to the mosque and Umar took hold of his garment, listing the man's crimes and reminding him that Allah had forbidden seeking forgiveness for the hypocrites, the Prophet replied that Allah had given him a choice in the matter, quoting the verse that says whether he seeks forgiveness for them or not, seventy times will not avail them, and said that if he knew seventy-one would work he would do it. He prayed over him and, according to al-Tabari, even went down into the grave. It was only afterwards that Surat At-Tawbah 84 was revealed forbidding him to pray over any of them or to stand at their graves.

questions.question: A whole tribe of several hundred came to Medina to become Muslims and then needed provisions for the journey home. Who was told to supply them, and how did he manage it?
questions.reference_answer: This was the tribe of Muzaynah, about four hundred people. The Prophet told Umar ibn al-Khattab to give them what they needed for the return journey. Umar protested that he only had a single bag of dates at home, but when the Prophet repeated the order he agreed, went home, and found his room piled to the ceiling with dates. All four hundred filled their sacks, and the last man out reported that the pile looked untouched, exactly as it had been before they started.

questions.question: A tribal chief once turned up in Medina with a hired killer, meaning to have the Prophet stabbed during the audience. Why did the plan fall apart, and what became of the two men afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: Amir ibn Tufayl of Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'a arranged with Arbad ibn Qays that he would keep the Prophet talking and Arbad would strike on a signal. Amir first pressed for a private audience, which the Prophet refused unless he accepted Islam, and Arbad never moved despite three signals; afterwards Arbad explained that once inside he could see nothing but Amir, so he had no target. Amir then made three arrogant demands, including a share of power and a threat of war, and was refused, and the Prophet prayed that Allah suffice him against Amir while guiding his people. On the way home Amir was struck overnight by a spreading disease and, humiliated at where he was dying, rode off into the dark and was never seen again; Arbad reached his people, said something blasphemous about Allah, and the next day was incinerated along with his camel by lightning in front of everyone, which the books of tafsir connect to Surah ar-Ra'd 11-13.

questions.question: The most respected man in Ta'if became a Muslim after the siege and insisted on going back to preach to his own people, even after being warned not to. What happened to him, and what did the Prophet say when the news came?
questions.reference_answer: This was Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi, who accepted Islam on the road as the Muslims withdrew from Ta'if. The Prophet warned that his people might kill him; Urwa answered that they loved him more than their own daughters and would not even wake him if they found him asleep. Back home he announced his Islam, was cursed, and at dawn climbed onto his roof and gave the adhan, at which an arrow came out of the dark and fatally wounded him. Dying, he forbade his family to seek blood money or revenge, called his death a gift Allah had honoured him with, and asked to be buried with the martyrs of Hunayn; when the news reached the Prophet he said Urwa was to his people what the man of Surah Ya-Sin was to his.

questions.question: Who ended up killing the false prophet Musaylimah, and why did that particular man want to be the one to do it?

questions.question: What price did Musaylimah name for submitting to the Prophet, how was he answered, and what earlier dream did the Prophet say now made sense to him?
questions.reference_answer: Musaylimah came with the delegation of Banu Hanifa and made his condition that he be put in charge after the Prophet's death and be given a share in prophethood, the way Harun shared with Musa. The Prophet, who happened to be holding a branch, told him that he would not give him even that worthless stick, and that Allah would deal with him and humiliate him. He added that Musaylimah was the fulfilment of a dream he had been shown: he had seen himself wearing two gold bracelets, was troubled by them, was inspired to blow on them, and they broke off and flew away, which he interpreted as two liars who would arise after him, one from Yamama and one from San'a.

questions.question: Talk started going around Medina about Maria the Copt and a servant who had arrived with her from Egypt. What did the Prophet do about it, and how did the matter end?
questions.reference_answer: The servant was Ma'bur, said in some reports to be a distant relative of hers. The Prophet told Ali to take his sword and go to him. Ali asked whether he should go simply as one carrying out an order or as one who would look and listen for himself, and was told to go as one who investigates. He found Ma'bur, who panicked, and in the process his body was exposed, making it plain that he had been mutilated and could not possibly be the subject of the rumour, so Ali came back and reported this. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Hazm take Ali's question as evidence he was sent to frighten and interrogate rather than to execute, though others hold he was sent to carry out the killing.

questions.question: The Prophet's baby son died in the last year of his life. What did he say to the companions who were startled to see him in tears, and how did he respond when people linked the darkening of the sun that same day to his grief?
questions.reference_answer: Ibrahim died at around a year and a half. The Prophet went to Maria's house in al-Awali and held the child as he was dying, and his tears fell; when a companion exclaimed that even he wept, he answered that the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves but we say only what pleases our Lord, and that were it not for Allah's decree and the certainty that those who remain will follow those who have gone, the grief would have been far worse. A solar eclipse occurred within hours of the death, and word spread that the sun was mourning the Prophet's son. Rather than let the claim stand, he gathered the people and preached that the sun and the moon are two of Allah's signs which do not eclipse for anybody's birth or death, and that when people see an eclipse they should turn to remembrance of Allah and prayer.

questions.question: The Prophet once swore he would keep away from his wives for a month. How long did the separation actually last, and what did he say when this was pointed out to him?
questions.reference_answer: He had sworn an oath (ila) not to go near them for a month, and he came back on the twenty-ninth day. Aisha, who had been counting the days, told him that his oath was for a month and it was only the twenty-ninth. He answered that a month can also be twenty-nine days, which is where the fiqh point comes from that an oath of one month is fulfilled by either twenty-nine or thirty days.

questions.question: When Umar finally got in to see the Prophet during the trouble with his wives, what did he find inside the room, and what passed between the two of them?
questions.reference_answer: Umar had to ask three times before being let into the upper chamber where the Prophet had withdrawn. Inside he saw almost nothing: about a handful of barley, a half-tanned leather water bag and a chamber pot, with the Prophet lying on a fibre mat that had left its marks on his side. Umar first asked whether he had divorced his wives and was told no, only that he had made an oath to stay away for a month, at which Umar said Allahu Akbar. Then he broke down and asked why the Prophet did not pray for wealth for himself and the ummah when Allah had given so much to Persia and Rome, describing the mat's marks on his back. The Prophet sat up and asked whether Umar was in doubt, and whether he was not content that they should have the next world while those others were given this one for their enjoyment; Umar asked for forgiveness for what he had said.

questions.question: After Mecca was taken, why was the city left under a man who had only just accepted Islam rather than one of the senior emigrants?
questions.reference_answer: Attab ibn Asid, of Banu Abd Shams, a Meccan who converted at the conquest, was appointed governor. The senior Companions could not take the post because the Muhajirun were bound by the terms of their emigration: a muhajir was not permitted to go back and resettle in the town he had left, or his hijrah would be void. So only those who had never emigrated, that is the Meccan converts themselves, could remain in charge of the city.

questions.question: Why did the Prophet stay away from the pilgrimage in the ninth year and send Abu Bakr in his place, and what was proclaimed to the crowds that season?
questions.reference_answer: He refused to take part because pagans were still circling the Kaaba naked, and he said he would not perform Hajj until that was stopped. So he sent Abu Bakr at the head of about three hundred people with twenty-five sacrificial animals. A few hours after they left, the opening passage of Surah at-Tawbah was revealed and Ali was sent to catch up and recite it, since the Prophet insisted that only a member of his own household should annul his treaties. Ali, joined by Abu Hurayrah, made four proclamations: that no one enters Paradise but a believer, that no one may circle the Kaaba naked, that no idolater will perform the pilgrimage after that year, and that all open-ended treaties with the pagans would expire in four months. The ban on naked circumambulation was enforced that very year; the ban on pagans performing Hajj took effect the year after.

questions.question: How many animals did the Prophet slaughter with his own hands on the Day of Sacrifice during his pilgrimage, and was there anything behind the number?
questions.reference_answer: He slaughtered sixty-three camels himself, out of the hundred that Ali had brought up from Yemen, one for each year of his life. He then handed the remaining thirty-seven over to Ali to slaughter, making a hundred in all. He had a piece of meat taken from each animal and cooked together, then ate some of it and drank of the broth.

questions.question: During the Prophet's pilgrimage, the Meccans assumed he would stop short of Arafah. Why did they expect that, and what did he actually do?
questions.reference_answer: The Quraysh had invented an elitist practice for themselves: as the people of the sanctuary they refused to leave the boundary of the Haram during Hajj, and instead of standing at Arafah, which is sacred but lies outside the Haram, they would stop at al-Mash'ar al-Haram in Muzdalifah and leave Arafah to everyone else. When the Prophet ordered his tent pitched at Namirah, which is just outside Arafah, the newly Muslim Quraysh assumed he was going along with their custom. Instead he passed al-Mash'ar al-Haram, camped at Namirah, waited until the sun had passed its zenith, and then entered Arafah itself, where he prayed Dhuhr and Asr together and delivered his sermon.

questions.question: What did the Prophet do with the small amount of money left in the house in his last days?
questions.reference_answer: On the Sunday before he died he asked Aisha how much money he had; she gathered everything in the house and came up with seven silver dirhams. Holding them, he said what would he say to Allah if he met Him with these coins, and told her to give them to the poor. He kept asking whether she had done it every time he regained consciousness until she gave away all the money in the house. questions.question: In his final illness the Prophet insisted that Abu Bakr lead the congregation. Why did Aisha try to talk him out of it, and how did he answer her?
questions.reference_answer: He had tried seven times to stand and lead Isha and collapsed each time, so he told Aisha to have Abu Bakr lead the people. Aisha objected that her father was too soft-hearted and would break down weeping when he recited, so the people would not like it, but her real motives were that she did not want anyone to think Abu Bakr was pushing himself forward, and she feared that if the Prophet died people would forever associate Abu Bakr's leading of the prayer with his death. When her stalling failed she brought in Hafsa to press the same point. The Prophet saw through it, told them they were behaving like the women around Yusuf, and repeated that Allah and His Messenger would allow no one but Abu Bakr; when Abu Bakr could not be found at once and Umar started the prayer, he heard Umar's voice and sent for Abu Bakr again.

questions.question: Umar would not accept the news that the Prophet had died. What was he doing in the mosque, and what finally brought him round?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Bakr had seen the Prophet lift the curtain and smile at Fajr, assumed he was recovering, and went home for the first time in a week, which left Umar as the senior figure in the mosque when the news broke. In shock, Umar strode about as if brandishing a sword, shouting that hypocrites were spreading lies, threatening to behead anyone who said the Prophet had died, and insisting he had gone to his Lord as Musa did for forty days and would return. Abu Bakr galloped back, went straight to Aisha's house, uncovered the Prophet's face, kissed his forehead and said how beautiful he was in life and in death. Coming out, he told Umar to sit down, and when Umar only stared at him, Abu Bakr stood on a lower step of the pulpit and declared that whoever worshipped Muhammad should know that he had died, while whoever worshipped Allah should know that Allah is ever-living and never dies, and he recited Al Imran 144. At that Umar collapsed to the ground, saying it was as though he had never heard the verse before.

questions.question: Why was the enclosure eventually raised over the Prophet's grave given five sides instead of being left as a plain square?
questions.reference_answer: The chamber itself had been walled in with thick black blocks of the same kind used for the Kaaba, so a five-sided outer structure was built around it in the time of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz for two stated reasons: so that nobody praying in the mosque could face the grave squarely as if praying towards it, and so that recent converts would not look at a black cube in Medina and imagine there was a second Kaaba there.

questions.question: An Umayyad caliph had the apartments of the Prophet's wives pulled down to enlarge the mosque in Medina. What reasons are given for that decision, and did anyone in the city object?
questions.reference_answer: Al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik, around 90 AH, decided to extend the mosque in all four directions and to buy up the wives' apartments so that the grave would be enclosed within it. One explanation is simply that rulers like to leave their mark by building great mosques. The other, which the corpus finds more persuasive, is political: a decade after Karbala, Ali Zayn al-Abidin was back in Medina, deeply loved, and used to sit in the Prophet's house, which was his by inheritance, and even preach from there into the mosque, so removing the houses removed his platform. Senior scholars of Medina objected, foremost Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, but not on theological grounds about the grave; he wanted the houses left standing so that people could see for themselves how rough and simple the Prophet's living quarters had been and take the lesson to heart. He was overruled, and the young governor of Medina at the time, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, took part in the demolition himself.

questions.question: In his final illness the Prophet asked for something to write with and then let the matter drop. What actually happened in the room, and what do Sunni scholars say he had meant to write?
questions.reference_answer: On the Thursday before he died, as his pain worsened, he asked for writing material, saying he would write something after which they would never go astray. Umar said the Prophet was overcome by pain and that the Book of Allah was enough for them; others said to ask him what he wanted; voices rose in disagreement, and the Prophet told them to leave him, since it was not fitting for people to argue in his presence. Scholars from al-Khattabi and al-Maziri to al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar read Umar's stance as compassion and caution rather than defiance, arguing he saw something in the circumstances that turned the command into a request, or feared something being recorded that the ummah could not fulfil. As for the content, one view is that it was the three final instructions he later gave verbally; another, held by Sufyan ibn Uyayna and Ibn Taymiyyah, is that he meant to write in favour of Abu Bakr, based on an earlier Bukhari and Muslim report from the same illness in which he asked Aisha to call Abu Bakr and her brother so he could write a letter lest anyone claim leadership. Against the claim that he meant to name Ali, the strongest argument offered is that he lived nearly four more days, was visited by Ali and Fatima among others, and said nothing further about it, which would be impossible had the matter been that important.

questions.question: How did Abu Bakr actually come to be accepted as leader after the Prophet died, and what happened at the gathering of the Ansar where it was settled?
questions.reference_answer: Within hours of the death on Monday the Ansar drifted to their customary meeting place, the roofed shelter in the garden of Banu Sa'ida, and the conversation turned to who would take charge; the name that came up was Sa'd ibn Ubadah, the senior figure of the Khazraj, who was lying there wrapped up with a fever. Abu Bakr, Umar and Abu Ubaydah went over. An Ansari spoke first, arguing the Ansar's greater numbers and their record as the defenders of Islam. Umar had a speech ready but Abu Bakr pulled him down and spoke instead, opening by praising the Ansar with every hadith he could recall, then turning to Sa'd and reminding him that he too had heard the Prophet say that this affair of leadership belongs to Quraysh, and adding that the Arabs would not follow anyone else. Sa'd conceded, saying they had spoken the truth and that Quraysh were the leaders and the Ansar their helpers. Abu Bakr then took the hands of Umar and Abu Ubaydah and told the gathering to choose between those two; when an Ansari proposed one leader from each side and voices rose, Umar called on Abu Bakr to stretch out his hand and gave him the pledge himself, and the Muhajirun and Ansar followed. The general public pledge was taken in the mosque after Fajr the next day, before the Prophet had even been buried.

questions.question: What tipped off the Meccans that their returning caravan was in danger, and how quickly did they raise an army?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Sufyan, already nervous after the near-miss on the outbound journey, sent parties out to check whether he was being watched; at an abandoned camp he broke open camel dung and found Madinan date seeds, confirming that Muslim scouts had been following him. He immediately switched to a route nearer the coast and dispatched his fastest rider, Damdam ibn Amr al-Ghifari, to Mecca with an exaggerated appeal that the caravan was already under attack. The Quraysh convened a council and mobilised within about a day, in what the lectures describe as the largest and quickest gathering Mecca had ever assembled, with essentially every household sending or hiring a man.

questions.question: The Prophet's aunt Atika had a frightening dream shortly before Badr. What did she see, and did anything come of it?
questions.reference_answer: Three days before the crier reached Mecca, Atika bint Abd al-Muttalib dreamt of a man arriving on a camel who called out three times that the traitors should go and meet their death in three days, and who then rolled a boulder down from Abu Qubays that shattered so that a fragment struck every house in Mecca. Abbas told her to keep it quiet but leaked it himself, and Abu Jahl publicly mocked the Banu Hashim for now having a prophetess. The dream was borne out twice over: essentially every Meccan household ended up sending someone to Badr, and after the defeat every house in Mecca was filled with wailing women.

questions.question: Utbah ibn Rabi'a spent the whole build-up trying to stop the Meccans from fighting. Why did he end up drawing his sword after all?
questions.reference_answer: Utbah first refused to march at all, but his brother Shayba argued that abandoning their people at such a moment would leave them mocked for the rest of their lives, so he went. At Badr he offered to pay the blood money for Amr al-Hadrami out of his own pocket to buy off the demand for revenge, and rode a red camel through the ranks urging the Quraysh not to kill their own relatives, even offering to have the cowardice blamed on him. Abu Jahl then taunted him publicly with having lost his nerve at the sight of the Muslim ranks; enraged, Utbah called his brother and his son Walid out for the duel, and all three were killed by Ubayda, Hamza and Ali.

questions.question: Bilal's old master tried hard to stay out of Badr. How was he pushed into going, and what happened to him there?
questions.reference_answer: Umayya ibn Khalaf hired a substitute so he would not have to march, but Abu Jahl pressed him and, when that failed, sent Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt to hand him a woman's perfume burner in the public assembly, shaming him into going. He still had no intention of fighting, telling his wife to buy him the fastest camel so he could slip away. On the field he was captured by his old business friend Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and offered a huge ransom for his life, but Bilal recognised him and called the Ansar, who killed him and his son; his body could not be lifted for burial, so he was covered with the same kind of hot desert pebbles he had used to torture Bilal.

questions.question: The Prophet once warned Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt what would happen the next time they met outside Mecca. Was that warning fulfilled?
questions.reference_answer: After Uqba spat in his face in Mecca, the Prophet told him that when they met outside the valleys of Mecca he would have him killed, and Uqba was frightened enough that he did not want to leave the city for Badr until he was given the fastest camel and shamed into going. In the rout his camel was the first to bolt, leaving him stranded on the open plain with nothing, and he was taken prisoner. He was one of only two Badr captives executed; when he pleaded about who would care for his children, the Prophet answered simply 'the fire', and Ali carried out the execution.

questions.question: Before and during Badr the Meccans asked God for victory. What exactly did they ask for, and how did that turn out?
questions.reference_answer: Before leaving Mecca the Quraysh gathered at the Kaaba, held its covering and rings, and asked God to help whichever of the two armies was more noble and honourable. On the morning of the battle Abu Jahl repeated the same idea out loud, asking that whichever side had brought more evil, cut the ties of kinship and introduced the stranger doctrine should be destroyed that day. On both counts the lecturer notes they were supplicating against themselves, and this is what Surah al-Anfal 19 addresses: if you are asking for victory, the decision has already come, and it is not in your favour.

questions.question: There is a story that Satan walked with the Meccan army disguised as a man. Why did he appear, and what did he do when the fighting was about to start?
questions.reference_answer: As the Quraysh left Mecca they panicked that the Banu Bakr, with whom they had an unresolved blood feud, would attack their undefended city, and a large part of the army was about to turn back. Iblis then appeared in the form of Suraqa ibn Malik, a chieftain of the Banu Kinana whom they knew and trusted, guaranteeing that Mecca would be safe and even accompanying them as a kind of live hostage. When the two armies faced each other and he saw the angels descending with Jibril, he pushed away al-Harith ibn Hisham who tried to hold him, said that he could see what they could not and that he feared God, and fled.

questions.question: What was decided about the men captured at Badr, and is it true the Prophet was told afterwards he had chosen wrongly?
questions.reference_answer: Roughly seventy captives were taken and, since this had never happened before, the Prophet consulted Abu Bakr and Umar: Abu Bakr urged mercy on grounds of kinship, while Umar wanted each man executed by his own relative. The Prophet accepted Abu Bakr's view and ransomed the prisoners, but the next day Umar found him weeping under a tree, and he recited the verses saying it was not fitting for a prophet to hold captives until he had established power in the land, and that they had wanted the goods of this world. Even so, the ransom went ahead, prices were set according to each man's means, poor and illiterate captives could go free or buy freedom by teaching children to write, and the Prophet ordered that they be treated kindly.

questions.question: Uthman missed Badr entirely, so why is he counted among its participants?
questions.reference_answer: Uthman stayed behind in Medina on the Prophet's instructions because his wife Ruqayya, the Prophet's daughter, had fallen gravely ill. He was one of about nine men given a full share of the Badr spoils despite not being on the field, and is reckoned a Badri. Ruqayya died while the army was away; Uthman was at Baqi', having just finished burying her, when he heard Zayd ibn Haritha riding into Medina calling out the takbir with news of the victory.

questions.question: Abu Lahab stayed home while the rest of Mecca marched to Badr. How did he get out of it, and what became of him?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Lahab sent a substitute instead of going himself: al-As ibn Wa'il owed him four thousand dirhams, and he cancelled the debt in exchange for the man taking his place. The lecturer suggests he could not bring himself to fight his own sub-clan, since most of the Quraysh Muslims were Banu Hashim. When the news of the defeat reached Mecca he sank into depression, then flew into a rage on hearing Abbas's slave rejoice at the Muslim victory, beat the slave and then Umm al-Fadl, and was so shamed by her rebuke that he fled the house; he fell sick and died within a few days.

questions.question: How did the Muslims end up fighting outside Medina at Uhud when the Prophet's own preference was to stay inside the city?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet's proposal, backed even by Abdullah ibn Ubayy on purely military grounds, was to use Medina's natural fortifications and force the attackers into street fighting. A group of younger companions who had missed Badr pressed to march out and meet the enemy in the open, the senior companions kept silent, and the Prophet took that as the majority view and went in to put on his armour. When Hamza came to say they had changed their minds, he refused, saying it is not fitting for a prophet who has put on his armour to remove it before fighting. He then led the army out on the Friday afternoon, travelling secretly through the date-palm groves rather than the main road so the Meccan scouts would not learn his position before he reached Uhud.

questions.question: What were the archers at Uhud told to do, and why did most of them leave their position?
questions.reference_answer: Fifty archers were stationed on Jabal al-Ainain to cover the one stretch of ground the mountains did not protect, and were told to keep the enemy off with their arrows because horses will not charge into arrows. The order was absolute: they were not to move even if they saw birds picking at the Muslim dead, and regardless of whether the Muslims were winning or losing, until the Prophet sent for them. When the Quraysh fled and the other Muslims began gathering the spoils, the archers argued among themselves for some time; Abdullah ibn Jubayr insisted on staying, but about forty came down, leaving only ten on the hill, which is the opening Khalid ibn al-Walid exploited.

questions.question: How exactly did Khalid ibn al-Walid turn the battle around at Uhud, and is the usual account of his route believable?
questions.reference_answer: Khalid was commanding the Meccan right, next to Jabal al-Ainain, and even while withdrawing he was watching the field; when he saw the archers come down he gathered perhaps a hundred to a hundred and fifty men and struck the exposed flank. The lecturer rejects the common medieval claim that he rode the whole way around Mount Uhud, arguing that anyone who has seen the mountain knows that would take many hours; following Shaykh Safi al-Rahman al-Mubarakpuri he holds that Khalid used a concealed rain-water ravine near the hill to get close unseen. The blow cut the Muslim force in two, with the Prophet's camp on one side and the men collecting spoils on the other.

questions.question: How was Hamza killed at Uhud, and what happened to his body afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: Wahshi, an Abyssinian slave promised his freedom by Jubayr ibn Mut'im, stalked Hamza through the fighting, waited behind a bush until Hamza had struck down an opponent, and threw his javelin at point-blank range into his back through a gap in his armour; Hamza turned to fight but collapsed. Hind bint Utba then mutilated the corpse, slitting the stomach and chewing the liver and cutting off the extremities. After the battle Safiyya, Hamza's full sister, sent two cloths with her son Zubayr to shroud him, though one was given by lot to an Ansari who had none; the Prophet wept, first threatened to mutilate thirty bodies in return, and then, after the verse on equivalent retaliation was revealed, forbade mutilation altogether. Back in Medina he remarked that Hamza had no women to weep for him, and the Ansari women came to mourn him outside his house.

questions.question: Where did the rumour that the Prophet had been killed at Uhud come from, and what did it do to the Muslims?
questions.reference_answer: Mus'ab ibn Umayr, who was carrying the banner and resembled the Prophet in complexion and features and may have been wearing a cloak of his, was cut down in Khalid's counterattack, losing first his right hand and then his left before being killed. Abdullah ibn Qami'a, who had also struck at the Prophet, assumed he had killed him and shouted that he had killed Muhammad, and the news spread through both sides. Many companions were demoralised, some sitting down and stopping fighting; Anas ibn al-Nadr rebuked them, saying that even if Muhammad had been killed the Lord of Muhammad had not, and threw himself into the fighting until his body was unrecognisable. The lecturer also notes the rumour worked to the Muslims' advantage, since it convinced the Quraysh their work was done.

questions.question: A former chief of the Aws showed up on the Meccan side at Uhud. Who was he, and what became of him and his son?
questions.reference_answer: Abd al-Amir ibn Sayfi, known as Abu Amir al-Rahib, had been a senior leader of the Aws before the Hijrah; refusing Islam, he left Medina for Mecca and offered Abu Sufyan to win his old tribesmen over. When he called out to them at Uhud they cursed him and told him he was not al-Rahib, the monk, but al-Fasiq, and he went back to Abu Sufyan saying his people had been struck with some disease. His son Hanzala fought on the Muslim side and was killed at Uhud; because he had left his new bride without performing ghusl, the Prophet said he had seen the angels washing his body, which is why he is remembered as Ghasil al-Mala'ika.

questions.question: Were there women present at Uhud, and what were they doing there?
questions.reference_answer: The Quraysh deliberately brought around two dozen of their women, including Hind bint Utba, both as an incentive to fight and to chant verses urging the men on with promises of the bedchamber if they won and nothing if they came back beaten. Abu Dujana came up behind one such figure with the Prophet's sword raised and withdrew when she screamed and he realised it was Hind. On the Muslim side, because Uhud was within walking distance of Medina, women such as Aisha and Umm Sulaym came out with water and tended the wounded, having tied their skirts up to move quickly; the lecturer stresses this was nursing and water-carrying, not fighting, and that it happened before hijab was revealed.

questions.question: If angels were guarding the Prophet at Uhud, why was he wounded at all?
questions.reference_answer: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas reported seeing two figures in the whitest of white fighting in front of the Prophet as he had never seen before or since, which the lecturer identifies as angels. He was nevertheless hit at least three times: a stone from Utba ibn Abi Waqqas that cut his lip, an arrow that went through a gap in his helmet into his cheek and dislodged a tooth and stuck fast, and a sword blow deflected by Talha that drove links of his own armour into the other cheek. The answer given is that the protection was real, since it kept him alive, but the wounds were by God's decree and for a purpose: the Prophet had to be shown struggling and bleeding like any other human being, so that victory is seen to come only through sacrifice and so that no one confuses him with the divine.

questions.question: When the tide turned at Uhud, where did the Prophet take cover and who stayed with him?
questions.reference_answer: He withdrew up the mountain into a narrow crevice, barely a cave, which the lecturer points out on the maps as the spot he fled to with only one or two companions at first. He had begun with nine men, two Muhajirun and seven Ansar; the Ansar were sent out one at a time as decoys to draw the Quraysh away, and all seven were killed, the Prophet each time holding Talha back for last. That left only Talha ibn Ubaydullah and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Talha insisting on shielding him with his own chest and losing fingers to a sword, and Sa'd shooting arrows that the Prophet handed him while telling him 'may my mother and father be your ransom, shoot' - a phrase the Prophet is said never to have used for anyone else.

questions.question: Mut'im ibn Adi had once given the Prophet protection in Mecca. How was that remembered later, and what part did his family play afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: When the Prophet was locked out of Mecca after Ta'if, Mut'im ibn Adi armed his own sons to escort him back in and announced publicly that he had granted him protection. Mut'im died shortly before Badr, but surveying the seventy-odd captives the Prophet said that if Mut'im were alive and had spoken a word for these men he would have released them all to him free of charge - repaying a debt to a man who never became Muslim. His son Jubayr ibn Mut'im took the opposite path: to avenge an uncle killed at Badr he promised his slave Wahshi his freedom if he killed Hamza, which is how Hamza came to be speared at Uhud. Jubayr himself later accepted Islam, saying faith first stirred in him when he heard the Prophet reciting Surah al-Tur while he was a prisoner in the mosque after Badr.

questions.question: Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman's father was kept out of one battle by a promise and killed by mistake in another. What happened?
questions.reference_answer: Before Badr the Quraysh captured Hudhayfa and his father and released them only on condition that they never fight alongside Muhammad; when they reported this, the Prophet told them to honour the undertaking, so both were kept out of Badr although they still received its reward. Yaman was by then so old that he had been excused from Uhud and left with the women and children, but he and another elderly man shamed each other into going and arrived just as Khalid's surprise attack was underway. In the confusion a group of Muslims who did not recognise him surrounded and killed him, with Hudhayfa shouting that it was his father; Hudhayfa forgave them, the Prophet paid the blood money from the public treasury, and Hudhayfa gave it away to the poor.

A group of them not recognizing Yaman, they surrounded him and they began using their swords.
the Prophet ﷺ paid him the blood money for his father from the Baitul Mal

questions.question: Only one prisoner was taken at Uhud and he was executed on the spot. Why him?
questions.reference_answer: Abu Uzza was a poet captured at Badr who pleaded that he was poor and had only daughters to support, so the Prophet released him without any ransom on the single condition that he never fight the Muslims again. Before Uhud, Abu Sufyan pressed him to compose war poetry and join the army, promising him a share of the spoils if they won and guardianship of his daughters if he died, and he broke his word. He was the single captive taken at Uhud, found cowering on the field, and was executed there - which the lecturer presents as the consequence of treachery, since one may repay many things in kind but never a broken covenant.

supporting_quotes.quote: So the Prophet ﷺ freed him with one condition, that you are never allowed to fight against us again.
Abu Sufyan said come on 3000 do you really think we're going to lose if we win you will join in the spoils

questions.question: The Muslims were famously helped by angels in their first great battle. Did the same help come the following year at Uhud?
questions.reference_answer: At Badr a thousand angels were sent in successive waves, and the corpus records several eyewitness incidents of their intervention, with Ibn Abbas holding that the angels only ever physically fought on the day of Badr and elsewhere merely served as reinforcements. Asked directly whether angels assisted at Uhud, the lecturer answers that there is no account of it in the Qur'an, and connects this to the contrast the Qur'an draws between the two days: at Badr the Muslims were kept from faltering and quarrelling, at Uhud they fell into exactly that. The one report of angelic presence at Uhud is personal rather than military - Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas seeing two figures in white fighting in front of the Prophet, understood as his protection rather than aid to the army.

supporting_quotes.quote: He said, never did the angels actually fight with the believers except on the day of Badr. In every other occasion, they merely were backups.
No, there isn't and we'll explain the wisdom. We'll explain the wisdom that will contrast. One of the lessons will be a contrast between Badr and Uhud.
I saw the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Uhud and there were two people in front of him wearing the whitest of white and fighting a fight that I had never seen before.

questions.question: How young was too young to fight in these battles, and were exceptions ever made?
questions.reference_answer: At Badr, when the army made its first camp, the Prophet reviewed the volunteers and sent back two boys, al-Bara' ibn Azib and Abdullah ibn Umar, who were under fourteen, the usual cut-off. At Uhud the threshold given is fifteen, and about a dozen were turned away, including Abdullah ibn Umar again, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Zayd ibn Arqam and Usama ibn Zayd, who at eleven or twelve had tried to smuggle himself in. Two fourteen-year-olds were allowed to stay after petitioning: Rafi' ibn Khadij because he was a skilled archer, and then Samura ibn Jundub, who argued that he was the stronger of the two and had beaten Rafi' at wrestling.

supporting_quotes.quote: he notices that there are two people who are too young to participate and these are Al-Bara' ibn Azib and Abdullah ibn Umar the both of them are younger than 14
In the battle of Uhud, you had to be 15 or older to participate. If you were less than 15, then you were rejected.

questions.question: The caravan the Muslims set out to intercept got away. What happened to it and to the money it made?
questions.reference_answer: The caravan Abu Sufyan was bringing back from Syria carried close to a thousand camels and is estimated at some fifty thousand dinars, with scarcely a household in Mecca that had not invested in it. He slipped past the Muslims by taking a coastal route and, once safe, sent word telling the army it could turn back - which Abu Jahl refused, so the battle happened without the caravan ever being touched. The goods reached Mecca and the profits were distributed to the shareholders; Abu Sufyan then went from door to door, with Ikrima and Safwan alongside him, demanding those profits back to finance the campaign that became Uhud, which the lecturer links to the verse about the disbelievers spending their wealth to block the path of God and then regretting it.

supporting_quotes.quote: And they reported to the Prophet ﷺ that it was under the command of Abu Sufyan that it had almost a thousand camels in its entourage.
Also Ibn Ishaq mentions that there was hardly any household in Mecca except that they had an investment in that caravan.

questions.question: The Prophet's uncle Abbas was on the wrong side at Badr. What changed for him, and how did that show later?
questions.reference_answer: Abbas was captured at Badr, and although the man who took him offered to hand him over as a gift, the Prophet insisted his ransom not be reduced by a single coin and that he also pay for his nephews Aqil and Nawfal. When Abbas protested that he had no money, the Prophet described the sum he and Umm al-Fadl had secretly buried and what he had told her each son should get, at which Abbas swore no one but God could have told him this. The lecturer holds that Abbas was at most a nominal Muslim until that moment and that real faith entered with the incident of the money; he returned to Mecca as a secret Muslim, and when the Quraysh marched out for Uhud he sent a trusted servant who reached Medina in three days with a detailed report of their numbers, horses and equipment.

supporting_quotes.quote: and the Prophet ﷺ said no, rather do not decrease his ransom by even one coin, one penny.
it appears that Abbas was a nominal Muslim up until the Battle of Badr. That he had said he's a Muslim, but that real Iman had not entered until the one incident.
immediately he sent a trusted servant to go to the Prophet ﷺ and inform him in explicit detail how many people, how much arms, how many horses, the entire layout of the army.

questions.question: Abu Jahl's son Ikrima was at both battles. What did he actually do in each, and where did he end up?
questions.reference_answer: At Badr, Ikrima was with his father's entourage and, as the young Ansari Mu'adh struck off Abu Jahl's leg, Ikrima's counter-blow severed Mu'adh's entire right arm. A year later he was one of the three senior commanders at Uhud, leading the Meccan left wing while Abu Sufyan led and Khalid ibn al-Walid took the right. After Uhud he was the loudest voice for turning back to finish the Muslims off, arguing they had neither killed Muhammad nor done anything worth boasting of, and was only overruled after Safwan's warning and Ma'bad al-Khuza'i's frightening report. He was later on the list of those to be killed at the conquest of Mecca, fled by sea, vowed to submit if he survived a storm, and accepted Islam with the Prophet at Tabuk, dying fighting the Romans.

supporting_quotes.quote: And Ikrimah's sword chops off the entire hand of Mu'adh. The entire right arm.
he put on the right flank, he put in charge Khalid ibn al-Walid, and on the left flank he put in charge Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahal.
And the most adamant amongst them was Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, the son of Abu Jahl. Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl. And he said that we need to go back and return.

questions.question: How did the Muslims find out that the Jewish tribe living inside Medina had gone over to the enemy during the siege?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet had a premonition and asked for a volunteer to check on the Banu Qurayza; Zubayr ibn al-Awwam went, and on his return the Prophet called him his disciple. Because Zubayr had only observed from a distance and was not an eyewitness to any conversation, the Prophet then sent a delegation of senior Ansar who had old ties with the tribe - the two Sa'ds, Abdullah ibn Rawaha and Khawwat ibn Jubayr - telling them to hint at bad news rather than announce it, so as not to spread fear. The tribe abused them and denied having any treaty at all, and the delegation returned with the coded reply 'Adal and Qara', the names of two treacherous tribes.

supporting_quotes.quote: it was none other than Zubayr ibn al-Awwam who came to the Prophet ﷺ to inform him of this treachery. That the Prophet ﷺ said, I fear something about the Banu Quraidah. Who will volunteer?
And the Prophet ﷺ said to them, go and confirm this news that has reached us. And if it is true, then indicate it to me indirectly.

questions.question: Was the chief of Banu Qurayza actually keen to break his agreement with the Muslims?
questions.reference_answer: No. Ka'b ibn Asad initially refused even to open his door to Huyay ibn Akhtab, saying he had a treaty with Muhammad which he could not break because he had only ever seen truthfulness and fulfilment from him. Huyay wore him down through the night with emotional blackmail and promises of overwhelming allied strength until Ka'b tore the treaty up. Once the confederates began to distrust one another, Ka'b turned on Huyay and cursed him, saying he had known all along that the man brought nothing but bad luck, and he recognised that if the allies left, nothing awaited his tribe but the sword.

supporting_quotes.quote: Ka'b said that I have a treaty with Muhammad sallallahu alayhi wasallam and I cannot break my promise for I have only seen from him truthfulness and fulfillment
And he began saying, Woe to me, woe to me, I knew this would happen. Wallahi this man, which man? This man brings nothing but bad luck.

questions.question: What became of Huyay ibn Akhtab after he talked the Banu Qurayza into switching sides?
questions.reference_answer: To close the deal, Huyay pledged that if the allied armies withdrew he would stay behind and share whatever fate befell the Banu Qurayza - a promise that ended up being his own verdict against himself. Later, when Abu Sufyan flew into a rage over the Sabbath excuse and swore the Jews were deceiving him, Huyay was frightened enough of Abu Sufyan that he slipped away back to the Qurayza fortress rather than return to the Quraysh camp. That choice sealed his death, because the confederates fled that same night while he remained inside the lines when the Muslims closed in.

supporting_quotes.quote: until finally he says and I shall be with you if they leave and I will face your own fate and that sealed his own fate
And Huyay was so scared of the consequences of Abu Sufyan, he decided not to return to the Quraysh and that decision proved to be his death.

questions.question: Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud came from a tribe that was besieging Medina - so how did he end up a Muslim?
questions.reference_answer: The corpus admits very little is recorded about him. What is known is that Abu Sufyan had earlier paid him, while still a pagan, to carry disinformation to Medina to keep the Muslims from turning up at the second Badr appointment, and that he later negotiated a small treaty with the Prophet on behalf of his sub-tribe. The lecturer's own theory is that these two encounters with the Prophet impressed him so deeply that he became a secret convert. Nu'aym's own first-person account, preserved in al-Waqidi, simply says that while camped outside Medina on the night of the siege Allah threw Islam into his heart, and he slipped away to the Prophet's camp and announced it there.

supporting_quotes.quote: My theory is that, and I think it's a pretty obvious theory, or it's an obvious thing to make a stretch, that these interactions impressed Nu'aym so much that he converted to Islam.
he said, Allah threw Islam into my heart. Alqa Allahul Islam fi qalbi. Like literally, it's as if he's saying, I have no idea where it came from.

questions.question: Why did the parties besieging Medina stop trusting one another?
questions.reference_answer: Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, who was trusted by all three parties, advised the Banu Qurayza privately that they should refuse to fight until the Quraysh handed over noblemen to live with them as collateral, since the Quraysh could always walk away while the Jews had everything to lose. He then warned Abu Sufyan that the Qurayza had second thoughts and were planning to hand over Quraysh nobles to be executed as an apology to Muhammad, and gave the Ghatafan a similar story. When the Qurayza emissary Azzal duly arrived demanding seventy noblemen, Abu Sufyan refused, saying they would not hand over so much as a baby camel, and each side concluded the other was plotting against it.

supporting_quotes.quote: my advice to you is, refuse to fight unless and until they guarantee you hostages from amongst them, that will live with you

questions.question: How bad did conditions get for the people inside Medina during the trench siege?
questions.reference_answer: There was a food shortage from the very first days of digging, attributed to the winter season, the lack of preparation for a siege and the halt of trade. Bukhari records that the Companions had only dried barley mixed with oil, which smelled bad; Jabir says at times they ate nothing but date pits, and he saw a stone tied to the Prophet's stomach against hunger. By the final night, as Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman described it decades later, they had endured a month of this on top of a bitter cold, a howling wind and darkness in which a man could not see his own fingertips - he said no night had ever come upon them darker, colder or windier.

supporting_quotes.quote: Bukhari mentions, Sahih Bukhari, he mentions that the Sahaba would only have dried barley with oil that they would have to mix together.
And no night had ever come upon us darker and colder than that night. And no night had ever come upon us as windy as that night.

questions.question: The Prophet spoke about conquering Persia and the Byzantine lands while the trench was being dug. How did people in Medina take that at the time?
questions.reference_answer: While striking an immovable rock in the trench line, the Prophet broke it in three blows and with each one declared that he had been given the keys of Syria, of Persia and of Yemen, saying he could see the red castles of Syria, the white pillars of Mada'in and the doors of Sana'a. The hypocrites treated such talk with open contempt: during the worst night of the siege one of them said aloud that Muhammad had been promising them the treasures of Caesar and Chosroes while they were now too frightened even to relieve themselves. The lecturer notes that within roughly seven years, at Yarmuk and Qadisiyya, the Muslims were eating off the plates of Chosroes and Caesar.

supporting_quotes.quote: He said, Allahu Akbar, I have just seen that Allah has given me the keys to Syria. Allah has given me the keys to Syria. By Allah I can see the red castles in Syria.
So one of them said, here was Muhammad ﷺ promising us the treasures of Kisra and Qaisar.

questions.question: How was the trench guarded at night, and who protected the women and children?
questions.reference_answer: Ibn Ishaq records that groups of Companions patrolled the trench in shifts through the entire night, calling out takbir so that anyone approaching would think a large force stood on the other side; Umm Salama said they could hear the takbirs until Fajr. The Prophet himself took a watch, and on one night Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas came and took over his shift so he could sleep. The women and children had been moved into the fortress of al-Fari', and once the Banu Qurayza's treachery became known the already thin patrols had to be split further, with Zayd ibn Haritha and Salama ibn Aslam sent with a contingent to guard that fortress and to let the Qurayza see they were being watched.

supporting_quotes.quote: And Ibn Ishaq mentions that a group of Sahaba in shifts, their job was to patrol the trench the entire night. And simply shout out, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar.
they sent Zayd ibn Harithah and Salama ibn Aslam with a contingent of fighters to go and protect the fortress that the Muslim women and the Muslim children were

questions.question: Why were the Quraysh so determined to keep the Muslims out of Mecca that particular year?
questions.reference_answer: It was purely a matter of pride. From the moment the first intermediary, Budayl ibn Warqa, relayed the Prophet's peaceful intentions, the Quraysh answered that they would never let him enter, because the Arabs would then say he had got the better hand over them. They repeated that same sentence to every envoy, including Uthman. The lecturer points out that this insistence actually exposed their insecurity: the fact that they were so obsessed with not being seen to lose face showed they knew the tide had turned and that the Muslims really did now have the upper hand.

supporting_quotes.quote: the Quraysh responded by Allah we will never allow him to enter Mecca and the Arabs will say that he had the better hand over us
Let not the Arabs say that you had the upper hand over us. What does that show? It shows that they did have the upper hand. But there is this arrogance.

questions.question: After refusing to talk for days, what finally pushed the Quraysh into negotiating at Hudaybiyya?
questions.reference_answer: Their support base fell away and then they took fright. Urwa ibn Mas'ud of Thaqif went as their envoy and came back convinced the Companions would never abandon their leader, which effectively removed Thaqif from the equation. Then al-Hulays of Kinana, seeing the sacrificial camels and the pilgrims in ihram, declared it unlawful to block them; when the Quraysh insulted him as an ignorant Bedouin, he swore that none of the Ahabish would stand with them, taking away a large part of their force. Finally, when word of the pledge of Ridwan reached Mecca, al-Bayhaqi reports that the Quraysh trembled with fear, and it was then that they sent a real delegation, first Mikraz and then Suhayl ibn Amr.

supporting_quotes.quote: as soon as they said this al-Hulay swore by Allah that none of the Ahabish would support the Quraish
he mentions that when the news reached the Quraysh about the bay'at al-Ridwan, they trembled. they got scared

questions.question: Why was Uthman the one sent into Mecca as the Prophet's envoy, and what happened while he was in there?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet first chose Umar, but Umar said his enmity with the Quraysh was notorious and his clan of Adi no longer had anyone left to protect him, so he suggested Uthman, who carried more standing in their eyes and had close Umayyad kin in the city. Uthman was stopped and mocked at the Baldah road until his cousin Aban ibn Sa'id gave him his own horse and personal protection to enter. The negotiations dragged on so long that the Muslims concluded he had been killed, which prompted the pledge of Ridwan; the Prophet took the oath on Uthman's behalf with his own hand. Uthman later insisted he would not have performed tawaf even had he stayed a year, while the Prophet remained shut out.

supporting_quotes.quote: So if you want me to go, I will go. But Uthman ibn Affan has more nobility in their eyes than I do.

he took his left hand and he said, this is for Uthman. And he put it in his right hand and he took the oath on behalf of Uthman ibn Affan.

questions.question: Who was Abu Jandal, and what eventually happened to him?
questions.reference_answer: He was the younger son of the Quraysh negotiator Suhayl ibn Amr, kept chained in a dungeon and tortured by his own father for about four years after his elder brother escaped to Medina. He broke out and threw himself on the Muslim camp in chains at the precise moment his father was insisting on the clause returning defectors, and Suhayl declared him the first case. The Prophet pleaded repeatedly for him to be gifted as an exception and, when refused, told him to be patient because Allah would make a way out. Later, after Abu Basir set up a camp outside the treaty's reach, Abu Jandal escaped and joined him, and when the Quraysh finally begged for the group to be taken into Medina, it was Abu Jandal who led them there.

supporting_quotes.quote: so Suhail locks up Abu Jandal and tells the servants and slaves to torture him throw him into the dungeon deprive him of food and water and he is chained since the battle of Badr up until now
