And the very Abu Jandal who was the cause of all of this is the one who led the camp back into Medina.

questions.question: What terms did the Quraysh negotiator get written into the agreement at Hudaybiyya?
questions.reference_answer: Suhayl ibn Amr first forced changes to the wording, objecting to 'Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim' and to 'Rasulullah'. He then insisted that no man defecting from the Quraysh to the Muslims be kept, even if he had accepted Islam, while anyone leaving the Muslims for Mecca would not be returned. The umrah was deferred to the following year, when the Quraysh would vacate the city for three days. Alongside these, the treaty set a ten-year peace, described as no armour and no swords between the two sides, and allowed either party to enter into alliances with other tribes, with the treaty's terms extending to those allies.

supporting_quotes.quote: so what was his condition that not a single man from us renegades or defects over to you even if he be on your religion except that you will hand him back to us
Of the conditions was that, there would be a peace for 10 years. For 10 years, neither side would fight. And they said, the exact phrase they said, no armor and no swords.

questions.question: Umar argued openly with the Prophet over the terms agreed with the Quraysh. How did he look back on that later?
questions.reference_answer: At the time Umar put a string of rhetorical questions to the Prophet - are you not the Messenger of Allah, are we not on the truth - and asked how they could accept humiliation in their religion; he then took the same questions to Abu Bakr, who rebuked him sharply. Once Surah al-Fath was revealed his view reversed instantly. Afterwards he performed extra deeds - freeing slaves, fasting and praying - hoping they would make up for what he had said, and during his caliphate he admitted that if any other leader had imposed such a condition on him he would never have accepted it. He also said he saw himself that day as almost rejecting the religion, and drew from it the lesson that a person should suspect his own opinion before he suspects the Qur'an and Sunnah.

supporting_quotes.quote: how can we accept the lower hand the humiliation ad-daniyata being disgraced in our religion how could we have allowed them to trample over us like this
He said that on the day of Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ put a condition on us. If any other leader had put it on me, I would never have accepted it.
Umar ibn Khattab said that I saw myself almost rejecting Islam meaning, what does he mean? my bad manners were so bad I worry that I might almost become a kafir on that day

questions.question: The agreement obliged the Muslims to send back anyone who fled Mecca for Medina. How did that clause actually work out?
questions.reference_answer: It backfired on the Quraysh. Abu Basir was the first to arrive and was handed over, but he killed one of his two escorts on the road, returned, and was told indirectly that he could not stay; he set up his own camp on the coast near the Meccan trade route. Abu Jandal and eventually some eighty stranded converts joined him, and since the Quraysh themselves had barred them from any treaty with the Prophet, they were free to raid Meccan caravans, which they did as a livelihood. Within about a year and a half Abu Sufyan sent a delegation begging the Prophet, by the ties of kinship, to take the whole group into Medina. The lecturer also stresses that the Prophet followed the letter of the clause only: he was never obliged to enforce it himself and did not hunt anyone down.

supporting_quotes.quote: And so, within a year and a half, the Quraysh sent a delegation. Abu Sufyan sent a delegation to Medina, begging the Prophet ﷺ, by the rights of kinship, please take these 80 people and put them in Medina.
the Prophet ﷺ was told that you're not going to allow somebody to live in your midst but he was not told it's your job to send them back

questions.question: Did women who escaped from Mecca after the treaty also have to be handed back?
questions.reference_answer: No. When Umm Kulthum bint Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt accepted Islam and fled to Medina, the Prophet did not know at first what to do, since returning a woman to persecution was far harder than returning a man. Surah al-Mumtahina verse 10 then instructed that believing women who migrate should be tested and, if genuine, not sent back to the disbelievers, though the dowries their husbands had paid were to be returned. The corpus draws a fiqh point from this: the treaty's wording said 'man', and the Muslims held strictly to the literal text even where that arguably cut against its spirit.

supporting_quotes.quote: it's one thing to return a man to be tortured to return a woman that's very painful as every one of us understands here it's very painful and even the Prophet ﷺ did not know what to do

Because the treaty said, no man shall come. And it's understood when you say generically man, with all respect to the feminists and what not, it is understood that when you say man, you mean woman as well.

questions.question: Hudaybiyya looked like a climbdown at the time, so why is it remembered as a great victory?
questions.reference_answer: On the road back Surah al-Fath was revealed whole, opening with the declaration of a clear victory; the Prophet said Allah had sent down a chapter more beloved to him than everything on earth, and Umar, told plainly that yes this was a victory, rode up and down the lines proclaiming it. The longer-term case is made by al-Zuhri, who said no victory before Hudaybiyya was greater than it, because peace let Muslims and pagans mix and talk freely and nobody of intelligence heard about Islam without entering it. Ibn Hisham's proof is arithmetic: 1,400 men gave the pledge at Ridwan, and two years later 10,000 marched on Mecca. The peace also freed the Prophet to deal with Khaybar and to begin writing to foreign rulers.

supporting_quotes.quote: And our Prophet ﷺ praised the surah and he said, Allah has sent down a surah that is more beloved to me than everything on this earth.
Ibn Shahab al-Zuhri said, there was no victory given to Islam before Hudaybiyah that was bigger than Hudaybiyah.
the proof for Al-Zuhri statement is that in Bayat al-Ridwan, there were 1,400 people. Two years later in the conquest of Mecca, there are 10,000 people.

questions.question: Was any blood actually shed while the two sides were camped facing each other at Hudaybiyya?
questions.reference_answer: None. Sahih Muslim records that eighty armed Quraysh came down from Tan'im to raid the Muslim camp around the time of Fajr, but the Muslims spotted them, surrounded them and forced their surrender without a single casualty; the Prophet pardoned all of them and sent them back to Mecca. Surah al-Fath verse 24 describes this as Allah restraining their hands and the Muslims' hands from each other in the valley of Mecca after giving the Muslims the upper hand. The corpus adds another reason blood was prevented: there were believers still hidden in Mecca whom the Muslims did not know about and would have killed in a battle, only to grieve over it afterwards.

supporting_quotes.quote: the Muslims actually surrounded them and forced them to surrender without causing any bloodshed. Which is an amazing miracle. Without killing one of them.
if there had been a battle they would have been forced to be on the side of the Quraysh because their Islam is secret and you would have been forced to kill them

questions.question: Why did the Muslims move on Khaybar so soon after making peace with the Quraysh?
questions.reference_answer: The peace removed the threat that had been absorbing all their attention, which left them free to deal with the one hostile power still on their doorstep. Khaybar sheltered the exiled Banu Nadir and elements of the Banu Qaynuqa, including Huyay ibn Akhtab, who had helped assemble the confederates and had talked the Banu Qurayza into breaking their treaty. There was no immediate plot, so the attack was preemptive; there was also no treaty with Khaybar. The march began within roughly two weeks of the return from Hudaybiyya, in Muharram of the seventh year, with about 1,600 to 1,700 men.

supporting_quotes.quote: First and foremost, the issue of the remaining Yahudi tribes. And that is in Khaybar now. And that's exactly why, less than one month after Hudaybiyah, Khaybar takes place.
And this shows us that the Muslims barely rested for two weeks after Hudaybiyyah. This shows us the process was thinking what is the next step.
it was a pre-emptive attack, so that the people of Khyber do not launch an attack against Medina.

questions.question: What arrangement did the people of Khaybar get once their fortresses had fallen, and how long did it last?
questions.reference_answer: After the last great fortress was surrounded they negotiated, arguing that the Muslims did not know how to work the land as they did. The terms were that they stay on and give half the produce to the Muslims, bear all maintenance and labour costs themselves, and accept that the Muslims could cancel the arrangement whenever they wished. They were also required to hand over all gold, silver, weapons and armour, and concealing any of it would void the agreement - which is what lay behind the interrogation of Sa'ya over Huyay's hidden treasure. The arrangement ran until late in Umar's caliphate, when he invoked the cancellation clause and had them relocate, ending the Jewish presence in central Arabia.

supporting_quotes.quote: that number one that the people of Khyber would give 50% of their produce to the Muslims now the people of Khyber had hundreds of acres of land and 50% is a massive amount
was that the tribes of Khaibah would hand over all of the gold and silver and weapons and armor. And they'd be allowed to keep their houses and lands for the time being.

questions.question: The daughter of Huyay ibn Akhtab ended up married to the Prophet. How did that come about?
questions.reference_answer: Huyay was the chieftain of Banu Nadir, described as the most evil of them, the man who slipped into Medina during the siege and persuaded the Banu Qurayza to betray their treaty; the corpus contrasts him with his daughter Safiyya as an example of how good and bad are not inherited. After the expulsion Safiyya grew up in Khaybar and married there. In the fighting her father, brother and husband were all killed, and she was taken as part of the captives and allotted to Dihya al-Kalbi until Companions argued she was too high-born for that and the Prophet bought her from him. Offered the choice of freedom and return to her people or Islam and staying, she said she had already inclined to Islam and believed in him before being asked, and he freed her and made her freedom her dowry.

supporting_quotes.quote: the Banu Nadir, they sent a secret emissary, Huyay ibn Akhtab, the father of Safiyyah. He was their chieftain and he was really the most evil of them.
And therefore Safiyyah was distributed along with everybody else. And she fell in the lot of Dihya al-Kalbi.
Ya Rasulullah, I was already inclined towards Islam even before you offered it to me. and I have already believed in you even before you asked me to convert.

questions.question: Did anyone who had not fought at Khaybar still receive a share of what was taken there?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, several groups. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib arrived from Abyssinia with around fifty emigrants on the very day Khaybar fell, and although they had taken no part in the fighting they were all given a share in recognition of the hardship of their long exile. Abu Hurayra and a small group of Daws arrived at the same time on their way to Medina, and the Prophet asked the Companions' permission before giving them a share too, which they granted. The Ansari women who had come along to treat the wounded and fetch water did not receive shares, since there was no battle share for them, but were given gifts; one of them was given a necklace she asked to be buried with. In addition, everyone who had been at Hudaybiyya was given extra, as Surah al-Fath had promised.

supporting_quotes.quote: And subhanallah, even though the people from Habasha, the Muslims, did not participate at Khaybar, they all got a share as well in Khaybar.
As for the people from Dawsi, he asked permission from the Sahaba. That would you mind if they also take a share? And they all agreed.

questions.question: How did the Prophet come to marry Abu Sufyan's daughter while she was living in Abyssinia?
questions.reference_answer: Ramla bint Abi Sufyan, Umm Habiba, had migrated to Abyssinia with her husband Ubaydullah ibn Jahsh, who reverted to Christianity there and died an apostate, leaving her alone with no family and no guardian in a foreign land. Since her father was not a Muslim, the Negus acted as her guardian: the Prophet sent the proposal through him, and Najashi conducted the marriage in his own palace, paid the dowry himself without being asked, and sent her off with lavish gifts, so hers was the largest dowry of any of the Prophet's wives. She most likely arrived with the returning Abyssinian emigrants around the time of Khaybar. The lecturer stresses the political weight of the match, since her father was the leader of the Quraysh.

supporting_quotes.quote: when Najashi heard he became so happy he was the one who conducted the nikah ceremony he acted as the wali for Ramla because Abu Sufyan is not a Muslim
So our Prophet ﷺ sent a proposal to her new wali, and her new wali was none other than Najashi himself, the emperor himself.

questions.question: Did the Muslims win at Mu'tah or lose?
questions.reference_answer: Scholars are divided three ways. Musa ibn Uqba, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Kathir call it a clear victory, resting mainly on the Prophet's own words in Bukhari, where after describing the deaths of Zayd, Ja'far and Ibn Rawaha he said that a sword from the swords of Allah then took the banner and Allah granted victory at his hands, and on the fact that under one percent of the three thousand were lost. Al-Waqidi, Ibn Sa'd and non-Muslim historians count it a defeat: three commanders killed, the banner lost and the Muslims forced to withdraw while the Romans held the field. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Qayyim call it a draw, since neither side pressed a final assault or took prisoners. The lecturer accepts each as true from its own angle, a victory in preserving the army rather than in taking ground.

supporting_quotes.quote: his eyes were crying until he said hatta akhadaha sayfun min suyufillahi ta'ala until a sword from the swords of Allah took it and Allah gave him victory at his hands
The third opinion is that it's neither a victory nor a defeat. It is in fact a draw. Neither side won clear cut.

questions.question: How did Khalid ibn al-Walid end up commanding at Mu'tah, and what did he do with the army?
questions.reference_answer: After all three appointed commanders were killed, Thabit ibn Arqam grabbed the fallen banner, pulled back and called the Muslims to regroup, then refused the command himself and told them to choose. Their eyes settled on Khalid, who had accepted Islam only a month or two earlier and had fought against them at Uhud, Khandaq and Hudaybiyya; he objected, asking how he could, but they insisted. Judging that outright victory was impossible and that the real objective was to save the army, he mounted a sharp attack with archers positioned to halt the Roman advance - he later said nine swords broke in his hand that day, leaving him only a Yemeni shield - and by nightfall the two armies had separated. The next day he created the impression that reinforcements were arriving, and in that pause the army withdrew intact.

supporting_quotes.quote: So all eyes turn to Khalid ibn al-Walid. And Khalid when he sees all of this, he says, how could I? Meaning, of course he understood, I am who I am.
He says that on the day of Mu'tah, nine swords broke in my hand. Nine swords, one after the other, kept on using nine swords until I finally only had left one Yemeni shield.

questions.question: How long did the Prophet have with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib after his return from Abyssinia?
questions.reference_answer: Barely a year. Ja'far arrived at Khaybar in the seventh year after more than a decade away; the Prophet stood to greet him, kissed him on the forehead and said he did not know which of the two things made him happier that day, the conquest of Khaybar or Ja'far's return. In Jumada al-Ula of the eighth year Ja'far was appointed second commander at Mu'tah and was killed there, fighting on after both hands were severed, his body found under a pile of the dead with more than ninety wounds. When the news came, Aisha says the Prophet had to sit down and his grief was plainly visible; Anas says he wept as he described the deaths.

supporting_quotes.quote: and he said I don't know which of the two things is making me happier today Fathu Khaybar or the return of Ja'far
Aisha says that when the news of the death of Ibn Harithah and Ja'far and Abdullah Ibn Rawaha came the Prophet ﷺ sat down and grief was clearly visible from him

questions.question: What happened to Ja'far's widow and children after he was killed?
questions.reference_answer: At first the women of his household fell into loud wailing, and a man came three times to the Prophet reporting that he could not stop them, until the Prophet, already in grief, told him to throw dust in their mouths - an Arabic expression of exasperation - at which Aisha rebuked the messenger for adding to the Prophet's suffering. The Prophet ordered that food be prepared for the family, since a matter had come upon them that would keep them occupied. After three days he visited, said no one should weep for his brother any longer, called for a barber for the children's neglected hair, told them their father had been given two wings in place of his two hands, and prayed for Abdullah's dealings to be blessed. When Asma bint Umays worried about the orphans, he told her he himself would be their guardian in this world and the next.

supporting_quotes.quote: So the Prophet ﷺ told him, go back and tell them to stop. So the man went. And then he came back again, and he said, Ya Rasulullah, I stopped them, I prohibited them.
the Prophet ﷺ said are you scared of poverty for them when I will be the one who will take care of them in this world and the next

questions.question: Did the trench actually keep the enemy out of Medina?
questions.reference_answer: Only partly, and it was never meant to do more. It ran about two kilometres along the one open approach, the rest of the city being shielded by volcanic rock and dense date plantations, and the lecturer describes it frankly as an act of desperation and a stalling tactic rather than a permanent defence. It stopped a mass charge, so the confederates settled into a siege instead, but it was not watertight: it could not stop a single man slipping through, which is exactly how Huyay ibn Akhtab got into the city to reach the Banu Qurayza. At one weakly held point five horsemen led by Amr ibn Abd Wudd flung their horses across, and Khalid ibn al-Walid and Ikrima also got over before being driven back.

supporting_quotes.quote: And this is, frankly it was an act of desperation because this is a temporary tactic. It's not a permanent tactic, right? And so immediately the Sahaba got to work non-stop.
the trench was not watertight right? the trench only protected large groups from entering Medina you can't stop one person from sneaking in, right?
a small group managed to break across. When there was nobody on the other side, they managed to fling their horses across, and it was five of them, and the leader of them was Amr ibn Abdu Wood.

questions.question: Why were the women and children moved into a fortress before the enemy had even arrived, and was that worry justified?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet ordered it at the same time he ordered the digging, thinking several steps ahead: every man would be tied up guarding the perimeter, and the loyalty of the one remaining Jewish tribe inside the city, the Banu Qurayza, could not be counted on. They were sent to al-Fari', the fortress of Banu Harithah, the largest the Ansar owned. The fear proved exact. Once the Qurayza flipped, their very first move was not against the fighting men but to work out how to get at the women and children, and they sent two scouts by night to see whether al-Fari' was defended. The only man there was Hassan ibn Thabit, who was not a fighter, so Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib went out herself, killed the scout and threw his head down, and his companion fled thinking the place was guarded.

supporting_quotes.quote: all of the men are going to be busy manning and guarding the perimeters. and inside of Medina there is still the tribe of the Banu Quraidah and the Banu Quraidah we don't know where their loyalties will lie
The first thing that they do is not to attack the men. it is to figure out how to execute all of the women and children think about that then put into perspective their punishment

All of the women and children go inside that fortress which is called Al-Fari' as we said. And the reason for this was the Prophet ﷺ was worried about the treachery that might come from the Banu Qurayza.

questions.question: Who put together the huge alliance that marched on Medina, and what were the tribes offered for joining it?
questions.reference_answer: The initiative came from the exiled Banu Nadir, who wanted their lands back and sent a high-level delegation of their noblemen, including Huyay ibn Akhtab and Salam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, to Mecca; the Quran exposed the deal in Surah al-Nisa verse 50, where they told the pagans that the Quraysh were better guided than Muhammad and his companions. The Quraysh had their own grievance in the ruined Syrian trade route, but Ghatafan had no such stake and had to be bought, so they were promised half of Khaybar's produce for a year - effectively hired as mercenaries. That mercenary character showed during the siege itself, when Ghatafan sent an emissary offering to sit out the fight in exchange for a third of Medina's produce, an offer the two Sa'ds rejected as a humiliation they had never accepted even in jahiliyya.

supporting_quotes.quote: And they said, we will pay you half of the produce of khaybar for one year. That's a fortune. Half of the produce of khaybar for one year for this one battle. Basically, they hired mercenaries.
And they said, these are the stakes. They've given us half of Khaybar to fight you guys. if you give us one third of Medina we won't fight you guys

questions.question: There seems to be disagreement about what year the battle of the trench happened. What is the argument on each side?
questions.reference_answer: One camp says Shawwal of the fourth year, resting on an explicit first-person report in Bukhari where Ibn Umar says he was fourteen at Uhud and turned away, and fifteen at Khandaq and allowed through; since Uhud was undisputedly the third year, the arithmetic gives the fourth. Bukhari himself, al-Zuhri, al-Nawawi and Ibn Hazm held this, Ibn Hazm saying there could be no doubt about it. The seerah specialists - Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Qayyim - say the fifth year, because the fourth was taken up by the second Badr appointment and because Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who by consensus died right after Khandaq, died in the fifth year; al-Bayhaqi tries to reconcile Ibn Umar's ages by noting nobody tracked birthdays precisely. The lecturer accepts the fifth year, with Ibn Sa'd differing only over whether it was Shawwal or Dhu al-Qa'da.

supporting_quotes.quote: so if we say that Uhud took place third year, then obviously simple math, Ibn Umar is saying I was 14 when I turned 15, Khandaq took place So then automatically, by default, that becomes Shawwal of the fourth year.
Sa'd ibn Mu'adh by unanimous consensus is Sa'ad dies right after Khandaq. By unanimous consensus, right? And the death of Sa'ad basically is marked to the fifth year.
Now, Ibn Sa'ad was of the opinion it took place in Dhul-Qa'dah and others Shawwal. But Shawwal and Dhul-Qa'dah is 1-2 weeks apart basically.

questions.question: What actually caused the truce with the Quraysh to collapse, and did the tribe that was attacked ever get to settle the score?
questions.reference_answer: The pagan Banu Bakr, allies of the Quraysh, launched a night raid on Khuza'ah at the pool of al-Watir in the eighth year, killing more than twenty people. The Quraysh did not merely know about it; their leaders gave the Banu Bakr weapons, which the corpus treats as a direct breach of Hudaybiyah. Khuza'ah's chief Amr ibn Salim rode to Medina and recited a poem recalling shared ancestry and old treaties, and the Prophet promised them help. After Mecca fell, he did let Khuza'ah take retaliation against Banu Bakr, but only until the Asr prayer that day, after which bloodshed in the Haram was forbidden again.

supporting_quotes.quote: So they consciously, knowingly approved of the raid and this goes against the treaty of Hudaybiyah. This is a very important point here. It's not as if the Banu Bakr did it and the Quraysh are innocent.
he allowed them to engage in a minor skirmish and he said you have until Asr and only Asr so they literally had few hours and most of the time is in the heat of the sun

questions.question: Abu Sufyan travelled to Medina to try to save the treaty. How was he received there, and how did he eventually end up accepting Islam?
questions.reference_answer: He was turned away by everyone. The Prophet gave him no answer at all; Abu Bakr said flatly he could not help; Umar mocked him; Ali would only advise him to stand up in the masjid and publicly ask for protection, which nobody granted. Even his own daughter Umm Habiba pulled the Prophet's bedding away so he would not sit on it. Later, on the night the Muslim army camped at Marr al-Zahran, al-Abbas found him scouting, put him on the Prophet's mule and brought him into the camp under his protection. After a whole night of argument with Abbas, he accepted the shahada reluctantly the next morning, saying that if the other gods were real they would have helped him by now.

supporting_quotes.quote: and Abu Bakr told him flat out لا استطيع I cannot help you at all flat out he said I cannot help you so he then sought out Umar who was his one time business partner in the days of Jahiliyyah
that Ya Abu Sufyan isn't it time for you to acknowledge that there is no God but Allah isn't it time come on how long are you going to deny this

questions.question: When did the Prophet's uncle Abbas become Muslim, and what part did he play in the takeover of Mecca?
questions.reference_answer: Scholars give as many as five opinions about when Abbas accepted Islam, and the corpus says the evidence is ambiguous, though it leans towards his heart having opened after Badr while he publicly declared his faith only now. He met the army near al-Juhfa emigrating with his family, and so is counted as the very last of the muhajirun, since there is no hijrah after the conquest. He then asked permission to go and negotiate to prevent bloodshed, found Abu Sufyan scouting at night, brought him in on the Prophet's mule, argued with Umar to spare him, and afterwards urged Abu Sufyan to hurry back and warn the Quraysh not to fight.

supporting_quotes.quote: lo and behold, Abbas ibn Abdul Muttalib comes to do hijrah. And Allah had written for him the honor, the sharaf, that nobody else got after him, and that is the last human being ever to enter into the realm of the muhajirun.

So we see here, Abbas is acting as an intermediate between the Quraysh and the Prophet ﷺ. Remember, he's the recent convert. His loyalties are with Allah and His Messenger, but his heart is still somewhat attached to the Quraysh.

questions.question: How was the target of the march kept hidden from the Meccans, and did anyone manage to get word to them?
questions.reference_answer: Secrecy was extreme: the Prophet did not even tell Abu Bakr or Aisha where the army was going, and he sent a scouting party of eight men northwards to create the impression that the target was Syria, announcing Mecca only about a day before departure. One companion, Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, did try to warn the Quraysh by paying a woman to smuggle a letter to Mecca hidden in her braided hair. Jibril informed the Prophet, who sent Ali and Zubayr to intercept her; they recovered the letter, and Hatib confessed that he had acted to buy protection for his family in Mecca, not out of disbelief. Umar wanted him executed but the Prophet spared him because he had fought at Badr.

supporting_quotes.quote: the Prophet ﷺ intentionally sent out a small expedition up north as a scouting party to give the impression that the massive army is gonna go up north towards Syria

Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala sent Jibreel down and Jibreel told the Prophet sallallahu alayhi wa sallam exactly what happened that Hatib wrote a letter and this lady is taking the letter and you had better stop her

questions.question: Once the Prophet had control of the Kaaba, what did he do with the statues around it, and who was told to give the call to prayer from its roof?
questions.reference_answer: Riding his camel, he made tawaf while pointing a staff at each of the more than three hundred idols set around the Kaaba, and each one fell as he pointed at it, while he recited that truth has come and falsehood has vanished. He then had the doors unlocked, went inside and removed the pagan objects and images he found there, including a picture of Ibrahim holding divination arrows. Afterwards he told Bilal to climb to the top of the Kaaba and give the adhan there, which the corpus presents as the reward of a man who had proclaimed Allah's oneness while being tortured in the same valley years earlier.

supporting_quotes.quote: Every time he passed by an idol, Ibn Ishaq mentions, he would point towards that idol with the staff. And if the idol had the face forward, it would fall forward.
and at this point in time he then instructs Bilal the famous instruction and that is to climb up to the top of the Kaaba and to give the Adhan from the top of the Kaaba

questions.question: A handful of Meccans did try to resist when the army entered the city. Who were they and what became of them afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: The brief, chaotic resistance was led by Ikrimah the son of Abu Jahl, joined by Safwan ibn Umayyah and Suhayl ibn Amr; it collapsed at once, with roughly a dozen to two dozen Qurayshis and two or three Muslims killed on Khalid ibn al-Walid's flank. Ikrimah fled by ship towards Abyssinia, and a storm at sea convinced him that only Allah could save him; he vowed to become Muslim, returned, and later died a martyr. Safwan also fled and spoke of killing himself, but his cousin Umayr ibn Wahb brought him back with the Prophet's own turban as a token of safety; he was given four months' grace and only accepted Islam after being given an enormous share of the Hunayn spoils. Suhayl shut himself in his house in terror and sent his son Abdullah to ask for protection; he was granted it and accepted Islam somewhat later, after Hunayn and Ta'if.

supporting_quotes.quote: the one in charge of it was Ikrimah the son of Abu Jahl Ikrimah ibn Abu Jahl he could not imagine refusing and along with him he gathered together the two most famous leaders that were still alive Safwan ibn Umayyah and Suhail ibn Amr
So Suhail came to the Prophet ﷺ and after a conversation he did not accept Islam immediately, but once again he was given some time, and eventually he converted to Islam after the conquest of Mecca

questions.question: Did the people of Medina ever worry that the Prophet would stay with his own tribe now that they had accepted Islam, and how did he reassure them?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, twice. In Mecca, after the men and women had given their oath of allegiance, some of the Ansar muttered that softness for his own relatives had overtaken him and that he would forget them. Jibril informed him, yet he still asked them directly whether they had said it; when they admitted it he reminded them of the promise made at Aqaba, saying his life was their life and his death their death, and they wept and were excused. The same anxiety surfaced again at Ji'ranah after Hunayn, when the huge gifts of booty went to Quraysh dignitaries and the Ansar got nothing; he gathered them alone in a tent, said he would go with the Ansar if all mankind went one way and they went another, and asked whether they were not content that others go home with sheep and camels while they go home with the Messenger of Allah.

supporting_quotes.quote: and one of them says now that he has returned here softness has overtaken him for his people meaning khalas he's forgotten about us

questions.question: What went wrong when Khalid ibn al-Walid was sent out to the Banu Jadhima, and how did the Prophet respond to it?
questions.reference_answer: Khalid, a very new Muslim, was sent to invite the tribe to Islam, but he had an old blood feud with them and they took up arms when they saw him coming. When others of the tribe declared their submission they used the old expression sabana rather than aslamna, and Khalid, not recognising the reference, had innocent men killed; senior companions such as Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf refused to obey his order. The Prophet faced the Kaaba, raised his hands and publicly disowned what Khalid had done, sent Ali with money to pay blood money and compensate the families, and rebuked Khalid with the words not to curse his companions. The corpus adds a further detail: one young captive who was executed had recited love poetry to his betrothed just before dying, and when the Prophet heard of it he became even angrier and asked whether there had not been one merciful man among them to stop it.

supporting_quotes.quote: The first thing the Prophet ﷺ did, he stood up, he faced the Ka'bah, he raised his hands and he said, Allahumma inni abra'u layka bima fa'ala Khalid.
When the Prophet ﷺ heard this story, he became enraged even more. And he said, أَلَيْسَ مِنْكُمْ رَجُلٌ رَحِيمٌ Wasn't there anybody that had mercy in his heart to stop this, Khalid doing this?

questions.question: How long did the Prophet remain in Mecca after taking it, and where did he live while he was there?
questions.reference_answer: Bukhari's report of nineteen days is the one the corpus follows, and he left Mecca on the sixth of Shawwal to face the gathering at Hunayn. He did not move back into any family house: Abu Talib's property had been inherited by his non-Muslim sons Talib and Aqil, and Aqil had sold it all, so when Ali suggested returning there the Prophet asked whether Aqil had left them anything. Instead he pitched a tent in the small valley of al-Hujun near the Kaaba, the same place where the Quraysh had drawn up the boycott document against him years before. Through those days he prayed all five prayers at the Kaaba, shortening the four-rak'ah prayers, and taught the new Muslims.

supporting_quotes.quote: he sets up a tent in his own city of Mecca situation has changed now He sets up a tent to live in for the next 19 days. And the place that he chooses is the famous mini valley close to the Kaaba, literally five minutes walk away. It's called Al-Hujun.
and the Prophet ﷺ left Mecca on the 6th of Shawwal on the 6th of Shawwal he left Mecca after having been in Mecca for 19 days

questions.question: The Muslims had never fielded a larger army than at Hunayn, so how did they end up almost losing the battle?
questions.reference_answer: Their very numbers were the problem. With about twelve thousand men, well rested and well armed with borrowed weapons from Mecca, some boasted that they could not possibly be defeated, and the Prophet warned them against that arrogance. Hawazin and Thaqif, who knew the terrain, planted a small decoy force at the end of a valley and hid archers in the crags on both sides; when the Muslims charged and the decoy pretended to break, volleys of arrows came from above and the main body charged from the front. Many of the troops were brand-new converts without helmets or armour, and they fled in panic. The Prophet stood firm on his mount, had Abbas call the tribes back by name, threw a handful of dust towards Thaqif, and the Qur'an later described how their numbers availed them nothing until Allah sent down calm and unseen armies.

supporting_quotes.quote: and the goal was that the Muslims be lured in and once they're inside the false contingent of Hawazin pretend to be defeated and this would cause more Muslims to rush in because now this is victory
and the Muslims for the first time in their lives felt overconfident never before had they felt overconfident and so much so that they remarked that how can we possibly be destroyed

questions.question: Why were the enemy's families and livestock brought onto the battlefield at Hunayn, and what happened to them in the end?
questions.reference_answer: Their young chief Malik ibn Awf ordered the women, children, herds and property brought along so that every man would fight harder with his family behind him. The blind elder Durayd ibn al-Simma, brought along for his blessing and counsel, heard the babies and the animals and told him this was foolish, since a losing man is not saved by his wife standing behind him; Malik mocked him and threatened to kill himself if he was not obeyed. When the enemy fled, roughly six thousand captives, some twenty-four thousand camels and forty thousand goats fell to the Muslims and were gathered at Ji'ranah. The Prophet waited there for around a month for Hawazin to come back, and when they did he made them choose between their property and their families and then arranged, tribe by tribe, for the captives to be released, so they got their families back but not their property.

supporting_quotes.quote: why is it that I can hear the babies crying and the goats bleating and the mules braying why have you brought the entire civilization of faqif, men, women children, property, the flocks why have you brought them
It is estimated that at least 6,000 prisoners of war were taken, women and children. 6,000. That is a massive amount.

questions.question: Why did the people of Ta'if take up arms after Mecca fell, and how did the campaign against their city finish?
questions.reference_answer: Thaqif understood that with Mecca in Muslim hands paganism had no future, and they also saw an opening to replace the defeated Quraysh as custodians of the Kaaba, so they sent emissaries to every pagan tribe and gathered around twenty thousand men. After their defeat at Hunayn they fell back inside Ta'if, which had thick walls, burning-oil devices on the ramparts and about a year's stored supplies. The Muslims used catapults, battering rams and a shield the corpus calls a turtle, all learned in advance from the tribe of Jurash, but the siege failed; they burned crops as pressure and then stopped when the townspeople begged. After roughly under two weeks the Prophet withdrew, and when the companions asked him to curse Thaqif he prayed instead that Allah guide them and bring them in.

supporting_quotes.quote: the tribe of Thaqif understood that the conquest of Mecca meant what? The end of idolatry, the end of paganism.
And he said, اللهم اهد ثقيف اللهم اأتي بثقيف Oh Allah, guide the people of Taqif. Oh Allah, bring the people of Taqif to us. And he made dua for them rather than against them.

questions.question: Did any non-Muslims march out with the Muslim army against Hawazin, and what was the arrangement over Safwan ibn Umayyah's armour?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. A number of prominent Meccans who had not yet accepted Islam walked with the army, Safwan ibn Umayyah among them, which the corpus notes raises the theological question of non-Muslims in a Muslim force. The Prophet asked Safwan for a hundred coats of armour, and Safwan asked whether it was being seized or borrowed; the Prophet answered that it was a guaranteed loan he would make good, from which the jurists derive that a borrower is liable for what he borrows. Weapons and money were also borrowed from Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith and Hakim ibn Hizam, and everything was repaid. Safwan finally became Muslim afterwards at Ji'ranah, when the Prophet gave him a whole valley of the captured animals and he said such a gift could only come from the heart of a prophet.

supporting_quotes.quote: So the Prophet ﷺ said, لَأْبَلْ عَارِيَةٌ مَأْمُونًا Or عَارِيَةٌ مُؤَدَّى I'm asking you for a loan that I guarantee I will pay back.
And he says, Yes, of course, who wouldn't be? And so the Prophet ﷺ said, All of this is yours, go take it.

And Safwan said that, Wallahi, the Prophet ﷺ gave to me when he gave, and he was the most despised person on earth to me. But he continued to give, and give, and give, and give, until he became the most beloved person to me.

questions.question: Who paid for the northern campaign in the ninth year, and who gave the most towards it?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet stood on the minbar appealing for funds and promised Paradise to whoever financed the army of hardship, because the wealth taken at Hunayn and Ta'if six months earlier had already all been spent. Uthman ibn Affan gave the largest share: he had pledged three hundred camels with their loads, and when his caravan came back from Syria he sold the whole thing on the spot for around a thousand gold coins and poured them out in front of the Prophet, who turned the coins over in his hands and said nothing Uthman did after that day would harm him. Umar brought half of everything he owned, hoping at last to beat Abu Bakr, but Abu Bakr brought everything and said he had left his family Allah and His Messenger. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf also gave two hundred measures of grain.

supporting_quotes.quote: Whoever finances the Jais al-Usra, he shall be given Jannah. If you help in financing Jais al-Usra, you will be given Jannah.
So he had financed an entire caravan to Syria. And when the battle of Tabuk, the call began for finances, that was the time when his caravan returned from Syria

questions.question: The companions remembered the march to Tabuk as the hardest thing they ever did even though no fighting happened. What made it so hard, and why was the destination announced beforehand instead of being concealed as usual?
questions.reference_answer: It was the largest force ever assembled, so food and water ran out; it set off in the blazing heat of late July; it was the furthest distance the Prophet ever led an army; and it fell right on the harvest, which for an agrarian Medina was effectively the whole year's income. Men slaughtered camels to squeeze water from their stomachs, and two or more people shared a single date a day, until the Prophet made du'a and rain fell. Ka'b ibn Malik's own account explains the break with normal practice: because of the severe heat, the long journey, the desert and the great number of the enemy, the Prophet told people plainly where he was going so that they could prepare themselves and provide for those left behind.

questions.question: Some men in Medina genuinely could not afford to go north with the army and others simply invented reasons. Were the two groups treated differently?
questions.reference_answer: Sharply differently. A group known as the weepers had neither money nor a camel, and when the Prophet told them he had nothing to mount them on they turned away with their eyes streaming with grief, and the Qur'an records their excuse as valid, with the reward of the intention. The hypocrites, by contrast, were delighted to stay, told each other not to march out in the heat, mocked those who gave charity, and produced flimsy excuses such as al-Jadd ibn Qays claiming he could not resist the Roman women. When the army returned, more than eighty men lined up with excuses, which the Prophet accepted, leaving their inner state to Allah, and Allah then gently chastised him for accepting them. Only Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah and Hilal confessed that they had no excuse at all, and it was those three, not the hypocrites, who were punished with a boycott.

questions.question: If no army ever turned up to fight at Tabuk, what did the Prophet and his men actually do during the weeks they camped there?
questions.reference_answer: They stayed roughly twenty days, praying shortened prayers throughout. On arrival the spring had almost dried up; the Prophet rebuked two men who had touched the water first, then rinsed his hands and face into it and it gushed enough for the whole army, and he foretold that Tabuk would one day become green and populated. He reorganised the army into battalions and appointed commanders, gave sermons, and told the men of five things granted to him that no prophet before him had. Politically he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to Dumat al-Jandal, where the Christian Arab king Ukaydir of Kindah was captured and agreed to pay jizya and break with Rome, and similar treaties with other northern tribes followed. Heraclius also sent a second letter with a messenger from the tribe of Tanukh, who was told to check three signs and returned with all three answered. Abdullah Dhul Bijadayn died there and the Prophet personally handled his burial at night.

questions.question: What happened on the journey home from Tabuk, and is the famous song about the rising moon really connected with the arrival in Medina at the Hijrah?
questions.reference_answer: On the way back the army passed al-Hijr, the rock-cut dwellings of Thamud; the Prophet called everyone together, forbade them to enter the homes of a punished people except in tears, covered his face and hurried through the valley, and ordered that water and dough taken from those wells be given to the animals rather than eaten. Rain came after his du'a and some hypocrites credited a star instead of Allah; his camel went missing and a hypocrite mocked him for it before Allah told him where it was; another group joked about his prediction that Rome and Persia would be conquered and were exposed by revelation before they could excuse themselves; and about fourteen masked men tried and failed to push him off a cliff at night. The corpus argues that the poem about the moon rising over Thaniyat al-Wada' belongs to this homecoming, not to the Hijrah, because Thaniyat al-Wada' lies north of Medina while the Hijrah came from the south, and because at the Hijrah most of the city was not yet Muslim.

questions.question: Why did the Prophet march a thousand miles north in the worst heat of the year when there turned out to be no enemy waiting?
questions.reference_answer: The corpus reviews and rejects the usual explanations. The report that Jews goaded him into going to Syria is dismissed because no Jews remained near Medina and because Surah al-Isra is Meccan. The claim of forty thousand Roman troops is called implausible, since Rome had no interest in the Arabs, and a Ghassanid threat would hardly be timed for July. The conclusion offered is that it was a direct command from Allah to test the believers, which is why participation was obligatory, why the destination was announced openly, and why the commands to march out in Surah at-Tawbah are so blunt. Its wisdom is seen in what came next: it was the last expedition of the Prophet's life, it opened up northern Arabia, and it pointed the Muslims towards Sham, which is why he prepared Usama's army on his deathbed and why the first conquests went that way.

questions.question: What sort of things were the hypocrites saying around the Tabuk campaign, and how did they get found out?
questions.reference_answer: In Medina they refused to contribute a penny and jeered at those who did: when a poor Ansari worked all night drawing water and brought a handful of dates, one of them asked whether Allah needed that quantity of dates, and Allah answered them in Surah at-Tawbah. They produced absurd excuses to avoid marching and quietly built a rival mosque near Quba as their own base, which the Prophet was later commanded to have destroyed. On the campaign itself one of them sneered that a man who claims revelation from the heavens does not know where his own camel is, and the Prophet announced the camel's location by Allah's word. Another group laughed at the prediction that Rome and Persia would fall and insulted the reciters of the Qur'an; a companion galloped forward to report it, but revelation exposing them was already being recited before he arrived, telling them to offer no excuses because they had disbelieved after believing.

questions.question: The siege of Ta'if never succeeded, so how did that city eventually come over to Islam?
questions.reference_answer: It came over by negotiation rather than conquest, exactly as the Prophet had prayed when he refused to curse Thaqif and asked instead that they be guided and brought in. Their leading nobleman Urwa ibn Mas'ud accepted Islam on the road back to Medina after the siege, insisted on returning to preach to his own people despite being warned they might kill him, and was shot dead with an arrow while giving the adhan for Fajr from his roof; the Prophet compared him to the man of Surah Yasin. Terrified of the consequences, the leaders of Ta'if then sent a delegation of six or seven senior men to Medina in Ramadan of the ninth year. They negotiated for days, trying to keep interest, fornication and wine and asking for years of delay before their idol was destroyed, and were refused; they finally accepted, fasted Ramadan with the Muslims, and the young Uthman ibn Abi al-As was made their leader. Al-Mughira and Abu Sufyan were then sent to demolish al-Lat.

questions.question: Not every tribe that sent representatives to Medina came in good faith. Which of them came meaning harm, and how did that turn out?
questions.reference_answer: Two stand out. Amir ibn Tufayl of Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, one of the men behind the massacre at Bi'r Ma'una, came with a henchman named Arbad ibn Qays and a plan to kill the Prophet while he distracted him with questions; Arbad never acted on the signal because he could not see him. Amir then demanded either a share of rule, or the succession after the Prophet, or war with a thousand camels, was refused, and the Prophet prayed that Allah suffice him against Amir and guide his people. Amir died shortly after and Arbad was struck dead by lightning. Musaylimah of Banu Hanifa came openly declaring that he would only follow if he were given authority after the Prophet's death and a share in prophethood; the Prophet, holding a stick, told him he would not give him even that stick, and identified him with the two gold bracelets he had seen in a dream, meaning false claimants after him. Musaylimah went on to parody the Qur'an and was killed in the Ridda wars.

questions.question: How did Islam reach Yemen, and why is Yemen spoken of so warmly?
questions.reference_answer: It began with Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi, chief of the Yemeni tribe of Daws, who came to Mecca during the persecution with cotton stuffed in his ears to avoid hearing the Prophet, heard him anyway, accepted Islam, and was told to be gentle with his people while the Prophet prayed three times that Allah guide Daws. He converted about eighty families and later emigrated to Medina with them, bringing Abu Hurayrah among them. Later a Himyarite king accepted Islam and Mu'adh ibn Jabal was sent as deputy and judge, with Abu Musa sent to another province, and Mu'adh was told to call them first to tawhid, then prayer, then zakah, and to make things easy rather than difficult and give glad tidings rather than drive people away. Yemen took to Islam far more readily than central or northern Arabia, and the corpus links this to hadiths praising the softness of Yemeni hearts, faith and wisdom being Yemeni, and the Yemenis having first access at the Prophet's fountain.

questions.question: Which earlier prophets did Muhammad meet as he was taken up through the heavens, and what did they say to him?
questions.reference_answer: At each of the seven gates Jibril asked permission and the gatekeeper checked who was with him. In the first heaven was Adam, who welcomed him as a righteous son and a righteous prophet; in the second Yahya and Isa; in the third Yusuf, of whom he said it was as if he had been given half of all beauty; in the fourth Idris; in the fifth Harun; in the sixth Musa, who wept because a younger man sent after him would have more of his followers enter Paradise; and in the seventh Ibrahim, leaning against al-Bayt al-Ma'mur, who greeted him with the same words Adam had used. All except Adam and Ibrahim greeted him as a righteous brother. Ibrahim also asked him to convey his greeting of peace to this ummah and to tell them that the soil of Paradise is fertile but bare, and that its seedlings are the words of glorification and praise.

supporting_quotes.quote: And Jibreel says, this is your father Adam, so say salam to him. So the Prophet ﷺ said salam and Adam responded and said, marhaban bil ibn al-salih wa nabiyy al-salih.
And he told me, Ya Muhammad, O Muhammad ﷺ, أَقْرِئْ أُمَّتَكَ مِنِّ السَّلَامِ give my salams to your ummah. So Ibrahim is telling his salams to us.

questions.question: How did the daily prayers end up being five, and why is that number treated as a mark of honour for this community?
questions.reference_answer: In the audience beyond Sidrat al-Muntaha, where he could hear the pen writing the decree, fifty prayers a day were prescribed. Coming back down he passed Musa, who told him to go back and ask for a reduction because he had experience of the Children of Israel and knew this community could not manage it; the Prophet first glanced at Jibril for a second opinion and Jibril nodded. He went back and forth several times, the reports differing over whether it dropped by five or by ten each time, until at five he said he was too embarrassed to ask again and was content. A voice then announced that the obligation had been fixed and lightened, that it is five in deed but rewarded as fifty. The corpus treats this as showing the superiority of this ummah over the ummah of Musa, since Musa said his people could not manage five and this community by and large does pray five times a day.

supporting_quotes.quote: أَمْضَيْتُ فَرِيضَتِي وَخَفَّفْتُ عَنْ عِبَادِي My faridah has been established, and I have made things easier for my servants. It is five, but it shall be rewarded with fifty.

questions.question: When Muhammad told the Meccans he had gone to Jerusalem and back in a single night, how did they react, and what convinced anyone?
questions.reference_answer: He woke anxious about how to tell people, and Abu Jahl found him sitting in that state, asked sarcastically what had happened, and then gathered the Quraysh so he would repeat it publicly. Some clapped in disbelief, some put their hands on their heads and some laughed. One man who had been to Jerusalem demanded a description; the Prophet said he became confused and terrified until Bayt al-Maqdis was raised up in view for him and he answered every question. He also described three Quraysh caravans he had passed, and one of them entered Mecca just as he had said, at which Abu Jahl called it plain sorcery. Abu Bakr, told of the claim by a Meccan, said that if he said it then it is true, and that he believed him in something far more astonishing than that, namely revelation coming to him from above the heavens, and it is from this that he was called al-Siddiq. The corpus also argues that the Quraysh's outrage and Abu Bakr's testimony only make sense if the journey was physical rather than a dream, and rejects the unsourced report in Ibn Hisham that some Muslims apostatised over the story.

questions.question: The man who killed Hamza eventually became a Muslim. Did he ever do anything to make up for it?
questions.reference_answer: Wahshi, the Abyssinian slave who speared Hamza at Uhud to earn his freedom, fled to Ta'if the moment Makkah fell because he knew he was on the list of those not to be spared. He only came to the Prophet about a year later, with the delegation of Ta'if; the Prophet forgave him but told him to keep out of his sight, which Wahshi had to do for the rest of the Prophet's life. He was also punished repeatedly by Umar for drinking. His attempt at making amends came in the wars of apostasy, when he killed Musaylimah the liar, deliberately using the same javelin, saying he wanted to atone for what he had done.

questions.question: Abu Jahl's son was at his father's side when he was cut down at Badr. How did he himself eventually die?
questions.reference_answer: Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl was guarding his father at Badr and, while trying to defend him, severed the arm of Mu'adh, one of the young men attacking Abu Jahl. He remained a leading enemy through Uhud, and when Makkah was conquered he was on the short list of people not to be pardoned; he fled to Jeddah and took a ship for Abyssinia, vowed during a storm at sea that he would submit if he were saved, came back and accepted Islam. He died fighting the Romans. In the aftermath of Yarmuk he was one of three dying men who each sent a cup of water on to the next because he thought the other needed it more, and all three died before any of them drank.

questions.question: Safwan ibn Umayya once bankrolled a plot to have the Prophet murdered. What was his position by the time of the conquest of Makkah and Hunayn?
questions.reference_answer: After Badr, in which his father and brother were killed, Safwan offered to clear the debts of his cousin Umayr ibn Wahb and provide for his family if Umayr would go to Madinah and kill the Prophet; Umayr went, was told of the secret conversation by the Prophet himself, and became Muslim instead. When Makkah fell, Safwan tried to fight, then fled towards the sea saying he would throw himself into it; Umayr obtained a guarantee of safety for him and brought him back. He was still not a Muslim, having asked for and been given a couple of months' grace, when the Prophet borrowed his stock of armour and weapons for Hunayn. He converted only after Hunayn and Ta'if.

questions.question: The Prophet's eldest daughter stayed behind in Makkah with a husband who was still a pagan. How did the two of them end up back together?
questions.reference_answer: Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi fought at Badr and was taken prisoner; the Prophet released him on the condition that he send Zaynab to Madinah, and he kept his word. Two or three years later Zayd ibn Haritha's expedition captured a caravan he was travelling with, and at the dawn prayer Zaynab called out from the women's side that she had granted him protection; the Prophet honoured her guarantee and the Ansar returned his goods. He refused to accept Islam in Madinah so no one could say he had done it for the money, went back to Makkah, returned every deposit to its owner, and only then declared his faith publicly. The Prophet returned Zaynab to him without a new marriage contract, and she died that same year.

questions.question: Was the king of Abyssinia already a Muslim when he gave the emigrants refuge, or did that come later?
questions.reference_answer: According to the corpus he was not. When Ja'far spoke to him and recited the opening of Surah Maryam the Negus wept, said the recitation and the messages of Moses and Jesus came from the same source, and refused to hand the Muslims back to Amr ibn al-As, but he did not embrace the faith then. The argument given is that the Prophet would not have written him an invitation letter years later, after Hudaybiyyah, if he had already been Muslim; he was sympathetic and open, and it was the letter that brought him to Islam. He died in the ninth year, and the Prophet announced his death the same morning and led the only funeral prayer in absentia recorded in the Seerah.

questions.notes: Lecture 71 explicitly argues against the popular view that the Negus converted at Ja'far's audience, which is what lecture 17 describes.

questions.question: Amr ibn al-As once went to Abyssinia to get the Muslim refugees handed back. What took him there a second time?
questions.reference_answer: The Quraysh had sent Amr as one of two envoys with gifts to persuade the Negus to extradite the emigrants, and he was sent away empty-handed. Years later, after Khandaq convinced him that Makkah would fall, he decided to emigrate to Abyssinia and live under the Negus rather than under the Prophet. While he was there he asked the Negus for permission to kill the Prophet's messenger, and the king reacted with fury, told him this man was upon the truth and would prevail, and urged him to follow him. Amr gave his pledge of Islam to the Negus on the spot, then returned towards Makkah, where he met Khalid ibn al-Walid and Uthman ibn Talha on the road, also on their way to the Prophet.

questions.question: What did the Prophet do about the woman who had mutilated Hamza's body, once she came to give her pledge of allegiance?
questions.reference_answer: Hind bint Utbah had cut open Hamza's body at Uhud, taken out his liver and bitten into it, and made a necklace from his fingers, purely to hurt the Prophet. When Makkah was conquered she came veiled among the women taking the pledge and gave a sharp comment to nearly every condition, until a remark about taking Abu Sufyan's money gave her away and the Prophet asked whether she was Hind. She asked him to forgive the past. He neither punished her nor told her she was forgiven; he simply passed over it and moved on to the next condition, which the lecture contrasts with the way he told Wahshi to keep out of his sight.

questions.question: Who was the woman who looked after the Prophet when he was a small child, and what became of her later in life?
questions.reference_answer: Umm Ayman was the servant Abdul Muttalib gave to Abdullah and Aminah when they married. She travelled with Aminah and the six-year-old boy to Yathrib and arranged Aminah's burial at Abwa when she died on the way home. The Prophet inherited her, and she became a foster mother figure to him. She later married Zayd ibn Haritha while both were slaves, and their son Usamah was born in the Prophet's own house. She accepted Islam, outlived the Prophet, and lived on into Abu Bakr's caliphate as almost the last person alive who had known both Abdullah and Aminah.

questions.question: Ka'b ibn Malik is remembered for the weeks he spent shunned by everyone after Tabuk. What had he done at Uhud years before that?
questions.reference_answer: At Uhud, when the rumour spread that the Prophet had been killed, Ka'b ibn Malik was the first of the survivors on the battlefield to recognise him, identifying him by his eyes because he was wearing a helmet, and he shouted out that the Prophet was alive. He then swapped armour with him so that the enemy would not identify the Prophet, which left Ka'b himself as the target, and he was wounded many times over. Years later he was one of the three who honestly admitted they had no excuse for staying behind from Tabuk, and the Prophet ordered that they be boycotted for fifty days.

questions.question: One of the Prophet's wives said her father recognised him as the awaited prophet the very day he arrived in Madinah. Who was her father, and what happened to him in the end?
questions.reference_answer: Safiyyah bint Huyayy remembered being a little girl when her father Huyayy ibn Akhtab, chief of Banu Nadir, and her uncle came home crushed after going to see the newly arrived Prophet; her uncle asked whether this was the one and her father swore by the Lord of Moses that he was, then said they would oppose him for as long as he lived. Huyayy was exiled with Banu Nadir, later talked Banu Qurayzah into breaking their pact during the Trench, and shut himself inside their fortress with them. When they surrendered he was led out in his best clothes and told the Prophet he had never regretted his enmity, and he was executed with the men of Banu Qurayzah. Safiyyah was widowed and orphaned at Khaybar and became the Prophet's wife.

questions.question: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib was away from the Prophet for well over a decade. Where had he been, and how long did he live after he came back?
questions.reference_answer: Ja'far led the emigrants in Abyssinia and was their spokesman before the Negus, answering Amr ibn al-As and reciting the opening of Surah Maryam. He stayed there for around thirteen years and only returned in the seventh year, arriving on the very day Khaybar was conquered, where the Prophet embraced him and said he did not know which of the two made him happier. He was killed a short time afterwards at Mu'tah, where he was named second in command after Zayd; he fought until both his hands were severed and his body was found with about ninety wounds, and the Prophet said he had seen him in Paradise with two wings in place of his hands.

questions.question: Zayd ibn Haritha's father found him in Makkah and offered to buy him back. What did Zayd decide, and how did his life end?
questions.reference_answer: Zayd had been kidnapped as a boy, sold at the fair of Ukaz and ended up as Khadijah's servant, then as the Prophet's. When his father and uncle came with a ransom the Prophet left the choice to Zayd, who said he could never choose anyone over him and that this man was more to him than a father and an uncle combined. The Prophet then freed him publicly and adopted him, and he was known as Zayd ibn Muhammad until the verse of Surah al-Ahzab told people to call children by their fathers. He was killed roughly thirty years later at Mu'tah, where the Prophet had appointed him first of three commanders; he took the flag, charged, and was surrounded and killed. Aishah said that had he been alive when the Prophet died, no one would have been chosen over him.

So Zayd took the flag and he charged in from the front. And he was in the charge of the middle of the flank. And he was attacked from every side until he was surrounded by the enemy.

questions.question: The leader of the hypocrites in Madinah had a son who was a sincere believer. How did that son deal with his father?
questions.reference_answer: Abdullah, the son of Abdullah ibn Ubayy, offered to kill his father himself after the insult on the way back from Banu al-Mustaliq, and the Prophet forbade him, telling him instead to be a good companion to his father. He then stood at the entrance to Madinah and refused to let his father in until the Prophet gave him permission. Years later, when Ibn Ubayy died, his son asked the Prophet for his shirt to use as a burial shroud, and asked him to lead the funeral prayer, which he did over Umar's protests until the verse of Surah at-Tawbah forbidding prayer over the hypocrites was revealed.

supporting_quotes.quote: his own son became basically the preventer how dare you say this and then you're gonna come back to the city I'm not gonna let you do this until the Prophet ﷺ himself gives you permission
after he died, his son Abdullah ibn Abdullah his son Abdullah ibn Abdullah ibn Ubay asked the Prophet ﷺ for his shirt

questions.question: The Quraysh chief who stonewalled the Prophet over the treaty at Hudaybiyyah had been a Muslim prisoner years earlier. Where was he held, and what happened to him when Makkah fell?
questions.reference_answer: Suhayl ibn Amr was the most senior surviving Quraysh leader captured at Badr, and the chiefs were lodged with their captors, Suhayl in the Prophet's own house; that is where Sawdah walked in and reproached him for surrendering rather than dying honourably, an outburst she immediately regretted. He was later the Quraysh negotiator at Hudaybiyyah. When Makkah was conquered he was terrified even though his name was not on the death list, and locked himself in his house, sending his son Abdullah to beg for protection while listing his own record at Badr, Uhud, Khandaq and Hudaybiyyah. The Prophet granted it and told the companions to receive him respectfully and not to stare at him. Suhayl did not accept Islam immediately; he converted in the month after Hunayn and Ta'if.

supporting_quotes.quote: So the senior most members of the Quraysh, they are housed in the house of the Prophet ﷺ. Foremost amongst them, Suhail ibn Amr.
So when the Sahaba conquer Mecca, Suhail becomes terrified. He locks himself in his house. He's terrified. He doesn't flee, he locks himself in his house.

questions.question: Khalid ibn al-Walid was still commanding Quraysh cavalry against the Muslims on the road to Hudaybiyyah. What finally brought him over, and what did the Prophet call him afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: The Quraysh posted Khalid with a force at Ghumaym to block the road to Makkah, and the Prophet avoided him by taking a difficult side route to Hudaybiyyah. Khalid later concluded the matter was settled and this man was a prophet; when he told Ikrimah he wanted to accept Islam, Ikrimah panicked and roused the Quraysh chiefs, and swords were drawn, so Khalid slipped out of Makkah that night with Uthman ibn Talha and met Amr ibn al-As on the road, all three heading for the Prophet. At Mu'tah, describing the battle as it happened, the Prophet said the banner was finally taken up by a sword from the swords of Allah and that Allah granted victory through him, and the title stuck so firmly that Byzantine chroniclers recorded him as the one they call the sword of God.

supporting_quotes.quote: they have sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to camp at Ghumaim. And Ghumaim is on the road right outside of Mecca when you're coming in from Medina.

Khalid and Uthman ibn Talha, they decide to leave Mecca without telling anybody. And both of them basically start walking. And within the next day or so, they bump into Amr ibn al-Aas who's on his way back from Habasha.
Until a sword from the sword of Allah took it and Allah gave them victory.

questions.question: The bedouin who chased the Prophet and Abu Bakr for the bounty during the migration turned up again at the Farewell Pilgrimage. What did he want to know there?
questions.reference_answer: Suraqah ibn Malik had ridden after the two of them hoping for the hundred camels the Quraysh had offered, and after his horse repeatedly sank into the ground he asked instead for a written guarantee of safety, which he produced years later at Hunayn when he accepted Islam. At the Farewell Pilgrimage, after the Prophet told those who had not brought sacrificial animals to complete only an umrah and leave the state of ihram, Suraqah stood up and asked whether this ruling applied just to that year or to every year. The Prophet interlaced his fingers and answered that hajj and umrah had been joined together until the Day of Judgement.

supporting_quotes.quote: Suraqa ibn Malik says that, I ask permission from the Prophet ﷺ to give me protection in writing.
Suraqa ibn Malik stood up and he said, Ya Rasulullah, is this rule only for this year or is it for every year?

questions.question: Umm Salamah was pulled away from her husband and her little boy when she tried to leave Makkah. How did that end, and how did she come to be married to the Prophet?
questions.reference_answer: When Abu Salamah set out for Madinah, her own clan stopped her from going and his clan seized the child, dislocating the boy's arm in the struggle. She was separated from both of them for more than a year, going out every day to Al-Abtah to weep, until her relatives relented and returned her son. She set off alone and was escorted the whole way to Madinah by Uthman ibn Talhah, still a pagan, who walked while she rode. Abu Salamah was badly wounded at Uhud, never fully recovered, and died of those wounds some months later, having asked her to remarry and prayed that Allah give her a husband better than himself. After she turned down Abu Bakr, the Prophet proposed to her directly, answering her worries about her age, her jealousy and her children.

supporting_quotes.quote: she said for more than 16 months, every day, year and a half. I would go to Al-Bathha, which is the farthest place outside of Mecca that is still within view of the city.
And in the battle of Uhud, Abu Salama was wounded very severely. He also was carried back. He recovered from Uhud, but never fully.

questions.notes: The transcript spells the place Al-Bathha; it is Al-Abtah.

questions.question: When Abu Sufyan came to Madinah trying to shore up the treaty, he called on his own daughter first. Why was she living there, and how did she treat him?
questions.reference_answer: Ramlah, known as Umm Habibah, had emigrated to Abyssinia during the Makkan years. Her husband Ubaydullah ibn Jahsh abandoned Islam for Christianity and died there, leaving her a widow with nobody to look after her, so the Prophet sent a marriage proposal through the Negus, who acted as her guardian, paid the dowry himself and held the wedding feast in his palace; she came to Madinah with the returning emigrants around the time of Khaybar. She had not seen her father in well over a decade. When he came to her house and went to sit down she snatched the bedding away, and when he asked whether she was protecting him from the mattress or the mattress from him, she told him it was the Prophet's bedding and he was an idolater who would not sit on it.

supporting_quotes.quote: So our Prophet ﷺ sent a proposal to her new wali, and her new wali was none other than Najashi himself, the emperor himself.
And so, Umm Habiba says, no, this is the blanket of the Prophet ﷺ. This is the bed, the sareer of the Prophet

questions.notes: Lecture 18 also mentions the marriage arranged through the Negus.

questions.question: Thumamah ibn Uthal became Muslim after being tied to a pillar in the mosque for three days. What became of his tribe after that?
questions.reference_answer: Thumamah was the chief of Banu Hanifah, captured by accident on his way to umrah; after three days of being treated generously he accepted Islam, was the first to enter Makkah calling the pilgrimage formula free of idolatry, and when the Quraysh threatened him he swore that not a grain of wheat would reach them from Banu Hanifah until the Prophet ordered otherwise, which forced the Quraysh to write and beg the Prophet to lift the embargo. His tribe as a whole never followed him. Banu Hanifah was the tribe of Musaylimah, who demanded a share of prophethood as his price for submitting, and it became the largest and worst of the apostate tribes in Abu Bakr's caliphate.

supporting_quotes.quote: wallahi not a single seed of grain will come to you from the Banu Hanifa and from up north until the Prophet ﷺ explicitly commands me to do so.
And by the way, the Banu Hanifa were the largest and the worst of the Murtad tribes in the time of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq.

questions.question: Abu Sufyan later said that faith first stirred in him while he was abroad, years before he actually submitted. What happened there, and where did he finally accept Islam?
questions.reference_answer: While trading in Syria he was summoned to Jerusalem and questioned by Heraclius, who seated his companions behind him so they could contradict him if he lied, which is why he answered honestly. After the letter was read out there was uproar in the court and Abu Sufyan left saying that the affair of this man had grown so great that even the emperor of the Romans feared him, and he said that was the first time the realisation that Islam would prevail entered his heart. He remained an opponent for years more. He only pronounced the testimony of faith on the night before the conquest of Makkah, brought into the camp by al-Abbas on the Prophet's own mule and told bluntly that it was that or execution. To satisfy his pride the Prophet declared that anyone who entered Abu Sufyan's house would be safe.

supporting_quotes.quote: Then Abu Sufyan says, that was when for the first time in my heart I realized that this matter Islam would eventually prevail and this was the first time Islam entered my heart after 20 years of opposing
And so with reluctance, Abu Sufyan said the shahada.

questions.question: The Muslims who fled Makkah for Abyssinia were gone a very long time. Where and when did they finally rejoin the Prophet?
questions.reference_answer: The Prophet told the persecuted Muslims in Makkah to cross over to Abyssinia because a just Christian king ruled there who would not interfere with their worship. The group under Ja'far ibn Abi Talib stayed away for more than a decade and only came back in the 7th year after the Hijrah, arriving with roughly fifty men and women on the very day Khaybar fell. The Prophet stood up to greet Ja'far, kissed him on the forehead, and said he did not know which of the two made him happier that day, the conquest of Khaybar or Ja'far's return. The returnees also debated with Umar over who had the greater claim, since they had made two migrations and he had made one.

questions.question: Amr ibn al-As worked hard against the Muslims before he became one. What was the biggest thing he tried to do to them, and what did the Prophet later put him in charge of?
questions.reference_answer: While still a pagan, Amr ibn al-As was the Quraysh's chosen diplomat and was sent with a second envoy to Abyssinia to persuade the Negus to hand the Muslim refugees back; the Negus refused outright and told them to leave. Amr accepted Islam only in the last batch of converts before Makkah was taken, together with Khalid ibn al-Walid and Uthman ibn Talha. Within a few months of converting the Prophet summoned him, looked him over, and appointed him commander of the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil, telling him he expected much booty for him; Amr replied that he had not become a Muslim for wealth.

questions.question: The Christian king who gave the Muslim refugees asylum refused to extradite them. Did he ever become a Muslim himself, and what did the Prophet do when he died?
questions.reference_answer: The Negus refused the Quraysh delegation outright, telling them to go away because he would not hand the refugees over and would not even consider it. He later accepted Islam; the Prophet corresponded with him by letter, and a delegation he tried to send to Madinah was lost when the boats sank. When he died in the ninth year after the Hijrah, the Prophet announced the death to the companions on the very morning it happened, said their brother had died in Abyssinia, and led a funeral prayer for him with no body present. The corpus presents this as the one and only time the absentee funeral prayer was performed.

supporting_quotes.quote: go away from me because I'm not going to hand these people over to you and I'm not even going to think about it
