questions.question: When the Banu Nadir were made to leave Madinah they were allowed to carry off what they could. Where did they settle, and did they leave the Muslims alone after that?
questions.reference_answer: Most of the Banu Nadir went north and settled in Khaybar, which the corpus flags in advance as the site of a second catastrophe for them. They did not stay quiet: wanting their lands back, their chieftains sent a full delegation of noblemen to Makkah to build the coalition that became the Battle of the Trench. Their chief Huyayy ibn Akhtab then went into the Banu Qurayza's stronghold and pushed them to break with the Muslims, and when Qurayza surrendered he was led out in his finest red silk garment and executed along with their men.

supporting_quotes.quote: Where did they go? Majority of them went to Khaybar. What's gonna happen at Khaybar? Another catastrophe for them.

questions.question: Did Bilal ever come face to face with the man who used to torture him, and what happened?
questions.reference_answer: Bilal's owner in Makkah was Umayya ibn Khalaf, who would personally drag him into the desert at midday and have a heavy rock placed on his chest; Amr ibn al-As, then still a pagan, said the rocks were hot enough to cook raw meat on. At Badr, Abdur Rahman ibn Awf had taken Umayya and his son as prisoners for ransom when Bilal saw them, shouted that the head of disbelief would not escape, and called a group of Ansar over. They surrounded Umayya and killed him despite Abdur Rahman's protests. His body ended up buried under a mound of pebbles, which the corpus treats as a fitting requital for the way he had tortured Bilal on the stones.

Amr ibn al-As, he himself narrates that when he was not a Muslim, Amr was not a Muslim. I passed by Bilal when he was being punished upon the rocks of the desert.

questions.question: A Makkan pagan once escorted the Prophet back into the city under armed guard. Did the Prophet ever repay that favour?
questions.reference_answer: After the rejection at Ta'if, the Prophet could not re-enter Makkah without a protector; two men gave excuses, and the third, Mut'im ibn Adi, armed his own sons and sent them out to bring him in and stood publicly in the sanctuary to announce the protection. Mut'im died a pagan a few months before Badr. Surveying the seventy-odd prisoners taken at Badr, whose ransoms were worth a fortune, the Prophet said that if Mut'im ibn Adi were alive and asked him for these men he would have released all of them to him for nothing.

questions.question: Why had Salman al-Farisi never fought in a battle before the trench was dug?
questions.reference_answer: Salman had left Persia, passed from one monk to another in Syria, and was finally told to look for the awaited prophet in a land of date palms. He joined an Arab caravan heading for Khaybar, but the traders kidnapped him and sold him to Jews living in Yathrib, where he toiled as a slave for years, even after the Prophet arrived. Because he was still owned and it took years to buy his freedom, the Trench was the first battle he was able to take part in, and it was there that he proposed digging the ditch.

supporting_quotes.quote: Salman is taken as a slave. And instead of ending up in Khyber, he is sold to a group of Yahud who happen to live in Yathrib.
And this was the first battle that he was able to participate in. It took a few years to free him.
Until finally, as we all know, Salman al-Farisi.

questions.question: The Quraysh once sent a nobleman from Ta'if to talk terms with the Prophet outside Makkah. What became of that man?
questions.reference_answer: Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi was the first envoy to volunteer from the Quraysh side during the Hudaybiyya negotiations, and he went back and reported how the companions revered the Prophet. Years later, after the siege of Ta'if and Hunayn, he caught up with the returning army and accepted Islam, then insisted on going home to preach despite the Prophet warning him that his people might kill him. He announced his Islam that night, was cursed, and at dawn was struck by an arrow while giving the call to prayer from his roof. He refused any blood money or revenge and asked to be buried with the martyrs of Hunayn, and the Prophet compared him to the believer of Surah Yasin.

questions.question: What happened to the man who killed Hamza, once the Muslims had the upper hand?
questions.reference_answer: Wahshi was the slave of Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who promised him his freedom if he killed Hamza, both as revenge for an uncle Hamza had killed at Badr and so the Prophet would lose an uncle too. When Makkah was taken Wahshi was on the short list of people not to be spared, so he fled to Ta'if and only converted when Thaqif finally submitted, coming to Madinah with their delegation. The Prophet made him recount the killing in full, wept until his beard was wet, and told him he was forgiven but should keep out of his sight.

questions.notes: Lecture 96 adds that Wahshi later killed Musaylima with the same javelin to atone.

questions.question: Who led the very first Friday prayer in Islam, and how did his life end?
questions.reference_answer: It was Mus'ab ibn Umayr, whom the Prophet picked out of some 250 converts and sent to Yathrib to teach the Qur'an and lead the prayers after the first pledge at Aqaba; the first Friday sermon was delivered by him in the house of As'ad ibn Zurara, with about forty people present, before the Prophet himself had ever led one. He was killed at Uhud while holding the banner: his right hand was cut off, he took the flag in his left, that was cut off too, and he held it with his stumps until he was stabbed to death.

supporting_quotes.quote: The Prophet ﷺ chose Mus'ab ibn Umayr to send back with them to go to Yathrib. He chose Mus'ab ibn Umayr to teach them the Qur'an and to lead them in salah.

So his right hand is cut off, and he then holds the flag with his left hand.

questions.question: When the Ansar first pledged themselves to the Prophet they asked what they would get out of it. Years later they felt cheated over a share-out of spoils — what did he say to them then?
questions.reference_answer: At the second pledge at Aqaba a voice from the crowd asked what they would get in return, and the Prophet answered with the single word Paradise, saying he could promise them no money or fame. After Hunayn the huge booty was used to win over Quraysh chiefs and the Ansar were the one group given nothing extra, and their younger men began complaining that they were called for war but forgotten when money was handed out. Sa'd ibn Ubada raised it with him, the Ansar were gathered alone in a tent, and after praising them the Prophet asked whether they were not content that others go home with sheep and camels while they go home with the Messenger of Allah; they wept and said they were content with Islam and with him.

questions.question: The Prophet turned down an offer to have Ta'if crushed between its two mountains because he hoped for its future generations. Did that hope come true?
questions.reference_answer: After Ta'if stoned him, the angel of the mountains offered to crush the city and he refused, saying he hoped Allah would bring out of their offspring people who would worship Him alone. Ta'if was besieged unsuccessfully after Hunayn and the Prophet withdrew, saying to leave them and they would come. Thaqif ended up the last pagan tribe in the region, and in Ramadan of the ninth year they sent a delegation of six or seven of their leaders to Madinah. They negotiated for days, tried to be excused from interest, adultery and wine, then asked for three years' grace for their idol al-Lat and were bargained down to nothing; the Prophet had it destroyed by their own kinsman al-Mughira along with Abu Sufyan, and refused to excuse them from prayer.

supporting_quotes.quote: Rather, I hope that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala will extract from their progeny, from their children, those who will eventually worship Him without associating partners with Him.

questions.question: Khalid ibn al-Walid was called the Sword of Allah. Which battle earned him that, and what had he done to the Muslims before he was on their side?
questions.reference_answer: As a pagan commander Khalid led the Quraysh cavalry at Uhud; while pulling back he kept watching the archers' hill, and the moment most of them abandoned it he took the opening and swept round behind the Muslims, inflicting the only genuine defeat they ever suffered. Years later at Mu'tah, after Zayd, Ja'far and Abdullah ibn Rawaha were killed, the Prophet described the fighting and said that a sword from the swords of Allah took the banner and Allah granted victory through him. The corpus notes that the title spread far enough that the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes recorded the escaping commander as the one they call God's sword.

supporting_quotes.quote: this is the fursa, this is the opportunity that Khalid ibn al-Walid saw

questions.question: After Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf was killed, another group of Ansar asked for a mission of their own. What was driving that, and who did they go after?
questions.reference_answer: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf was dealt with by men of the Aws, with Muhammad ibn Maslama volunteering partly because the Aws had old ties with Ka'b's tribe and the Khazraj did not. The Khazraj felt the Aws were now one up on them, so they volunteered for a target of their own and proposed Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, a wealthy Khaybar chief who had been a main financier of the Trench coalition. Five Khazraji men led by Abdullah ibn Atik took it on, a far riskier three-day journey than the hour Ka'b had been away, and the Prophet's only stipulation was that they kill no women or children.

They felt that the Aus had beaten them by taking care of Ka'b ibn Ashraf.

questions.question: The Prophet's uncle Abbas was captured at Badr and insisted he had been a Muslim all along. Was he believed, and when did he actually move to Madinah?
questions.reference_answer: Abbas was taken prisoner at Badr and told the Prophet he was already a Muslim who had been forced out to fight. The Prophet answered that only Allah knew his inner state but that he had to be judged by his actions, and refused to reduce his ransom by even a single coin when his Ansari captor offered to gift him back; he also had to pay for Aqil and Nawfal. He did not migrate until years afterwards: the Muslim army marching secretly on Makkah ran into him at the valley of Juhfa coming the other way with his wives and children, and the corpus says he was the last person ever to earn the status of a muhajir.

questions.question: Suhayl ibn Amr negotiated the truce for the Quraysh. Had he ever been in Muslim hands before that, and did he ever accept Islam?
questions.reference_answer: Suhayl ibn Amr was captured at Badr and was housed as a prisoner inside the Prophet's own home; Sawda walked in, saw the chief of the Quraysh sitting bound in the corner, and lost her composure at the sight. He was ransomed, went on to negotiate the treaty at Hudaybiyya, and was still resisting when Makkah fell, joining Ikrima and Safwan in the one chaotic skirmish against the entering army. He held out even after the conquest and is treated in the corpus as one of the last senior Quraysh leaders to convert, along with Safwan ibn Umayya.

questions.notes: Lecture 41 itself contains a forward reference to Suhayl negotiating Hudaybiyya, so that link is not exclusive to the later lectures; the conversion is only in 79-80.

questions.question: Zayd ibn Haritha was given the chance to go home with his own father and turned it down. What did he go on to become?
questions.reference_answer: When his family found him in Makkah and came to buy him back, the Prophet left the choice to Zayd, who answered at once that he could never choose anyone over him and that the Prophet was more to him than a father and an uncle combined. He became the only companion named in the Qur'an, and Aisha said he was never sent on an expedition except as its commander, never second to anyone. At Mu'tah the Prophet appointed him leader and, uniquely, named two successors after him, Ja'far and then Abdullah ibn Rawaha, and all three were killed.

He appointed Zayd ibn Harithah as its leader.

questions.question: Umm Salama had already been widowed once before she married the Prophet. Where did that happen, and what was her most famous piece of advice to him afterwards?
questions.reference_answer: Her first husband Abu Salama went with her to Abyssinia in the first migration and was the first companion to die there, leaving her cut off from her relatives in Makkah with no support, which is why the Prophet sent her a proposal. Her best-known intervention came at Hudaybiyya: after the treaty the Prophet ordered the companions three times to slaughter and shave, and nobody moved. He went back into his tent visibly upset and told her; she suggested he simply go out and do it himself without saying a word, and when they saw him they would follow. He did, and they did.

supporting_quotes.quote: Abu Salama would be the first Sahabi to die in Abyssinia, and Umm Salama would be left all alone without any support.

questions.notes: Lecture 4 also notes a different report about her first husband apostatising in Abyssinia; the corpus is not fully consistent on this point.

questions.question: Which clause of the truce with the Quraysh ended up giving the Muslims their reason to march on Makkah?
questions.reference_answer: One of the terms agreed at Hudaybiyya was that either side could make treaties with any other tribe, and the truce conditions would then extend to that tribe as well. Khuza'a allied with the Muslims and Banu Bakr with the Quraysh. Banu Bakr asked the Quraysh for permission to settle an old score with one night raid, and the Quraysh not only approved it but leaders such as Suhayl ibn Amr and Safwan ibn Umayya supplied them with weapons, on the assumption that a night attack would never be traced back. That made the Quraysh, not just Banu Bakr, guilty of breaking the treaty.

supporting_quotes.quote: Both Quraysh and the Muslims can engage with treaties with any tribe that wants to enter into alliances.
some amongst them such as Suhail ibn Amr and others and Safani ibn Umayyah actually gave them weapons
The Quraysh not only knew, not only approved, their elders actually gave weapons to the Banu Bakr.

questions.question: Why were the Banu Qaynuqa allowed to walk out of Madinah alive when the Banu Qurayza were not?
questions.reference_answer: When the Banu Qaynuqa surrendered after a siege, their two old Khazraji allies reacted differently: Ubada ibn as-Samit renounced the alliance, while Abdullah ibn Ubayy physically grabbed the Prophet's armour and would not let go until he was promised their lives, saying he feared misfortune if his business partners were harmed. The verdict was three days to pack and leave, with what remained going to the Muslims. The Banu Qurayza's case ended differently: the Prophet let their old allies the Aws choose an arbitrator and named their own leader Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, whose judgement was that the adult men be executed, and they were taken out in batches.

supporting_quotes.quote: And then the verdict came, you have three days, to pack your stuff and leave.
So he said, thaka Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. I have chosen for you Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, your leader.
all of the male adults were basically taken batches by batches and they were executed
